system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.
runtime: Anthropic API, effort medium, no seed or temperature, so runs do not repeat exactly

position.recommendation: Do not build a new consumer brand or direct-to-consumer business yet. recommendation.detail: 4 sources, 4 conditions that would change it

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product build yet. Run the proposed installer-channel pilot first, to test whether a branded retrofit kit can hold a premium over imported kits through installers. Treat the existing OEM and boat/caravan heater business as the base case. Establish whether Ebersparcher already sells retrofit heaters to individual owners through any channel before deciding, since public sources did not confirm this.

frame.objective: Decide whether Ebersparcher should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example, a consumer-facing heater, climate or mobility product sold to individual vehicle owners or aftermarket buyers) beyond its current OEM and specialist-dealer business, and identify what evidence would justify the investment. The question is what causes individual buyers to value and pay for such a product, and whether Ebersparcher can capture that value.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no company contact or non-public contractual or financial detail
Company's existing consumer reach is unknown and must be established from sources, not assumed
Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget of 8 searches (7 remaining); evidence must be read before it is cited
Any numbers cited as observed must come from a source read; proposed test parameters must be labelled as proposed
Simulated results are not evidence and will not be cited in the final recommendation
alternatives: No expansion: keep the business as OEM and specialist-dealer supplier of exhaust, heaters and thermal management, with no consumer proposition
Aftermarket retrofit: sell existing fuel-operated or electric heaters and parking climate products as accessories via independent workshops or online to individual owners, without redesign
Product redesign for a consumer use case: adapted heater or thermal product for camper vans, motorhomes, boats or off-grid living

Different route to buyers: partner with an existing consumer brand, leisure-vehicle dealer network or online retailer rather than building an own consumer channel, or license the technology to a consumer brand
Different customer group: target fleet or commercial operators (taxi, delivery, ambulance, utility) whose purchase is made by a business rather than an individual
Adjacent consumer product outside vehicles: portable or stationary heating/thermal units using the same core technology for households or outdoor use

T1.claim: Individual camper and leisure-vehicle owners already want the proven brand heater as an upgrade or retrofit, because they trust its safety and reliability. A consumer-grade version sold through leisure-vehicle dealers and installers would earn a premium that OEM-only supply does not capture.
T1.who_benefits: Motorhome and camper owners who retrofit heating, and Ebersparcher if it sells a branded consumer kit through installers and leisure dealers
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Owners value heat reliability, safety and certified installation more than price, and the established brand names give them confidence. When a trusted name is available through an installer they can trust, they pay for it instead of a low-cost import.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Ebersparcher sells branded kits or accessory heaters with installation support and warranty through leisure-vehicle installers or dealers, earning a margin above component price
assumptions: A meaningful number of individual owners want to retrofit or replace a heater, not just buy one with a new vehicle
Installers or dealers will carry a consumer product with the Ebersparcher brand
Owners will pay a premium over cheap imports for certified installation and warranty
Current demand is visible through the brand name, as the company's own booth account suggests
predictions: Sales of an installer-sold branded retrofit kit should hold a price premium over unbranded imports of similar output
Installer and dealer willingness to stock the kit should be measurable in a pilot with a small set of partners
Owners who buy the branded kit should cite safety, warranty or installation as the reason, not price
T1.first_claim: Individual camper and leisure-vehicle owners already want the proven brand heater as an upgrade or retrofit, because they trust its safety and reliability. A consumer-grade version sold through leisure-vehicle dealers and installers would earn a premium that OEM-only supply does not capture.

T2.claim: Individual owners of camper and leisure vehicles buy the cheapest heater that works, because the consumer aftermarket is driven by price and DIY installation. Low-cost imported kits set the price, so a premium branded consumer product cannot capture much value unless it competes on price.
T2.who_benefits: Budget-conscious DIY owners and low-cost importers, who capture the value through cheap kits sold online
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Owners who can install a heater themselves compare the total kit price, not the brand. A cheap kit with a reasonable output meets their need, so they have little reason to pay for a brand or installer network.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Low-cost importers sell complete kits online and capture the margin; Ebersparcher would only win if it matched price, which its cost structure as a Tier-1 supplier may not allow
assumptions: Most individual retrofit buyers are DIY and buy on price
Imported kits deliver adequate output and safety for the owners who buy them
Ebersparcher cannot profitably undercut imported kits at consumer price points
predictions: Online sales of unbranded kits should grow faster than installer-sold branded kits in the same market
Owners in price-comparison forums should cite cost as the main reason for choosing an import
A branded kit priced near import levels should show low margin or low uptake
T2.first_claim: Individual owners of camper and leisure vehicles buy the cheapest heater that works, because the consumer aftermarket is driven by price and DIY installation. Low-cost imported kits set the price, so a premium branded consumer product cannot capture much value unless it competes on price.

assessments.quote: People simply know the Airtronic and Hydronic, many have them installed in their own camper or car.
assessments.does_not_show: It is the company's own account from a trade fair booth, not market data. It does not show how many individual owners want a retrofit, whether they would pay a premium over cheaper imports, or whether installers would stock a consumer kit. It says brand awareness and installed base exist, not willingness to pay.

assessments.quote: FULL KIT = circa £114 off ebay. 5KW of heat. Bench tested first.
assessments.does_not_show: This is one 2019 forum post from the UK about a single kit, with no sales volumes, no market share, and no evidence of how many owners buy these kits instead of branded heaters. It shows that low-priced imitation kits existed and were offered as comparable, not that price drives most buyers.

assessments.quote: Caravan and motorhome owners are tempted to purchase these units because of the huge price difference between them and the name brand equivalents.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a 2024 Australian advice article, not survey data. It shows that price difference tempts owners, which cuts against my assumption that owners pay a premium for the brand. It does not show how many owners actually buy cheap units, and the same article says the cheap units are inferior, which is consistent with a quality-based premium that my theory needs. The evidence weighs against the premium assumption but does not refute the quality mechanism.

X1.name: Installer-channel retrofit pilot with price-parity and premium arms (proposed)
X1.method: Over 12 weeks, list a branded retrofit heater kit (existing product, no redesign) through 8 to 10 independent leisure-vehicle installers or dealers in one German-speaking market. Randomly assign partners to one of two price arms: a premium arm priced above comparable imported kits with warranty and certified installation included, and a parity arm priced near the imported kit. Track enquiries, quotes, and completed sales. Run a small online ad test in the same region with identical product pages to measure click-to-enquiry at each price point.
X1.sample: 8 to 10 installers or dealers (proposed) and about 3,000 targeted impressions per arm for the online test (proposed), all in one region
X1.measure: Share of installers willing to stock the kit at the offered margin; enquiry-to-sale conversion by price arm; share of buyers citing safety, warranty or installation as their reason, asked at point of sale

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium arm converts at a similar rate to parity arm, most buyers cite warranty or safety, and at least half of installers agree to stock the kit at the premium price
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium arm converts far below parity arm, buyers cite price, and fewer than a third of installers agree to stock at the premium price

X1.decision_rule: Keep T1 as the working theory only if at least half of approached installers agree to stock the premium kit AND premium-arm conversion is at least 70% of parity-arm conversion. Reject T1 if fewer than a third of installers stock the premium kit or premium conversion is below 50% of parity. Between these thresholds, treat as inconclusive and do not commit investment.

revisions.reason: SYN-D is a simulated result about a warehouse label printer. It measured nothing about wearers, buyers or heater demand, so it bears on neither T1 nor T2 and I am not citing it. The read sources still leave T1 uncertain: the company's booth account shows brand recognition and installed base, but the RV Daily article shows owners are tempted by price gaps, which cuts against the premium assumption. Nothing changes; the installer pilot remains the test.

Treating SYN-D as a what-if: a simulated warehouse label-printer test says nothing about wearers, buyers or heater demand, so even if it were real it would not move T1 or T2. It is not evidence and I do not cite it for any claim. T1 stays uncertain pending the installer pilot.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product build now. Run the proposed 12-week installer-channel pilot first, with a branded retrofit kit at premium and parity price arms, and decide only if it clears the decision rule. Keep the existing OEM, specialist-dealer and boat/caravan heater business as the base case. The public evidence shows an established brand with some owner awareness and an installed base in camper and car use, but it does not show that owners will pay a premium over cheap imports or that installers will stock a consumer kit.
final.target_customer: Owners of camper vans, motorhomes and small boats who want to retrofit or replace a heater, and the independent installers and leisure dealers who fit them
final.value_proposition: A recognised-brand heater kit with certified installation and warranty, offered through installers, as a safer alternative to low-priced imported kits. This is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.
final.next_action: Confirm first whether Ebersparcher already sells retrofit or accessory heaters to individual owners through any channel, using non-public company information if available. Then run the proposed pilot (X1, 20,000 EUR and 12 weeks, both proposed) to test installer stocking and the premium-arm conversion against the thresholds in the decision rule.
final.uncertainty: High. No public data on the company's current consumer sales, channel contracts, margins or unit costs. No market size or share of retrofit buyers was found. The only consumer-market evidence is one company trade-fair account, one 2019 forum post about a cheap kit, and a 2024 Australian advice article that says owners are tempted by price. None measures willingness to pay. The SIMULATED result SYN-D was not used as evidence. Search budget was spent on the company's consumer footprint and the cheap-import challenge, not on market size.
would_change_if: Public or company information shows Ebersparcher already sells retrofit heaters to individual owners with stable margins, which would change the question from building to scaling

The pilot shows fewer than a third of installers stocking the premium kit, or premium conversion below half of parity, which would reject T1 and point to no expansion or a price-led aftermarket alternative
Evidence that owners are mainly DIY buyers who choose on price, with installers having no role, which would favour T2 and make the consumer proposition uneconomic against imported kits
Credible market data showing the retrofit buyer base is too small to recover development and channel costs

arguments.name: Installer-channel retrofit pilot with price-parity and premium arms (proposed)
arguments.method: Over 12 weeks, list a branded retrofit heater kit (existing product, no redesign) through 8 to 10 independent leisure-vehicle installers or dealers in one German-speaking market. Randomly assign partners to one of two price arms: a premium arm priced above comparable imported kits with warranty and certified installation included, and a parity arm priced near the imported kit. Track enquiries, quotes, and completed sales. Run a small online ad test in the same region with identical product pages to measure click-to-enquiry at each price point.
arguments.sample: 8 to 10 installers or dealers (proposed) and about 3,000 targeted impressions per arm for the online test (proposed), all in one region
arguments.measure: Share of installers willing to stock the kit at the offered margin; enquiry-to-sale conversion by price arm; share of buyers citing safety, warranty or installation as their reason, asked at point of sale

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium arm converts at a similar rate to parity arm, most buyers cite warranty or safety, and at least half of installers agree to stock the kit at the premium price
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium arm converts far below parity arm, buyers cite price, and fewer than a third of installers agree to stock at the premium price

arguments.decision_rule: Keep T1 as the working theory only if at least half of approached installers agree to stock the premium kit AND premium-arm conversion is at least 70% of parity-arm conversion. Reject T1 if fewer than a third of installers stock the premium kit or premium conversion is below 50% of parity. Between these thresholds, treat as inconclusive and do not commit investment.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product build yet. Run the proposed installer-channel pilot first, to test whether a branded retrofit kit can hold a premium over imported kits through installers. position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. frame.objective: Decide whether Gühring KG should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its industrial precision rotary cutting tools. The real objective is to find out whether individual or small-workshop buyers have a distinct, reachable need that Gühring could serve profitably without damaging its B2B core, and what evidence would justify that investment.

alternatives: A. No expansion: remain purely B2B precision tooling and invest in core automotive, aerospace, medical and mechanical engineering accounts

C. Different route to buyers: direct-to-consumer or online retail channel for existing or lightly adapted products, bypassing distributors

T1.claim: Small workshops, makers and training shops are a real but unserved segment that wants professional-grade precision cutting tools in small quantities. Gühring's B2B channels (distributors, key accounts, punchout ordering) do not reach them, so a simplified range sold through an online shop could capture margin without changing the industrial core.
T1.who_benefits: Small machine shops, repair shops, vocational training workshops and advanced makers who cannot get engineering support or small quantities from industrial channels; Gühring if it captures a premium for quality in a segment it does not serve now.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who need one or two precision drills or reamers at short notice currently pay high distributor markups or substitute cheaper tools with worse results. A direct online offer with known-quality tools and small-quantity ordering reduces search cost and makes quality visible, so they switch to the premium product.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring sells existing or lightly simplified SKUs direct online at a premium over commodity tools, using its existing manufacturing and brand, with marginal cost mainly in catalogue, e-commerce and returns handling.

T2.claim: Gühring's value lies in engineering-intensive B2B relationships, not in product sales to a new buyer type. T2.who_benefits: Industrial key accounts in automotive, aerospace and medical technology who pay for application support, tool-life guarantees and consistent quality; Gühring itself, which keeps its premium pricing and avoids channel conflict with distributors.

A consumer-facing line would signal commoditisation to those buyers and would not earn that premium from hobbyists or small shops, who buy on price and convenience. X1.name: Small-buyer pre-launch test of a simplified precision drill range
X1.method: A 10-SKU range of existing or lightly simplified drills and reamers in one category is listed on a separate landing page, outside the B2B punchout shop, and promoted with paid search and workshop forums. Price is randomised across two premium levels (A and B, about 15% apart, proposed) to test price sensitivity. In parallel, 15 to 20 structured interviews are held with existing industrial key accounts about the value of application engineering and regrinding services. Only the buyer-side channel is opened, with a waitlist for orders, to limit fulfilment cost.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 2,000 unique visitors from small workshops, training shops and makers over 8 weeks; 15 to 20 key-account contacts for interviews.
X1.measure: Orders and conversion rate from non-key-account buyers; share of orders under a proposed minimum value; price response between the two levels; repeat purchase within 12 weeks; return and support-ticket rate per order; interview ranking of engineering support versus product price as the reason for buying from Gühring.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Non-key-account buyers convert at a meaningful rate and accept the premium price level with limited price sensitivity; repeat purchase is comparable to distributor buyers; support cost per order is modest.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Conversion from small buyers is low or price-sensitive; orders carry high returns or support cost per unit; key-account interviews rank engineering support and tool-life above product price, and the premium rests on services rather than a product sold to new buyers.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed: proceed to a larger B2C-style pilot only if at least 150 orders from non-key-account buyers are placed in 8 weeks, the premium price level shows no more than a 20% drop in conversion versus the lower level, repeat purchase within 12 weeks is at least 15%, and support tickets are under 10% of orders. If orders are below 50, or support tickets exceed 25% of orders, or key accounts rank engineering support above product price, stop the consumer line and direct effort to the service proposition.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the B2B precision-tooling core. Treat the small-workshop segment as an unproven hypothesis (T1) and fund only the proposed 20000 EUR, 12-week pre-launch test as a decision gate. Examine services for industrial customers (T2) in parallel.
final.target_customer: Not chosen. Test candidate only: small machine shops, training workshops and advanced makers buying single or small-quantity precision drills and reamers. Industrial key accounts remain the core.
final.value_proposition: Untested. For small buyers: professional-grade drills and reamers in small quantities, sold direct online. For key accounts: application engineering, tool-life optimisation and regrinding. Neither has been shown to earn a premium.
final.next_action: Confirm whether the online shop and distributor channels already serve single-unit buyers and what minimum order sizes apply. Obtain channel and service revenue splits if available. Then decide whether to run the pre-launch test.
final.uncertainty: Large. All Gühring sources are company claims (B2B punchout shop, customer description, company size). No independent evidence of small-buyer demand, brand dilution, or channel or service margins. The ALPEN-MAYKESTAG source is a different company, used only as an analogy. Brief details (family owned, fourth generation) unverified. Financial and contractual detail not found.
would_change_if: Evidence that existing channels already sell small quantities to workshop or individual buyers at scale
Independent data showing small workshops buy precision tools with own money at a brand premium

Pre-launch test meeting the rule: at least 150 non-key-account orders in 8 weeks, no more than 20% conversion drop at the higher price, at least 15% repeat purchase, support tickets under 10% of orders
Key-account interviews ranking product price above engineering support, weakening T2
Evidence a consumer line damages key-account pricing or distributor relationships, favouring no expansion

position.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep Gühring as an industrial B2B supplier. Before any product decision, run the low-cost listing test (X1) to see whether origin and guidance earn a premium with light-duty buyers. Only if T1 survives should a narrow kit or accessory line through a machine-vendor channel be considered.

frame.objective: Decide whether Guehring KG should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific individual-buyer use case, such as home workshop or hobbyist metalworking, or remain an industrial B2B supplier. Identify the evidence that would justify the investment.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only. The company has not asked this question and nothing here describes its intentions.
Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining. No direct company contact.
Test budget of 20000 EUR and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state what could not be found.
Company claims are not proof of demand. SIMULATED results are not cited as evidence.
alternatives: No expansion: stay purely industrial B2B in automotive, aerospace, mechanical engineering and medical technology.
Product redesign: adapt existing industrial tool lines with smaller shanks, simpler geometry and lower cost for light-duty users through the current channel.
Different route to buyers: sell existing or adapted tools through retail, online marketplaces or distributors that serve hobbyists and small workshops.
Different customer group: serve small job shops, prototype makers or repair workshops rather than individual consumers.
Consumer kit line sold through third parties, or licensing the brand to a consumer tool company.

T1.claim: Home and small-workshop CNC owners buy cutting tools as consumables and are short of reliable application knowledge. A tool maker with proven industrial reputation, offering application guidance for light-duty cuts, could earn a premium with them through the channel they already use, such as CNC machine vendors.
T1.who_benefits: Gühring (premium pricing and brand reach); small-workshop owners (fewer tool failures); machine vendors such as Tormach (a stronger accessory offer)
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who cannot judge tool quality rely on trusted brands and vendor recommendations. Industrial reputation lowers their perceived risk, so they will pay more for a tool they trust.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring sells premium-priced tools or application kits through machine-vendor accessory catalogues or its existing distributors, earning a margin without building a retail brand.
assumptions: Hobbyists and small shops buy tools in small quantities and care about brand trust.
Machine vendors will list a third-party premium tool brand.
Gühring's industrial reputation transfers to light-duty users.
predictions: Forum and review sites will show hobbyists asking for or praising industrial-grade brands in drills and end mills.
Hobbyists will pay a premium for a tool when its industrial origin is shown.
A vendor-channel listing will sell at a higher price than a generic equivalent.
T1.first_claim: Home and small-workshop CNC owners buy cutting tools as consumables and are short of reliable application knowledge. A tool maker with proven industrial reputation, offering application guidance for light-duty cuts, could earn a premium with them through the channel they already use, such as CNC machine vendors.

T2.claim: Home and hobby metalworkers choose tools mainly on price and on brands that are already familiar to them in that hobby, such as Proxxon, Alpen and S&R. An industrial brand's quality does not carry over to them, so a premium industrial reputation gives little advantage in this segment.
T2.who_benefits: Existing hobby brands and retailers, which keep the consumer margin; hobbyists, who get low prices without needing a premium tool
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists judge tools by price, availability and forum recommendations within their own community. They are not moved by industrial credentials, so a premium-brand entry would need a price cut that erases the margin.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Gühring would capture little value. Hobby brands and retail channels would keep the consumer margin, so a consumer product would need a low-price, high-volume model that does not fit Gühring's cost base.
assumptions: Hobbyists weigh price and community recommendation above industrial origin.
Gühring's cost base cannot match the price points of hobby brands.
Hobby brands already dominate the consumer channels.
predictions: Forum discussions will recommend hobby brands over industrial brands for home use.
Price-sensitive buyers will not pay a premium for an industrial brand when a cheaper hobby brand is available.
Consumer sales channels will show hobby brands in top positions over industrial brands.

X1.name: Price-and-origin listing test for light-duty drill sets
X1.method: Assemble a small set of existing Gühring small-diameter drills (proposed: 6-piece set in a case) and list it in two controlled conditions through a third-party online channel used by home and hobby metalworkers, or through a CNC machine vendor's accessory catalogue if one agrees. Condition A shows the industrial origin and application guidance at a premium price. Condition B shows a price near comparable hobby brands with the same product and no origin message. Run the listings in matched periods or split-traffic where the platform allows. This is a demand test, not a product launch.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 2,000 unique product-page visitors per condition, or a minimum of 40 sales per condition over the test, whichever comes later, within 12 weeks. Channel availability is unknown and must be confirmed first.
X1.measure: Conversion rate per 100 visitors, units sold, revenue per visitor, and the share of buyers who open the origin or guidance content. Also record unsolicited buyer comments on quality and price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A converts at least as well as Condition B despite the higher price, and buyers cite industrial origin or trust in their comments. Revenue per visitor is higher in A.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition A converts clearly worse than Condition B, because buyers respond to price and familiar hobby brands. The origin message adds no lift and buyers cite price in their comments.

X1.decision_rule: Continue to a consumer proposition only if Condition A revenue per visitor is at least 1.2 times Condition B and conversion in A is at least 80% of B. Otherwise, treat T2 as favoured and do not build a consumer line. Results below 40 sales per condition are inconclusive and need a second round.

revisions.reason: SYN-D is a SIMULATED result about a label printer in a warehouse. It says nothing about hobbyist buyers, tool brands or price, so it does not bear on T2 and is not cited. T2 stays as it was, supported by the buying guide that names Proxxon, Alpen and S&R as popular, and limited by the lack of price or sales data.

SYN-D is a SIMULATED label-printer result that says nothing about buyers or tools, so it does not bear on T1 and is not cited. T1 stays uncertain. The forum comment that quality is top notch but price is the only trouble weakens its premium-capture part, and the buying guide shows hobbyist opinion on brand quality is divided.

Supposing SYN-D were real, it would still bear on neither T1 nor T2. It describes a label printer reducing packing errors in a warehouse and measures nothing about buyers, tool brands or price. It is SIMULATED and is not evidence, so the result changes nothing. T2 stays as it was.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep Gühring as an industrial B2B supplier. Run only a small, low-cost listing test (X1, proposed at about 15,000 EUR over 10 weeks) to see whether industrial origin and application guidance earn a premium with light-duty buyers. Revisit only if that test passes its threshold.
final.target_customer: None for now. If the test runs, the group is home and small-workshop CNC or hobby metalworkers who buy small drill and end-mill sets.
final.value_proposition: Not yet defined. The only candidate is industrial-grade reliability for light-duty cuts, with application guidance. The evidence so far does not show buyers paying for it.
final.next_action: Confirm with public sources whether Gühring already sells through any retail, marketplace or machine-vendor channel to individuals. Then, if exploration continues, confirm a channel for X1 before spending on it.
final.uncertainty: Large. I found no company source on Gühring's consumer sales, distribution, light-duty product range, pricing or financials. The evidence is four anecdotes and buying guides: a 2016 UK forum post, an undated German buying guide, a 2021 vendor blog about its own customers, and a 2019 article about Heller, a different company. None measures demand, willingness to pay or segment size. The SIMULATED result SYN-D was irrelevant and is not evidence. T1 is uncertain and T2 is only likely.
would_change_if: X1 shows Condition A revenue per visitor at least 1.2 times Condition B, with conversion at least 80% of B. That would support T1.
Public sources show hobbyists or small-workshop buyers paying a clear premium for industrial brands in drills or end mills.
Gühring's own public material shows an existing small-customer or light-duty channel that a consumer line could reuse at low cost.
A machine vendor confirms it would list a third-party premium tool brand at a margin Gühring can accept.
Evidence that price is not the main barrier for hobbyists, such as recent reviews citing quality over cost in purchase decisions.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Homebrewing is slow (about two weeks per batch in the LG example) and messy. A capsule appliance turns it into a convenience purchase, so the buyer pays for time saved and for variety, and then keeps buying consumables.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Recurring sales of proprietary capsules at high margin, on top of a one-off appliance price (LG example: about 3.99 million won, USD 3,386, per set-up)
assumptions: Buyers accept a high up-front appliance price

Capsule recipes can be protected or are hard to copy
Repeat purchase rates are high enough for lifetime value to exceed acquisition cost
predictions: Households pay for convenience and variety more than for cost saving, so willingness to pay rises with time saved per batch

X1.method: Run a landing page in Germany offering a refundable EUR deposit on a capsule beer appliance at a proposed price, with an opt-in for a capsule subscription. Separately, send a short licensing enquiry to 15 consumer brands and appliance retailers asking whether they would take the technology and sell it under their brand. Proposed design, not yet run.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 2000 landing-page visitors recruited from homebrewing and craft-beer channels, and 15 licensing prospects
X1.measure: Deposit conversion rate on the appliance, share opting into a recurring capsule subscription, and number of brand partners agreeing to a licensing discussion

prediction_by_theory.T1: Deposit conversion is high enough at the proposed price, and a large share opt into the capsule subscription, so the appliance and consumables can carry a recurring margin.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Direct deposit conversion is low or subscription opt-in is weak, while several brands show interest in licensing, so value sits with the brand owner rather than the hardware maker.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a prototype only if deposit conversion is at least 3 percent of visitors (proposed threshold) and at least 40 percent of depositors opt into the capsule subscription. If conversion is below 1 percent and at least 3 brand partners show licensing interest, pursue licensing instead. Otherwise stop.

X1.name: Hospitality demand test for an on-site brewhouse versus a consumer capsule appliance
X1.method: Two-arm pre-order test in one German region. Arm A: offer hospitality operators a priced, commercially rated small brewhouse with service and ingredient supply, asking for a refundable deposit or signed letter of intent. Arm B: offer consumers a capsule-brewing appliance concept at a stated price, asking for a refundable pre-order. Both arms use the same landing page and price framing, with a deposit refunded if the product is not built.
X1.sample: Proposed: 30 hospitality operators (restaurants, hotels, caterers with more than 50 covers or regular events) and 200 consumers reached through paid online ads, both in one region.
X1.measure: Proportion of contacted buyers who sign a letter of intent with a deposit (Arm A) or place a refundable pre-order (Arm B), plus number of enquiries about running costs and servicing.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hospitality operators sign deposits at a higher rate than consumers pre-order, and enquiries focus on guest-facing beer, service and ingredient supply.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Consumer pre-orders match or exceed hospitality deposits, and enquiries focus on price and capsule refills rather than service.

X1.decision_rule: Pursue the hospitality route (T1) if at least 6 of 30 operators (20 per cent, proposed threshold) sign a deposit and that rate is at least twice the consumer pre-order rate. Pursue neither if fewer than 3 of 30 operators sign. Otherwise treat as inconclusive and do not invest beyond the test.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer-facing proposition now. Run a low-cost hospitality test of a turnkey small brewhouse (proposed test X1) before any product build. The evidence is thin and mostly not about Krones.
final.target_customer: Hospitality operators (restaurants, hotels, caterers) as the hypothesis to test; consumers are rejected for now.
final.value_proposition: A commercially rated small brewhouse plus service and ingredient supply, so a venue can brew its own house beer. Unproven; the only supporting source is a Speidel marketing claim.
final.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed: 20,000 EUR, 10 weeks) with the decision rule: pursue only if at least 6 of 30 operators sign a deposit and that rate is at least twice the consumer pre-order rate. First establish how far Krones already sells to individual buyers, and any Speidel link, from company or non-public sources.
final.uncertainty: High. No source I read shows Krones selling to individual buyers or a Speidel-Krones link. The Speidel excerpt is marketing with no sales data. The USD 213.4m market figure is a research estimate covering consumers. The LG price is one 2019 list price, not demand. Krones contracts and margins are not public. Test sample and threshold are my proposals.

Test X1 shows fewer than 3 of 30 operators signing a deposit
Consumer pre-orders match or exceed hospitality deposits
Evidence that hospitality brewing operators fail at rates that make service revenue unreliable

X1.method: Offer a standardised compact brewhouse or small-batch line configuration to small craft producers as a fixed-price quote with a 2-week response window, and run a parallel consumer pre-order page for a home capsule appliance in one market. Log qualified quote requests and pre-orders.
X1.sample: Proposed: 40 craft breweries and small food producers in Germany and Austria (B2B arm); 1,000 home-brew enthusiasts reached via paid social for the consumer arm (proposed sizes, not observed).
X1.measure: B2B: number of qualified quote requests with stated volume and budget per 40 contacts. Consumer: pre-order deposits per 1,000 exposed.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer pre-orders should reach a meaningful deposit rate, and repeat-capsule intent should be high; B2B quote requests would be low because the value sits with consumers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Qualified B2B quote requests should be clearly above the consumer deposit rate, concentrated among producers with growing volume and a stated space constraint; consumer pre-orders should be low.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: pursue the B2B compact route only if at least 6 of 40 breweries submit a qualified quote request within 2 weeks (about 15%) and the median requested capacity is within the compact range. Pursue a consumer appliance only if consumer deposits reach at least 2% of exposed enthusiasts and repeat-capsule intent is confirmed in follow-up. Otherwise, do not expand.

revisions.reason: The simulated result SYN-D is excluded because it is a SIMULATED label-printer test that measured nothing about buyers, so it bears on neither theory. T2 is kept unchanged on the real evidence I read: the Steinecker MicroCube claim is company marketing, and the Compact Class release gives only the company's own description of a profitable, growing small-output business. Demand for compact lines is still untested.

Supposing SYN-D were real, it would show a label printer cutting packing errors in a warehouse. That bears on warehouse operations, not on whether individuals buy home beverage appliances or capsules, so T1 is unchanged. The result would not move T1 towards or away from being true. T1 stays very unlikely on the real evidence, which is a market-size estimate and one 2019 product price with no margin or repeat-purchase data.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer-facing proposition now. The public evidence I could read supports, at most, a cheap test of a standardised compact line for small producers, which fits Krones's existing industrial route to market. I found no public evidence that Krones sells to individual buyers: its material describes B2B machines and lines, and Steinecker's MicroCube is a brewhouse for craft brewers. The consumer appliance route rests on a market-size estimate and one 2019 product price, with nothing on margin or repeat purchase.
final.target_customer: Small craft breweries and small food and beverage producers that need compact plants (a company-claimed segment, not yet tested)
final.value_proposition: A standardised, fixed-configuration compact line that lowers the cost, space and lead-time barrier for small producers, sold through the existing industrial sales and service organisation.
final.next_action: Run the proposed B2B quote test (X1) with 40 small producers: a fixed-price compact configuration, a 2-week response window, about EUR 18,000 over 10 weeks. All figures are proposed. Pursue the compact route only if at least 6 of 40 submit a qualified quote request. Do not run a consumer pre-order arm unless the B2B result is positive and the consumer question is tested separately.
final.uncertainty: High. I could not find Krones's internal consumer reach, Compact Class margins or customer counts, or any buyer-behaviour data for compact lines. The market-size figures come from a paid research report, and the LG price comes from a single 2019 launch. The challenge search found a GEA compact brewhouse product and an older trade-fair press release, neither of which shows weak demand. SYN-D is simulated and excluded from the evidence.

T1.claim: Private EV owners pay a premium for a home charging product from an established industrial cable maker because it signals electrical safety and reliability, so a Lapp-branded home wallbox or cable set sold through its own shop can earn a margin above generic alternatives.
T1.who_benefits: Private EV owners who want a safe, reliable home charging installation and a seller they trust; Lapp Mobility, which captures margin on the product and the shop channel.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Owners worry about fire and installation risk in garages. A brand known for industrial-grade cables and connectors reduces that perceived risk, which justifies paying more than for a low-cost import.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp Mobility sells the wallbox and accessories directly through its online shop to private customers, keeping the retail margin and selling add-ons and cable sets.

Lapp's industrial reputation transfers to the consumer product

T2.claim: Private EV owners buy home charging on price and convenience, so a consumer-facing product from an industrial cable maker faces a commodity market with no premium. Value stays with B2B supply to OEMs and installers, not with individuals.
T2.who_benefits: Private EV owners, who gain low prices; installers and OEM buyers, who keep the volume; Lapp only if it stays in B2B supply.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The source describes a fiercely contested, price-sensitive market where start-ups have been pushed out. When many sellers offer similar wallboxes, buyers compare price and do not pay for brand.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Lapp earns margin on components and assemblies sold to wallbox makers, installers and OEMs, and does not need its own consumer margin or shop.

predictions: Lapp-branded wallboxes price close to or below generic equivalents, with weak sales at a premium

X1.name: Brand premium test on a home wallbox listing
X1.method: Run paid search and social ads for the same wallbox in two arms: one shows the Lapp brand and one shows a generic, unbranded listing, both at the same price. Then run a price step with the Lapp listing at about +10 percent versus the generic. Compare click-through, add-to-cart and purchase rates. Use the existing shop or a landing page with the same checkout (proposed design).

X1.name: Brand premium choice test for home charging cables
X1.method: Online discrete choice experiment with a matched set of charging cables that differ only in brand origin and visible certification, at three price points, plus 15 structured interviews with electricians who install home wallboxes. Price and brand presentation are randomised.
X1.sample: Proposed: 400 German private EV owners or buyers recruited through an online panel, and 15 electricians recruited through trade associations (estimated).
X1.measure: Share of respondents choosing the certified industrial-brand cable over the cheapest uncertified option at each price point; willingness to pay premium in euros; electrician-stated influence on brand choice.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Certified industrial-brand cable keeps at least 25 percent choice share with a premium of 10 percent or more over the cheapest option, and electricians report that brand and certification shape their recommendation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Choice share for the certified brand falls below 10 percent once the price gap exceeds about 10 percent, and electricians report that customers buy the cheapest adequate cable.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a consumer pilot only if the certified brand keeps at least 25 percent choice share at a 10 percent premium and at least half of electricians say brand affects their recommendation. If choice share is below 10 percent at a 10 percent premium, drop the consumer proposition and keep B2B supply to charger makers. Between these, keep investigating with a second wave.

final.recommendation: Do not build a standalone consumer brand now. Keep B2B supply of mobility components to charger makers and infrastructure operators as the core route. Test a private-buyer proposition with a proposed choice experiment (not yet run) before committing consumer investment. The test budget and timing are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
final.target_customer: Not yet chosen. Private EV owners are the candidate segment, but the evidence found so far does not show they buy on brand. Electricians and charger makers are the more likely buyers.
final.value_proposition: For now, a supply proposition to charger makers and operators: reliable, stock-backed mobility components from an established industrial supplier. A consumer proposition would need a visible certification or safety premium, which is unproven.
final.next_action: Run the proposed choice experiment (about EUR 18,000 over 10 weeks, estimated) with 400 private EV buyers and 15 electricians, using the decision rule set out in the test. Separately, ask the company, not the public web, for its consumer sales figures, which I could not find.
final.uncertainty: Very thin evidence. I found two trade-press items and one company claim. I found no public figures for Lapp's consumer sales, margins, channel shares, or contracts with charger makers. The competition source describes reduced attractiveness for consumers in price-sensitive markets but gives no numbers. The Mennekes source shows that a German industrial maker sells home wallboxes to private users, but it does not show whether brand commands a premium. Whether Lapp already sells to individual buyers at scale is unknown. The test is proposed only and nothing has been run.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Keep the core B2B model. If a consumer-facing move is pursued, test the installer and trade route (T2) first, because the sources read so far do not support a direct-to-consumer premium (T1), and no source shows that installers choose components on certification (T2 remains untested). Run the proposed two-offer test before committing more than the test budget.

frame.objective: Decide whether U.I. Lapp GmbH should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its industrial cables and connection technology, and identify the evidence that would justify that investment. The real objective is to find a consumer-facing value pool where Lapp's engineering know-how (cable reliability, connectors, safety, certification) earns a premium its B2B channel cannot capture, without damaging the core machinery business.
constraints: Outside analyst using only public sources; no company intentions or contractual detail known
Test budget EUR 20000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget of 8 in total, 7 left after read_brief, with 1 challenge search kept for theory challenge
Must not assume what Lapp already sells to individual buyers; must verify
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state the gaps
Family-owned, about 5700 staff and EUR 1.93bn sales in FY2025 limit the scale of any side venture
alternatives: A. No expansion: stay B2B in machinery, plant engineering, food, logistics, energy and mobility
B. Product redesign: adapt existing OELFLEX cable and connector lines for a consumer niche such as DIY, home charging, marine or camping
C. Different route to buyers: sell existing products to end users through online retail or a DIY distributor, with no new product
D. Different customer group: serve a specific consumer segment such as EV owners or solar prosumers with a bundled kit or service
E. Consumer-adjacent B2B: sell to installers who serve homeowners, for example wallbox installation kits, and leave the end consumer to them
F. Licensing or partnering with a consumer brand that uses Lapp cable technology as an ingredient

T1.claim: Private EV owners will pay a premium for Lapp-branded charging cables and accessories sold direct through Lapp's own shop, because the Lapp name signals industrial-grade safety and reliability that cheap consumer accessories lack.
T1.who_benefits: Private EV owners who want a safe, durable charging cable; Lapp Mobility, which would capture the margin by selling direct and keeping the brand.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers judge charging equipment on safety and durability once they know the risks of cheap cables. A recognised industrial brand reduces the perceived risk and justifies a higher price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp sells direct through its existing private-customer shop (Germany and Austria), keeping the retail margin and building a consumer brand on top of its existing product range.
assumptions: Lapp Mobility's shop already accepts private customers, so the route to buyers exists
Private buyers care more about safety and brand than about the lowest price
The price premium is large enough to cover the cost of marketing and returns to individuals
predictions: Private visitors to the Lapp shop buy at a higher average price than the market average for comparable EV cables
A test listing with a safety and reliability message converts at a higher rate than a price-led message
Repeat purchase and reviews mention safety or durability more than price
T1.first_claim: Private EV owners will pay a premium for Lapp-branded charging cables and accessories sold direct through Lapp's own shop, because the Lapp name signals industrial-grade safety and reliability that cheap consumer accessories lack.

T2.claim: Private EV owners do not choose their charging equipment; the installing electrician does. A Lapp product sold through trade channels to installers who serve homeowners captures value without consumer marketing, because the installer's safety and certification concerns drive the purchase.
T2.who_benefits: Installers and electricians, who need certified, traceable components to protect their liability; Lapp, which keeps its B2B model and sells into a trade channel.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Installers carry liability for installation faults. A component from a manufacturer with recognised certification and documentation lowers their risk, so they specify it and the homeowner accepts the installer's choice.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Lapp sells wallbox connection kits or cable assemblies through electrical wholesalers and installer accounts, using its existing B2B sales network and documentation, with no direct-to-consumer marketing cost.
assumptions: Homeowners follow the installer's recommendation on charging hardware
Installers value certification and documentation enough to pay a premium
Lapp's existing sales companies can reach electrical wholesalers without new channel investment
predictions: Installer-specified products carry a higher price than those bought by end consumers in the same category
Lapp sales to electrical wholesalers grow faster than direct sales to private buyers
Installers cite certification and documentation, not brand awareness among homeowners, as the reason for choice
T2.first_claim: Private EV owners do not choose their charging equipment; the installing electrician does. A Lapp product sold through trade channels to installers who serve homeowners captures value without consumer marketing, because the installer's safety and certification concerns drive the purchase.

X1.name: Two-offer demand test: private EV owners vs installers
X1.method: Run two parallel offers for the same certified charging cable kit. Offer A: a landing page aimed at private EV owners, with a safety and durability message and a price, linked to the existing Lapp Mobility shop. Offer B: a trade offer to electrical installers and wholesalers, with a certification and documentation pack and a trade price. Track enquiries and pre-orders from each. Use paid search and targeted trade mailings to a fixed list.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3000 unique visitors to the consumer page over 6 weeks through paid search, and about 150 installers and wholesalers contacted directly in Germany.
X1.measure: Pre-order or quote-request rate per 100 unique contacts in each arm, plus average quoted price and stated reason for choice in the trade arm.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer arm converts at or above 1 per 100 visitors, and the safety message beats the price message at similar or higher price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trade arm produces at least 3 quote requests per 100 installers, and installers ask about certification and documentation before price.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if trade quote requests are at least 3 per 100 contacts and at least twice the consumer conversion rate, and at least 10 installers ask for certification documents, favour T2 and build the installer route. If consumer conversion is at least 1 per 100 visitors with a safety premium over the price message, keep T1 as a parallel option. If neither arm clears its threshold, stop and do not invest.

revisions.reason: The simulated result SYN-D (label printer, packing errors) measured nothing about installers, wholesalers or buyers, so it changes nothing. It is not cited. T2 is kept because no read source contradicts it, but it is still untested: the Eon survey shows home charging is common, not who chooses the charger, and the test is needed.

The simulated result SYN-D (label printer, packing errors) measured nothing about private EV owners or buyers, so it does not bear on T1 and changes nothing. T1 is weakened by the price-sensitivity market source (lapp-ev-accessory-competition) and by the absence of any measured premium, but is not refuted. It is kept as an untested alternative, with the consumer arm of test X1 to check it.

Supposing SYN-D were real, it would say only that a label printer reduces packing errors in a warehouse. It would still say nothing about installers, wholesalers or homeowners, so it would change nothing for T2. It is recorded here only to close the update step and is not cited in the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Keep the core B2B model. The public sources show that Lapp Mobility already accepts private customers in its German and Austrian shop, but they give no evidence that private EV owners would pay a safety premium for Lapp cables. The one market source on consumer charging describes price-sensitive, fiercely contested buyers. If the company wants a consumer-facing move, test the installer and trade route (T2) first, using the proposed two-offer test (X1), at an estimated EUR 15000 over 6 weeks, inside the EUR 20000 budget.
final.target_customer: Electrical installers and wholesalers who fit home EV chargers for homeowners (for the trade test). Private EV owners are a secondary, untested segment (for the consumer arm of the test).
final.value_proposition: For installers: a certified, documented charging cable or connection kit from an established industrial manufacturer, which lowers their liability and installation risk. For private owners, untested: a safety and durability message at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run test X1: a two-offer test with a consumer landing page and a trade offer to installers and wholesalers, over 6 weeks at a proposed cost of EUR 15000. Decide on the pre-set thresholds: favour the trade route if trade quote requests reach at least 3 per 100 contacts, at least twice the consumer conversion rate, and at least 10 installers ask for certification documents. Otherwise do not invest.
final.uncertainty: High. Lapp's sales to individual buyers, its consumer revenue, its contracts and its margins are not public, so I could not check what it already sells beyond the Lapp Mobility shop. I found no source that measures how installers or homeowners choose charging components, so T2 is untested. The Eon survey (63 per cent charge most often at home) is company-commissioned, shows where charging happens and not who chooses the hardware, and its date should be checked. The one consumer market source describes price-sensitive buyers, which weakens T1. No simulated result was used as evidence.
would_change_if: Test X1 shows private consumer conversion at or above 1 per 100 visitors, with a safety message beating a price message at a higher price (supports T1 and reopens the direct route)
Installers and wholesalers do not ask for certification or documentation and choose on price (rejects T2)
Public or company data shows Lapp already sells substantial volumes to private buyers through its shop, changing the baseline
Evidence that homeowners, not installers, make the final charger choice in most cases
Non-public contract or margin data shows that the trade route would conflict with existing machinery-channel agreements

T1.claim: Lapp already reaches private buyers through its Lapp Mobility online shop for EV charging accessories, and a small consumer proposition in home EV charging can extend that channel because buyers of charging hardware value a simple, ready-to-use product from a known cable brand.
T1.who_benefits: Private car owners and homeowners installing EV charging, who want a simple and trusted purchase; Lapp, which already has a direct sales channel and cable know-how.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers of home charging cables and accessories face a fragmented market and want simple, checked, ready-made products. A cable brand they already associate with reliability can reduce perceived risk and make the purchase feel simple.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp sells existing or lightly adapted charging cables and accessories through its own shop, earning margin on products it already makes, without building a new brand or retail network.

The shop's current private sales are material enough to matter

T2.claim: Individual EV-charging buyers are price-sensitive and treat cables as interchangeable commodities, so a cable brand gains little direct consumer premium; value for Lapp lies instead in selling through installers and electricians who specify and recommend products.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product yet. The only evidence for a household-premium market is a vendor page, a market-research summary and one anecdotal review. Of the options, the cheapest informative step is the proposed deposit test (X1, about EUR 14,000 over 10 weeks, estimated). If the reliability arm clears the proposed thresholds, consider a small premium chamber unit on the existing tabletop platform. If not, stay B2B and pursue small-producer sales, not households.

frame.objective: Decide whether MULTIVAC should build a differentiated proposition aimed at individual or household buyers for a specific use case, beyond its current B2B packaging, labelling, inspection and food-processing equipment for food, medical, pharma and industrial producers. The decision should rest on evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay and a route to buyers that MULTIVAC can actually operate.

alternatives: No expansion: keep the B2B-only focus on food, medical, pharma and industrial producers, and reach small craft businesses through existing channels
Consumer-facing product redesign: a compact, lower-cost vacuum or sealing appliance for households, sold through existing or new retail channels
Different route to the same buyers: sell existing small-format machines or consumables online or via retail to craft food businesses and serious home users, without a new product
Different customer group: target small craft and artisan food producers, farm-direct sellers or micro-businesses as a 'prosumer' segment with a simplified offer
Ecosystem or service play: sell subscriptions, consumables, packaging-as-a-service or training to existing and prospective small users, keeping the machine within the B2B model
Adjacent consumer use case: food-preservation or meal-kit packaging partnerships with consumer brands, where MULTIVAC supplies machines to a brand that sells to households

T1.claim: Serious home cooks and micro-producers will pay a premium for a compact chamber sealer built on MULTIVAC's existing tabletop platform, because they want professional-grade, reliable liquid sealing that cheap consumer sealers do not deliver.
T1.who_benefits: Serious home cooks and sous vide enthusiasts; MULTIVAC, which would reuse existing C-series tabletop engineering and parts.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who already use sous vide or bulk food processing find consumer sealers unreliable with liquids, and the professional chamber sealing they see used by chefs signals quality and justifies a higher price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: MULTIVAC sells a direct or retailer-listed product at a premium above mass-market consumer sealers, using its existing tabletop design and manufacturing so that development cost is low.
assumptions: A meaningful number of households will pay several hundred euros or more for a chamber sealer
Existing tabletop engineering can be cut to a consumer price point without a new design
Serious home cooks value professional build quality over brand, app or recipe content
MULTIVAC can reach households through a retailer or e-commerce channel it does not yet operate

assessments.does_not_show: A vendor's page shows that one brand markets presets as a selling point. It does not show that buyers choose a machine for its presets, that brand owners would buy OEM hardware from a machine maker, or what share of the sale the software and brand capture.

assessments.does_not_show: This is one anecdotal review, hosted on the vendor's own page, so it is selected and unrepresentative. It does not give a price threshold, a sales figure, or any test of whether a premium MULTIVAC-built unit would sell. It shows only that at least one prospective buyer saw chamber sealers as too expensive.

X1.name: Premium-reliability landing-page and deposit test for a compact household chamber sealer
X1.method: Run a two-message landing-page test with a deposit option. Traffic comes from paid social and sous vide and bulk-cooking communities. Visitors are randomly shown one of two messages: (a) professional liquid-sealing reliability and build quality, or (b) presets, guided modes and app features. Both pages show the same proposed price, with a refundable deposit to reserve a unit. A second price arm tests a lower price point against a higher one. The test uses a concept render and no product is built or sold. (All volumes, prices and rates here are proposed or estimated, not observed.)
X1.sample: Proposed: about 6,000 to 8,000 qualified unique visitors across 8 weeks, split across message and price arms, recruited through paid ads (estimated budget)
X1.measure: Deposit conversion rate per arm (refundable reservation), and email signups as a secondary signal. Also a short exit survey asking the main reason for not reserving.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Reliability message converts at least as well as the presets message among sous vide and bulk-cooking visitors; deposit conversion stays meaningful at a premium price point, and exit reasons cite price fit with professional-grade quality rather than missing features.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Presets and app message converts clearly better than the reliability message; conversion falls sharply at any premium price, and exit reasons cite missing modes, recipes or app features rather than price or build quality.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: keep T1 for further work only if the reliability arm reaches at least 2% deposit conversion among qualified visitors at the premium price, and beats the presets arm by at least 1.5 times. Reject T1 if reliability conversion is below 0.5% at both prices, or if exit reasons are dominated by price. Favour T2 if the presets arm beats reliability by 1.5 times or more. If neither threshold is met, decline further spend and return to no-expansion or a partner-brand option.

final.recommendation: Do not build a household product now. MULTIVAC's public footprint is B2B: its tabletop chamber line is marketed to butchers, dairies, restaurants and direct sellers, not to households. The public evidence for a premium household chamber sealer is thin, so the next step is a low-cost deposit test (proposed, not run). Keep the B2B focus unless that test clears its thresholds.
final.target_customer: Provisionally, serious home cooks and sous vide users, with micro-producers as a possible adjacent segment. This is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.
final.value_proposition: Professional-grade, reliable liquid sealing in a compact unit built on the existing tabletop platform, at a price below professional machines. Whether buyers will pay the premium is unknown.
final.next_action: Consider running the proposed deposit test (X1: two messages, two price points, about EUR 14,000 and 10 weeks, all estimated). Before running it, confirm with MULTIVAC's own records whether it already sells small units to consumers or through dealers, and what its unit costs and channel costs are, since none of this is public.
final.uncertainty: Largely unknown. I could not find MULTIVAC's consumer sales, channel or dealer data, or its margins; the brochure I found dates from 2014 and is hosted by a dealer. Household market size comes from one market-research summary with no method or figures. The only consumer demand signal is a single vendor-hosted review that cites price. I have no evidence on what a MULTIVAC-branded unit would sell for or how many households would buy it. Theory T2 (brand and software capture the value) is not tested at all, and the test does not yet separate it cleanly from T1.

The presets or app message clearly beats reliability, or exit reasons cite price at every price point (supports T2 or no expansion)
MULTIVAC's own data show existing dealer or retail sales of small units to households, which would lower the cost of entry
Unit cost estimates show no margin at a consumer price point, even with existing tabletop engineering
A retail or brand partner offers a committed volume that would pay for the development

Visitors are randomly shown one of two messages: (a) professional liquid-sealing reliability and build quality, or (b) presets, guided modes and app features. Both pages show the same proposed price, with a refundable deposit to reserve a unit. A second price arm tests a lower price point against a higher one. The test uses a concept render and no product is built or sold. (All volumes, prices and rates here are proposed or estimated, not observed.)
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 6,000 to 8,000 qualified unique visitors across 8 weeks, split across message and price arms, recruited through paid ads (estimated budget)
arguments.measure: Deposit conversion rate per arm (refundable reservation), and email signups as a secondary signal. Also a short exit survey asking the main reason for not reserving.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Reliability message converts at least as well as the presets message among sous vide and bulk-cooking visitors; deposit conversion stays meaningful at a premium price point, and exit reasons cite price fit with professional-grade quality rather than missing features.

X1.name: Tabletop chamber pre-sale with a cooking-use screen
X1.method: Run a landing-page and pre-order test in two sales channels. Show a compact chamber machine at a premium price point to (a) home cooks who sous vide and (b) small food businesses (craft butchers, cheese dairies, delis). Each respondent gives a deposit or joins a waitlist and answers a screen: main use (liquid or sous vide cooking, storage, or product sealing for sale). Compare conversion, stated use, and deposit amount across the two groups. This is a proposed design; no results exist.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 400 home-cook visitors recruited through sous vide forums and about 150 small food businesses recruited through trade associations and dealer lists. Estimated, not observed.
X1.measure: Deposit or waitlist conversion rate by group; share of home-cook respondents whose main stated use is liquid or sous vide cooking; share of business respondents citing hygiene or product sale as purpose; average price accepted.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Home cooks convert at a meaningful rate, at least 3 percent, and most name sous vide or liquid sealing as their main use. Their accepted price is well above a clamp-type home sealer.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Business respondents convert at a higher rate than home cooks, at least twice as high, and cite product sale or hygiene. Home cooks convert below 1 percent.

X1.decision_rule: Favour T1 if home-cook conversion is at least 3 percent with at least half naming sous vide or liquid use. Favour T2 if business conversion is at least twice home-cook conversion and home-cook conversion is below 1 percent. If neither holds, the results are inconclusive and the consumer proposition is not supported. Threshold values are proposed, not from any source.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the B2B core and the tabletop line for small food businesses. Before any product investment, run the proposed 12-week pre-order test (estimated 20000 EUR) to see whether households buy a premium chamber machine for cooking. Nothing in the public sources shows that MULTIVAC already sells to individual buyers, so treat that as unknown.
final.target_customer: Small food businesses (craft butchers, cheese dairies, delis) as the current base. Serious home sous vide cooks as the only candidate consumer group, to be tested, not assumed.
final.value_proposition: A compact, professional-grade tabletop chamber machine with industrial hygiene and service, sold through existing dealer channels to food businesses. A household offer is unproven.
final.next_action: Find out whether MULTIVAC already sells tabletop machines to households, through its own shop or dealers, and get current sales mix. Then run the proposed pre-order test with the decision rule set out in the proposal.
final.uncertainty: Evidence is thin. The only company source is a 2014 dealer-hosted brochure, with no sales, price or margin data. Market sources are undated summaries. No evidence on household willingness to pay a premium, on dealer volumes, or on MULTIVAC's current consumer reach. Contract and internal financial detail is not public. Threshold values in the test are my proposals, not sourced figures.

arguments.name: Tabletop chamber pre-sale with a cooking-use screen
arguments.method: Run a landing-page and pre-order test in two sales channels. Show a compact chamber machine at a premium price point to (a) home cooks who sous vide and (b) small food businesses (craft butchers, cheese dairies, delis). Each respondent gives a deposit or joins a waitlist and answers a screen: main use (liquid or sous vide cooking, storage, or product sealing for sale). Compare conversion, stated use, and deposit amount across the two groups. This is a proposed design; no results exist.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 400 home-cook visitors recruited through sous vide forums and about 150 small food businesses recruited through trade associations and dealer lists. Estimated, not observed.
arguments.measure: Deposit or waitlist conversion rate by group; share of home-cook respondents whose main stated use is liquid or sous vide cooking; share of business respondents citing hygiene or product sale as purpose; average price accepted.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Home cooks convert at a meaningful rate, at least 3 percent, and most name sous vide or liquid sealing as their main use. Their accepted price is well above a clamp-type home sealer.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Business respondents convert at a higher rate than home cooks, at least twice as high, and cite product sale or hygiene. Home cooks convert below 1 percent.

arguments.decision_rule: Favour T1 if home-cook conversion is at least 3 percent with at least half naming sous vide or liquid use. Favour T2 if business conversion is at least twice home-cook conversion and home-cook conversion is below 1 percent. If neither holds, the results are inconclusive and the consumer proposition is not supported. Threshold values are proposed, not from any source.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Keep the B2B tabletop and small-business line as the base. T1.why_behaviour_changes: A parts department that searches shelves by hand loses time and stock visibility. Compact automated storage that condenses footprint and shows stock levels reduces wait times, which the company says leads to faster repairs and higher throughput.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex sells and services its own hardware and software to a segment reached through dealership groups or distributors, so it keeps the margin on hardware, installation and service without building a retail brand.
