X1.name: Small-operator versus household demand pilot
X1.method: Offer two compact, illustrative product descriptions (not a built product) to two groups: small service businesses with parts or tool counts (dealership parts counters, independent workshops, small healthcare or pharmacy back rooms) and households with high item counts (collectors, home offices). Each respondent sees a purchase price and a monthly rental price, and is asked for a refundable deposit or letter of intent. Track conversion and the stated reason for declining.
X1.sample: Proposed: 40 small-business contacts and 60 household contacts, recruited through trade associations, workshop networks and online collector groups. Analyst estimate, not company data.
X1.measure: Share of contacts who give a deposit or signed letter of intent at the stated price, split by purchase and rental option, and the stated reason for declining.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Small-business deposit or letter-of-intent rate is clearly higher than household rate, and small businesses mention time saved on parts or item retrieval as the reason to buy.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household rate is similar to or higher than the small-business rate on a rental basis, and rental is preferred to purchase; small-business rate is low because price, not use case, is the barrier.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 10% of small-business contacts give a deposit or letter of intent and this is at least twice the household rate, keep T1 and scope a small-footprint B2B variant. If household rental uptake is at least 5% and above small-business uptake, consider a rental model for households and revisit T2. If neither group reaches 5%, reject both and do not invest.

final.recommendation: Do not build a Nabtesco-branded consumer product now. Run the proposed clinic referral pilot (X1) for the existing Conpal home-use unit before any expansion. T1.claim: Nabtesco's advantage in welfare is the microprocessor-controlled knee, and its value reaches end users only through clinicians and reimbursement, so a consumer-facing sale would add little unless the product is sold through the clinical channel.
T1.who_benefits: Amputees and prosthetists who need a knee that adapts to walking speed; Nabtesco if prescribers and payers adopt its product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Prescribing clinicians choose components for fit and safety, and payers reimburse them. A patient's purchase decision is shaped by the prescription, not by brand preference.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Nabtesco sells the knee to orthotic and prosthetic fitters or manufacturers, earning component margin, while the end-user pays through the clinical and insurance route rather than a retail price.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumer robot makers choose joint suppliers on reliability and cost per unit. As unit volumes grow, they need suppliers who can meet volume and quality, and a proven reducer maker can offer that without the brand-building burden.

X1.method: Two-arm offer test over 12 weeks. Arm A: offer rehabilitation clinics and home-care providers a paid home-use trial or rental of a Conpal-style unit with a therapist support package, and measure signed letters of intent and paid pilot starts. Arm B: send a technical brief on precision reducer supply to consumer and service robot makers and measure requests for samples, quotes or meetings. Both arms are run only through Nabtesco's public contact channels and existing trade contacts, with no claim that the company has approved this.
X1.sample: Proposed: 30 rehabilitation clinics and home-care providers in one prefecture or market (Arm A); 40 consumer and service robot makers from public directories (Arm B). Estimated, not observed.
X1.measure: Arm A: number of clinics or providers giving a signed letter of intent or paying for a pilot start within 12 weeks. Arm B: number of robot makers requesting a sample, quote or technical meeting for reducers within 12 weeks.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A produces several signed intents or paid pilots, because clinics and home-care providers see value in extending therapy at home. Arm B produces few or no reducer requests, since T1 does not depend on component demand.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B produces multiple sample or quote requests from consumer robot makers, because they are buying components. Arm A produces few paid pilots, since home-use gait training is not the main route to value.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed: if at least 8 of 30 clinics or providers (about 27%) give signed intent or pay for a pilot, and Arm B yields fewer than 3 reducer requests, favour T1 and proceed to a costed pilot. If Arm B yields at least 5 requests and Arm A yields fewer than 4 signed intents, favour T2 and test reducer supply instead. Otherwise both stay uncertain and the investment is not justified.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer brand. Treat the compact professional-workshop tier as the only consumer-adjacent option worth testing, through existing Biesse dealers, with a service contract as the main offer. Run the proposed dealer and service-option pilot before committing any product development. Keep hobbyist and partner routes as a secondary probe.

frame.objective: Decide whether Biesse should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, and what evidence would justify the investment. The real aim is a profitable, defensible way to reach individual buyers, such as home makers, hobbyists or small craft workshops, without harming the core industrial franchise. A consumer brand for its own sake is not the goal.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked and its intentions are unknown. Search budget 8, 7 remaining. Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions.
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public and must be flagged as a gap. Do not assume Biesse already sells to consumers until verified.

Industrial channel (furniture, window and door, construction) is the core and must not be cannibalised. A consumer product needs safety certification, warranty, service and dealer support that a B2B firm may lack.
alternatives: No expansion: stay purely B2B with large industrial manufacturers
Product redesign: scale down an existing machine (compact CNC router or edgebander) for small workshops and professional craftspeople
Different route to existing buyers: sell through retail, online or partner channels to small shops and hobbyists without a new product
Different customer group: a dedicated consumer brand and product line for DIY or home fabricators

X1.name: Premium branded upgrade pre-order test in two-wheel and car enthusiast segments
X1.method: Run paid online traffic to a pre-order page for a Brembo-branded performance upgrade, in two market segments: car track-day enthusiasts and bicycle/e-bike riders. Show the same product at a premium price and at a discounted price, randomised, and compare pre-order rates. Use an unbranded comparator page offering a similar product as a control.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 20,000 targeted ad impressions per arm across two segments, in Germany and Italy, over 6 weeks (estimated).
X1.measure: Pre-order (deposit) conversion rate per 1,000 targeted visitors, and the share of buyers who choose the premium-priced branded version over the discounted or unbranded version.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Car enthusiasts convert on the premium Brembo-branded page at a rate close to or above the unbranded comparator, and the premium price holds with little discounting needed.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Conversion is low in both segments, especially bicycle buyers, and the premium version only sells when discounted; the branded premium does not hold.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed: keep T1 if the car-segment premium page converts at least 1.0 percent of targeted visitors and at least 70 percent of that rate on the unbranded comparator pricing, with buyers not needing a discount beyond 10 percent. Reject T1 if conversion is below 0.3 percent or the premium page needs more than 20 percent discount to sell. Bicycle results decide whether T2 holds in two-wheel retail.

final.recommendation: Do not build a new consumer proposition in two-wheel retail now. Brembo already sells a consumer upgrade kit for cars through its parts channel (company claim), so the open question is whether a branded premium holds for car enthusiasts. Run the proposed pre-order test (cost EUR 18,000 estimated, 8 weeks) on car enthusiasts before any wider investment. Do not commit to a new product line or channel until the test is run.
final.target_customer: Car track-day and performance-road enthusiasts who already modify their vehicles; bicycle and e-bike riders are a secondary, lower-priority segment.
final.value_proposition: A Brembo-badged braking upgrade sold direct or online, with the brand's racing and OEM credibility as the reason to pay a premium over generic kits. This is unproven and needs the test.
final.next_action: Run test X1 as proposed: premium versus discounted and unbranded pre-order pages in car and bicycle segments, Germany and Italy, 8 weeks. Before running it, confirm with Brembo's parts business how the existing GT kit sells today, since sales volume and channel terms are not public.
final.uncertainty: Brembo's consumer sales volumes, margins, channel contracts and OEM agreements are not public and I could not find them. Evidence used: SEMA (US general accessory market, not braking), Shimano and ZIV (bicycle market, not brakes), and one Brembo company claim about the GT kit. No source shows a brake-specific price premium or that direct sales would not damage OEM relationships. T1 and T2 are both still uncertain.

X1.name: Channel and price test for a branded upgrade kit (proposed, not run)
X1.method: Run a 10-week controlled listing test on Brembo's existing consumer channel and in 2 to 3 partner workshops in one European market. Offer the same UPGRADE-style kit at 2 price points (proposed: base and +15%) to randomised visitors on the direct site, and track sales through partner workshops at the same price points. Tests whether buyers respond more to brand-led direct marketing or to installer recommendation, and how price-sensitive they are.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 20000 unique visits to the direct product page over 10 weeks, plus 3 partner workshops with at least 150 owner enquiries combined. Estimated, not sourced.
X1.measure: Conversion rate per 100 visits by channel and price point; share of workshop enquiries that convert to an installed kit; repeat or replacement purchase within 6 months where data allows.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Direct conversion is meaningful at the premium price point and does not collapse by more than about 30% at +15%, because buyers pay for brand credibility; direct share of kit sales exceeds workshop share.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Workshop-sourced sales convert at a higher rate than direct visits, and most kit purchases come through installers; direct conversion is low regardless of brand.

X1.decision_rule: Favour T1 if direct conversion at the premium price is at least 60% of the base-price conversion and direct sales are at least half of total kit sales. Favour T2 if workshop conversion per enquiry is at least twice direct conversion per visit and workshops supply at least half of sales. If neither holds, conclude that consumer demand is too weak for a dedicated proposition and recommend no expansion beyond current aftermarket.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new differentiated consumer proposition yet. Brembo already reaches individual buyers through its own consumer-facing products (UPGRADE GT kit marketed to track-day enthusiasts on bremboparts.com, and the GR-PRO mountain-bike brake at about EUR 750). Test how that existing channel performs at premium prices before investing in a dedicated proposition. Keep the no-expansion option as the default if the test fails.
final.target_customer: Track-day and performance car enthusiasts, and mountain-bike or motorcycle enthusiasts who buy high-end upgrades, rather than mass-market owners.
final.value_proposition: Motorsport-proven braking performance and visual credibility under the Brembo name, sold as a premium upgrade.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 10-week channel and price test (X1, about EUR 20000, estimated) comparing direct sales with partner-workshop sales at two price points, and apply the decision rule.
final.uncertainty: I could not find sales volumes, retail-channel shares, margins or price elasticity for Brembo's consumer products; these are probably not public. The evidence on buyer willingness to pay is thin: one independent review of one mountain-bike kit that called the price hard to justify. The SEMA source is a US survey about accessories in general and does not bear on brakes or installer channels. T2 (workshop-led channel) has no direct evidence either way. Only one challenge search was used and it found nothing new against T1.

arguments.name: Branded vs unbranded performance kit and wear-signal pilot
arguments.method: Online stated-preference and click test with enthusiast owners. Show the same performance brake kit in two arms: branded Brembo versus unbranded equivalent, each at a price point. Measure add-to-basket and intent. Separately, a workshop pilot where owners receive either a standard service reminder or a clear wear indicator with an easy-fit kit option, and measure how many book brake work within 6 weeks.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 600 enthusiast owners (mountain-bike and sport-motorcycle forums and track-day lists) for the online arm, and about 200 owners across 4 partner workshops for the pilot. Sample sizes are estimates, not drawn from any source.
arguments.measure: Online arm: add-to-basket rate and stated purchase intent by arm and price. Workshop arm: share of owners booking brake work within 6 weeks, by reminder type.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The branded arm converts at or above the unbranded arm at a price premium of at least 15 percent, showing a brand premium holds for enthusiast buyers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Owners who receive the clear wear indicator book brake work at a higher rate than owners who get the standard reminder.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: keep T1 only if the branded arm keeps at least 90 percent of unbranded add-to-basket at a 15 percent price premium. Keep T2 only if the wear-indicator arm books at least 10 percentage points more than the standard reminder arm. If either fails, revise that theory and do not build a consumer kit on it.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a new differentiated consumer proposition yet. arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Brake modifications carry safety and legal risk, so buyers defer to a trusted fitter. The fitter's endorsement, not the brand alone, converts interest into purchase, and the fitter decides which brand to specify.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Brembo sells kits or components to specialist installers and tuners under trade terms, earning margin on volume without carrying consumer warranty, fitment support or liability exposure.

arguments.name: Direct versus installer-routed price test for a track-day brake kit
arguments.method: Run a 10-week controlled online test in two EU markets (proposed: Germany and Italy). Show the same Brembo track-day kit at three price points (proposed: list, list plus 10 percent, list minus 10 percent) on the existing consumer parts channel, and on a partner-installer booking page where the fitter recommends the kit. Randomise visitors to variants. Track add-to-basket, completed purchase and returns or fitment queries.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 3000 unique visitors per arm, with at least 1500 car owners who visited track-day or performance-car content. Sample size is an estimate and should be confirmed against the traffic available.
arguments.measure: Conversion rate to purchase by channel and price point; share of buyers who reach checkout via installer recommendation; returns and fitment-query rate per 100 orders; price elasticity between variants.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Direct channel converts at the list price at least as well as at lower prices, because buyers pay for performance identity; direct conversion exceeds installer-route conversion for the same kit; returns and fitment queries are low.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Installer-recommended variant converts well above direct variant at every price; direct-channel conversion falls sharply without the fitter's endorsement; fitment queries and returns are higher in the direct channel.

arguments.decision_rule: Favour T1 if direct-channel conversion at list price is within 20 percent of the installer-route conversion and fitment queries are under 5 per 100 orders. Favour T2 if installer-route conversion is at least 1.5 times direct conversion at list price, or direct fitment queries exceed 10 per 100 orders. Otherwise treat both as unresolved and do not invest beyond the test.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a new consumer business yet. Brembo already sells track-day kits to individuals through its own parts website, so the question is whether to deepen that existing channel. Run the proposed price and channel test before committing investment. Treat the premium-pricing claim as unproven.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Keep the core B2B model and treat the Com4recycling licence as the only evidenced route beyond machine sales, but only pursue it further if the proposed Phase 1 test shows a verified mill-level premium. Treat the hobby-spinner route (T2) as unsupported by the evidence read so far.

frame.objective: Decide whether Rieter should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case beyond its B2B spinning-mill business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The real question is whether value can be captured from individual buyers, or from a reachable consumer-adjacent segment, at a margin and risk that beat Rieter's core mill-customer model.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; the company has not been contacted and its intentions are unknown
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; flag gaps rather than fill them
Search budget of 8 (7 remaining); test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions
Core customers are industrial spinning mills (3,000+), a B2B capital-equipment and after-sales business
Must check whether Rieter already sells to individual buyers rather than assume it does
Barmag acquisition (Feb 2026) changes the portfolio and may shift attention and capital
alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the B2B machinery, components and after-sales model; invest in core efficiency or Barmag integration
B. Product redesign for a specific end use: adapt spinning technology or yarn outputs for a niche consumer-facing use, still sold to mills
C. Different route to buyers: brand-to-consumer channel (co-branded yarn or fabric made on Rieter-spun output), capturing value downstream of the mill
D. Different customer group: sell equipment, retrofit or service to small-scale, artisan or craft spinners, or micro-mills in emerging markets
E. Consumer-adjacent data or service: yarn-quality monitoring or traceability services sold to mills or to brands
F. Partnership or licensing: license a spinning process to a consumer-brand or textile partner rather than building a consumer offer in-house

T1.claim: Consumers pay a premium for verified recycled or traceable yarn in garments. Rieter can capture part of that premium by licensing its Com4 recycled-yarn process to mills, so the value reaches Rieter through licence and machine sales rather than through selling to consumers directly.
T1.who_benefits: Brands and retailers that sell labelled recycled garments; spinning mills that can charge more; Rieter, which earns licence income and machine demand from mills that must use its cards, draw frames and end-spinning machines.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A verifiable label (GRS certification plus a licence) lets a brand show recycled content, so the consumer's willingness to pay for a traceable sustainability claim is passed back up the chain to the mill that needs the premium to justify the certification cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter charges a licence for the Com4recycling process and sells the machines that the licence requires, so it earns on each licensed mill's output rather than on the consumer's purchase.
assumptions: Mills can pass the recycled-yarn premium to brands
Rieter's licence terms are not tied to measurable volume that is already public
Recycled-content labels drive purchases among a meaningful share of consumers
Mills that buy the process would not switch to a cheaper non-Rieter certified route
predictions: Licensed mill count and machine orders for recycling-capable equipment rise where brands publish recycled-content targets
Premium pricing of recycled yarn over virgin yarn is observable in brand or mill price lists
Mills without a Rieter licence who sell recycled yarn show a lower price premium or no licence-linked label
T1.first_claim: Consumers pay a premium for verified recycled or traceable yarn in garments. Rieter can capture part of that premium by licensing its Com4 recycled-yarn process to mills, so the value reaches Rieter through licence and machine sales rather than through selling to consumers directly.

T2.claim: Hobby and craft spinners buy small-scale spinning equipment for personal use when they move from buying yarn to making it. Rieter could capture value by selling a scaled-down or retrofit product to that group, which sits outside its mill-customer model.
T2.who_benefits: Individual craft and hobby spinners who want to produce their own yarn; a manufacturer that sells a small machine or kit to them at a margin that its industrial line cannot reach.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in handcraft, shown by the large share of recent crafters in the US survey, creates a population that wants control over fibre and yarn. Once a hobby becomes sustained, buying equipment is a rational next step, so demand for equipment follows the growth in craft participation.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells equipment or consumables direct to individual buyers or through craft retailers, earning a unit margin and possibly recurring consumable sales.
assumptions: The craft-yarn growth observed in the US is large enough to support a sustained equipment market
Craft spinners would buy equipment rather than rely on hand tools or second-hand machines
Rieter can build or source a small machine at a cost that allows a viable retail price
The buyers reached are not already served by existing hobby-spinning makers
predictions: Hobby spinning equipment sales grow where craft yarn purchases grow
Craft spinners who buy a wheel or spinner also buy consumables (fibre, bobbins) repeatedly
Price points that can be sold through craft retail are far below Rieter's industrial machine prices, so the product must be a different design, not a scaled copy
T2.first_claim: Hobby and craft spinners buy small-scale spinning equipment for personal use when they move from buying yarn to making it. Rieter could capture value by selling a scaled-down or retrofit product to that group, which sits outside its mill-customer model.

assessments.quote: To apply for a license, spinning mills must produce their recycled yarn on a Rieter card, draw frame and end-spinning machine. In addition, a Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certification is required.
assessments.does_not_show: This shows only that the licence is tied to Rieter machines and GRS certification. It does not show licence fees, how many mills hold a licence, the price premium for recycled yarn, or any consumer willingness to pay. It is Rieter's own description of its product terms, so it cannot prove the value capture is real.

assessments.quote: Two out of five crafters in the paid sample, representing approximately 50% of the respondents, say they started crocheting within the last two years.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a US survey of crocheters from a craft trade body, about crochet and not spinning. It says nothing about buying spinning equipment, the size of the spinning-hobby market, or whether those who started crocheting would buy a machine. It is a sample of paid respondents, so it cannot establish a market size.

X1.name: Two-route demand and value check: licence premium vs small-scale equipment intent
X1.method: Phase 1 (weeks 1-5): structured interviews with recycled-yarn mills and brand buyers to find whether the Com4 licence and GRS certification carry a price premium that reaches the mill. Phase 2 (weeks 4-10): a pre-order and waitlist test for a small spinning unit or kit, offered via craft and fibre-arts retailers and online hobby communities, with a refundable deposit, to measure paid intent among hobby spinners. Both phases are external; no Rieter product is built.
X1.sample: Proposed: 15 to 20 mill or brand buyers in recycled-yarn supply (Phase 1); 300 to 500 hobby-spinning or fibre-arts consumers reached through 3 to 5 partner retailers or communities (Phase 2). Sample sizes are analyst estimates.
X1.measure: Phase 1: share of buyers reporting a verified price premium for licensed recycled yarn over virgin yarn, and the premium size. Phase 2: refundable deposit conversion rate for a small spinning unit at a proposed price point, and repeat consumable purchase intent.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Phase 1 finds a clear, reported premium for certified recycled yarn passed up to mills, and mills say the Rieter licence is needed to claim it. Phase 2 deposit conversion is low, because hobby spinners are not the value route.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Phase 1 finds little premium reaching the mill for certified recycled yarn. Phase 2 deposit conversion among hobby spinners is meaningfully above a baseline, and respondents say they would buy consumables repeatedly.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: proceed with a licence-led (T1) investigation only if at least 60% of Phase 1 mills report a premium of 5% or more that they can attribute to certified recycled content. Consider a consumer route (T2) only if Phase 2 deposit conversion is at least 5% of visitors reached and at least 30% of depositors state repeat consumable intent. If neither threshold is met, do not invest further in consumer products; keep the B2B model.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer-facing proposition now. Keep the B2B model. The only evidenced route beyond machine sales is the Com4recycling licence, which ties mills to Rieter cards, draw frames and end-spinning machines plus GRS certification. Pursue it further only if the proposed Phase 1 mill test shows a verified premium. The hobby-spinner route is not supported by the evidence read so far.
final.target_customer: Core: spinning mills (existing B2B). Possible later option: recycled-yarn mills selling to brands. Hobby spinners are a hypothesis only, not a target.
final.value_proposition: For mills that want to sell certified recycled yarn: Rieter's process and machines are the licensed route to the Com4recycling label. Value to Rieter comes through licence and machine sales to mills, not from consumers directly. No consumer product is recommended.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 10-week Phase 1 interviews with 15 to 20 recycled-yarn mills and brand buyers, to test whether a verified premium for certified recycled yarn reaches the mill. Do not start Phase 2 consumer pre-orders until Phase 1 is read. Ask for Rieter's own licence and sales data, since none is public.
final.uncertainty: Major. No public data found on Rieter's licence fees, licensed mill count or licence revenue. The Com4 source is a company claim. No independent evidence of a consumer premium reaching the mill. The craft survey is about US crochet, not spinning equipment. The Maine source concerns wool mini-mills, not Rieter products. I did not establish whether Rieter sells to individual buyers; searches were limited (8). Rieter's 2025 sales fell 20% to CHF 685.1m, which may limit appetite for new ventures (an inference).
would_change_if: Phase 1 shows at least 60% of mills reporting a premium of 5% or more attributable to certified recycled content
Rieter's own licence or sales data show material, growing licence income
Evidence that Rieter already sells to individual buyers
Independent evidence of sustained consumer demand for recycled-content yarn at mill level
Phase 2 deposit conversion of at least 5% among hobby spinners with 30% or more repeat intent (would support T2, currently rated unlikely)

recommendation.detail: 4 sources, 5 conditions that would change it

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. The evidence I could find does not show consumer demand for spinning equipment, and the best-supported driver of Rieter's machine sales is still mill-side: certification and licence rules, technology and after-sales service. Keep the investment in the industrial channel. If management wants to test the consumer idea, run a low-cost pilot first (the proposed test X1) and treat it as an option, not a plan.

frame.objective: Decide whether Rieter should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its industrial spinning-mill business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Real objective: test whether individual or small-scale buyers (hobbyists, small makers, artisan yarn producers, niche textile users) represent a reachable, profitable demand for a Rieter product or service, rather than assuming they do.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions. Rieter's contractual, customer-level and margin detail may not be public, so state gaps rather than fill them.
Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; search budget is 8 searches, so evidence must be chosen carefully.
The 3,000+ industrial mill customer base is the core business; any consumer move must not put it at risk or divert capital from it.
The Barmag acquisition (Feb 2026) changes the group's scope and may absorb management attention and capital.
Rieter's products are large capital equipment; a consumer proposition would need a different price point, channel and service model.
alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the focus on industrial spinning-mill systems, components and after-sales services; monitor adjacent demand only.
B. Product redesign for existing industrial customers: a smaller or modular spinning/winding unit for mid-size or new-entrant mills, sold through the current B2B channel.
C. Different route to existing buyers: sell spare parts, digital monitoring or aftermarket services directly or through distributors to smaller mills and textile workshops.
D. Different customer group in the same value chain: small textile makers, artisan yarn producers, fibre-processing start-ups or education/research users, with compact machines or kits.
E. Consumer or direct-to-hobbyist proposition: a spinning or yarn-making product or service sold to individuals, the case the question names.

F. Adjacent-market move (not suggested by the question): use Barmag man-made fibre or fibre-preparation know-how for non-spinning uses such as nonwovens or technical textiles; or licensing know-how to third-party makers of small-scale equipment.

T1.claim: Hobby and craft makers are a growing buyer group that would pay a premium for compact, make-your-own yarn equipment or kits, so a differentiated consumer product could earn value Rieter's industrial channel does not reach.
T1.who_benefits: Hobby crafters and small yarn makers who want to produce their own yarn; Rieter, if it can sell a product through craft retail or online channels.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Craft participation is rising (recent crochet starters are common in US craft surveys), and crafters increasingly value made-by-hand or custom yarn, which raises willingness to pay for tools that let them make yarn.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells a compact spinning unit or kit through a consumer or craft channel at a price far above its industrial machines' unit price per output, or licenses its spinning know-how to a consumer brand.
assumptions: Craft participation growth translates into interest in spinning, not just knitting or crochet with bought yarn.
Crafters will pay a price that covers Rieter's engineering, certification and distribution costs.
Rieter can reach consumers without damaging its B2B relationships with mills.
Safety, support and warranty costs for consumer machines are manageable for a company selling large capital equipment.
predictions: A consumer-priced compact spinning unit shown to hobby crafters in a 12-week test will show a conversion rate that clears a set threshold in paid pre-orders.
Consumers who buy the kit will spin only occasionally, so repeat purchases of fibre or consumables are the real test of value, not the first sale.
Interest will be higher among people who already spin (drop-spindle or wheel users) than among general crocheters.
T1.first_claim: Hobby and craft makers are a growing buyer group that would pay a premium for compact, make-your-own yarn equipment or kits, so a differentiated consumer product could earn value Rieter's industrial channel does not reach.

T2.claim: Spinning-mill purchases are driven by compliance and certification lock-in, not by product price. Rieter's value comes from being the certified machine supplier that mills must use to produce recycled or certified yarn, so value is captured from mills, and a consumer product would not share that pull.
T2.who_benefits: Spinning mills that need recycled or certified yarn (for example GRS-certified yarn) and must run approved machinery to get the licence; Rieter, which holds the machine and licensing position.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Brands and retailers demand certified recycled content, so mills buy machines that meet the licence requirements. The purchase decision is driven by the licence, not by the unit price of the machine.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells machines to mills and earns licence-linked machine and component sales, plus after-sales service, from mills that need the certified process.
assumptions: The licence rule (machine must be a Rieter card, draw frame and end-spinning machine, plus GRS certification) is still in force and applies to most recycled-yarn mills.
Demand for certified recycled yarn is growing faster than the number of mills that can meet the rule.
Mills will not switch to non-Rieter machinery to avoid the cost premium of certification.
predictions: Mills that have not yet applied for the Com4recycling licence will show lower machine-purchase intent than mills that already hold GRS certification.
A consumer product offering would show no reduction in the mill-level lock-in, meaning industrial sales stay the main value source regardless of consumer demand.
Mills' willingness to pay for Rieter machines will track the size of certified recycled-yarn contracts, not the number of individual buyers.
T2.first_claim: Spinning-mill purchases are driven by compliance and certification lock-in, not by product price. Rieter's value comes from being the certified machine supplier that mills must use to produce recycled or certified yarn, so value is captured from mills, and a consumer product would not share that pull.

assessments.quote: Two out of five crafters in the paid sample, representing approximately 50% of the respondents, say they started crocheting within the last two years.
assessments.does_not_show: It is a US survey from 2022-23 of crochet and craft buyers. It does not show interest in spinning yarn, willingness to pay for spinning equipment, or any demand for a Rieter product. It supports only the premise that craft participation is growing, and only for crochet, not for making yarn from fibre.

assessments.quote: To apply for a license, spinning mills must produce their recycled yarn on a Rieter card, draw frame and end-spinning machine. In addition, a Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certification is required.
assessments.does_not_show: This is Rieter's own web page, so it states the licence rule but not how many mills hold it, what it earns Rieter, whether mills buy Rieter machines mainly for it, or how strictly the rule is enforced. The date is unknown. It does not show that compliance rather than price drives purchases.

assessments.quote: The world market for staple fiber machines relevant to Rieter has an annual volume of CHF 2 200 million to CHF 4 000 million. Rieter is the market leader with a share of about 30 percent.
assessments.does_not_show: This is Rieter's own investor-relations claim, with no date. It shows that about 70 percent of the market is held by other suppliers, so most mill purchases are not made under the Com4recycling licence rule. That weakens the claim that licence lock-in is the main driver of machine purchases. It does not show what drives those other purchases (price, service, technology), nor the split of licence-linked volume.

X1.name: Consumer pre-order and mill purchase-driver test
X1.method: Two parallel low-cost probes over 12 weeks. (a) A landing page describing a compact, consumer-priced spinning unit and kit, shown to hobby spinners and craft buyers through targeted online ads and craft forums, with a refundable deposit option and a waitlist. (b) Structured interviews with spinning mills that already hold or are applying for GRS certification, asking what triggered their last machine decision: licence or certification rules versus price, service and technology.
X1.sample: (a) Proposed: about 2,000 qualified ad-page visitors who self-identify as spinners or fibre makers, with about 8 weeks of paid traffic. (b) Proposed: 20 mills, half holding Com4recycling-style certification and half not, reached through trade contacts and industry associations.
X1.measure: (a) Deposit or waitlist conversion rate among visitors who identify as active spinners, and separately among crochet or knit buyers with no spinning experience. (b) Share of mills that name the certification or licence rule as the primary reason for their last machine purchase, versus price, service or technology.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Little deposit conversion among consumers (below 1%), and mills naming certification or licence rules as the main purchase trigger, so industrial lock-in, not consumers, drives value.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer product now. The public sources I read show no sales to individual buyers: the webshop is for spinning mills, and the calculator is a free company tool with no sales data. The only consumer-side signal, the 2023 Craft Yarn Council survey, is about crochet, not spinning. The licence route is a mill-side mechanism that fits the existing business. Run the proposed test before any consumer spend, and examine the licence route further.

frame.objective: Decide whether Rieter should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its industrial spinning-mill business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The real objective is to find out whether individual buyers (for example hobby, craft, small-batch or home-textile users) would pay enough, through a channel Rieter can reach, to justify the investment without damaging its core mill relationships.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions are known; direct reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established by search.
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public and must be reported as not found.
Test budget of EUR 20,000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; search budget is limited (7 searches left).
Industrial spinning machinery is capital-intensive and sold to mills in long cycles; a consumer product must not distort the core business or its service model.
Barmag acquisition (February 2026) adds man-made fibre equipment and may change the scope of options.
Only claims observed in sources I have read may be presented as facts; proposed numbers must be labelled as proposed or estimated.
alternatives: No expansion (including exit of the consumer idea): keep the industrial mill focus and deepen after-sales, components and digital services for existing mill customers.
Product redesign for a niche consumer use case: a small-scale or desktop spinning/winding unit sold to craft, hobby or small-batch yarn makers.
Different route to buyers: sell existing or lightly modified equipment or components through a third-party channel or online marketplace to small mills and independent yarn producers.
Different customer group: target small independent spinners, artisan yarn producers, or textile education and maker-space markets rather than individual consumers.
Adjacent play: license spinning know-how or yarn-quality sensor/software to small textile makers or brands, not a consumer machine.
Partner or licensing: co-develop and distribute a product with a consumer maker-equipment firm, keeping Rieter out of consumer marketing.

T1.claim: Individual craft makers who are newly taking up yarn-based hobbies would pay a premium for a compact, easy-to-use spinning or winding unit sold as a hobby product, so Rieter could earn consumer margins by designing for that use case.
T1.who_benefits: Hobby and craft makers who want to make their own yarn; Rieter, if it captures margin on a consumer-grade product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Craft participation is growing, and crafters who move from using yarn to making it want tools suited to home and small-scale use rather than industrial machines.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter designs and sells a small consumer unit, with accessories, direct or through craft retailers, at a price well above the cost of industrial components.
assumptions: Craft growth in the survey extends from crochet to yarn production.
Hobby spinners would buy a dedicated machine at a price Rieter can sustain.
Rieter can design a small unit without distorting its industrial business.
predictions: A demand test will show a measurable share of craft respondents willing to pay for a home spinning unit.
Buyers will prefer a compact unit with clear instructions over a scaled-down industrial machine.
Conversion will be low if the unit is priced near industrial equipment.

X1.name: Consumer deposit and mill-licence interest test
X1.method: Two-arm demand test over 12 weeks. Arm A: a landing page describing a compact home spinning unit for craft spinners, with a refundable EUR 50 deposit for priority waitlist, plus short interviews. Arm B: a short offer to spinning mills and recycled-yarn brands describing the Com4recycling licence route (Rieter machines plus GRS certification), with an expression-of-interest form and a call with a Rieter-side contact or a neutral intermediary. Traffic from craft-spinning communities and trade contacts. The product is described honestly as a concept; no product is taken money for beyond the refundable deposit.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 400 qualified craft-spinning visitors (people who say they spin or weave) for Arm A, and about 30 mills or brands contacted for Arm B.
X1.measure: Arm A: share of qualified visitors who place a refundable deposit. Arm B: number of mills or brands who request a licence call or submit an expression of interest, and whether any mention an existing Rieter machine fleet.

prediction_by_theory.T1: A meaningful share of craft spinners place deposits, roughly 3% or more of qualified visitors, and interview answers name a price and use case for a compact unit.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Deposits stay low, below 1%, while mills and brands show interest in the licence route, and most inquiries come from firms already running Rieter machines.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a consumer prototype study only if Arm A shows at least 3% deposit conversion among at least 400 qualified visitors and at least 5 interviews name a use case and price. If Arm A falls below 1%, drop the consumer idea and treat the licence route (Arm B) as the lead lead. Between 1% and 3%, do not invest further without a second round.

T1.claim: Homeowners who buy waterproofing and sealing products fail mainly at application, not at chemistry. A simplified, pre-mixed product with step-by-step guidance sold at retail would let Sika charge a premium for certainty of result, which its existing contractor-grade products cannot deliver to untrained buyers.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and DIY buyers who want a fix that works first time; Sika, which would capture a price premium on a product designed for them.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who have failed at a repair (leaking bathroom seal, roof patch) avoid repeat purchases and pay more for a product that reduces the risk of a second failure. Application guidance removes the skill barrier that currently pushes them to a professional or to giving up.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika sets a price above commodity DIY sealants by bundling a pre-measured or single-application format with guidance, and retains margin by owning the formulation rather than the retail shelf.

X1.name: Guided-format vs standard-format direct test, UK, 10 weeks
X1.method: Two-arm online test on a landing page with paid search and a partner-free direct checkout. Arm A offers a simplified, single-application guided kit at a premium price. Arm B offers the standard sealant at the existing consumer price. Both arms ask a short questionnaire on any previous failed home repair and what the buyer believes caused it. No retailer listing is used, so that channel effect (T2) is held out of this test and can be checked separately. All figures below are proposed, not observed.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors per arm drawn from paid search on homeowner leak and sealing terms, in the UK (the market where Sika already owns a merchant-channel consumer brand). Estimated size, not a sample from any source.
X1.measure: Primary: checkout conversion per visitor for each arm, and the price point at which the guided kit still converts. Secondary: share of respondents who report a prior failed repair, and the share who attribute that failure to application rather than product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Guided kit converts at or above the standard product at a premium of at least 25 percent (proposed threshold), and most prior failures are attributed to application error, not product failure.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Both arms convert at very low rates regardless of format or price, because without a retailer listing the homeowner does not see the product at the point of need, so format and price make little difference.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed: if the guided kit converts at 2 percent or more of visitors and at least 1.5 times the standard arm's rate, with at least 25 percent premium accepted, T1 is kept and a format pilot is justified. If both arms convert below 0.5 percent, T2 is favoured and the next step is a partner or retailer listing test, not a product build. Anything between these results is inconclusive and the test is extended, not decided.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer-branded product build yet. Sika already reaches homeowners indirectly: Sakrete is marketed to homeowners in Canada, and Everbuild, bought in 2013, was a UK merchant-channel brand. Bostik runs a retailer-served consumer range of over 2,000 products. The decision therefore turns on channel access to the homeowner, not on whether a consumer market exists. Run a low-cost direct-channel test first. Build a guided or simplified format only if the channel test shows homeowners will buy it at a premium.
final.target_customer: Homeowners who buy sealing and waterproofing products for their own repairs, initially in the UK, where Sika already owns a merchant-channel consumer brand. Not yet validated: no source describes these buyers' behaviour.
final.value_proposition: Not yet defined with evidence. The working hypothesis is a product that delivers a reliable first-time repair, but this is untested. Channel access is the prior question.
final.next_action: Run a 10-week, UK, direct-to-consumer test (proposed budget about 15000 EUR, within the 20000 EUR assumption) comparing a guided kit with a standard product, plus a separate check of retailer or merchant listing options. Decision rule as proposed in X1: keep T1 if the guided kit converts at 2 percent or more with a 25 percent premium accepted; if both arms convert below 0.5 percent, treat T2 as favoured and move to a partner or listing test.
final.uncertainty: Large. Four sources were read: two are company claims or company-hosted pages (Sakrete, Bostik), one is trade press on a 2013 deal, and one is a challenge search that returned only the same sources. None gives sales volumes, margins, consumer failure causes, retailer terms or online channel data. Sika's non-public contractual and financial detail was not available. X1.name: Pro-grade shelf range versus installed bundle, one UK-style retail market
X1.method: Proposed: a 10-week controlled listing test in 20 stores of one retail partner, comparing three arms: (a) an existing Pro Select-style sealant range with pro-grade claims on shelf, (b) the same range with a plain-claim shelf label, and (c) an online booking offer for a certified-applicator installed sealing job, priced against the product alone. Measure sell-through per store per week and bundle bookings.
X1.sample: Proposed: 20 stores (about 10 per arm pair) and an online traffic sample of about 2,000 homeowner sessions over 10 weeks
X1.measure: Units sold per store per week for arm (a) vs (b); number of installed-job bookings per 1,000 sessions in arm (c); return and complaint rate per 1,000 units

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm (a) sells more units per store per week than arm (b), by a clear margin, and the pro-grade label, not price, explains the gap
prediction_by_theory.T2: Installed-job bookings per 1,000 sessions are high enough to matter, and the product-only arms do not match the booking value per homeowner

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: continue with T1 (retail pro-grade line) if arm (a) sells at least 15% more units per store per week than arm (b) with no rise in complaints. Pursue T2 (installed bundle) if bookings reach at least 3 per 1,000 sessions and complaint rate in the bundle arm stays flat. Otherwise stop: neither route shows enough demand.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a separate consumer brand for a specific use case now. Sika already sells some products to homeowners through retail in some markets (US Pro Select, Canada DIY pages), so the cheapest next step is to test whether that existing pro-grade range sells better with a pro-grade claim, and whether a certified-applicator installed option attracts bookings. Run the proposed X1 test (about 18,000 EUR, 10 weeks, proposed figures) before any larger spend.
final.target_customer: Homeowners buying sealants, adhesives or patchers at retail who want contractor-grade performance (T1), and homeowners with a high-risk job who would pay for a certified installed application rather than a DIY product (T2). Neither segment is sized in the evidence.

position.recommendation: Do not build a new consumer brand or direct-to-consumer channel yet. Sika already sells consumer-labelled products through retail partners in North America (Pro Select in the US, Sakrete in Canada) and previously owned a UK sealant business with trade and merchant reach (Everbuild). The cheapest next step is a retail pack and labelling pilot on existing formulations in one market where a retail partner already exists, with a warranty arm to separate the pack effect from the warranty effect. Scale only if the test shows a clear sell-through and price premium.

frame.objective: Decide whether Sika AG should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case (for example DIY or homeowner sealing, waterproofing or repair) beyond its contractor, distributor and industrial channels, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions
Some financial and contractual detail (channel margins, distributor agreements, retail sell-through) may not be public
Test budget assumed at EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit; these are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget is 8 searches (7 remaining), so evidence gathering must be targeted
Must find out how far Sika already reaches individual buyers before assuming it does not
alternatives: No expansion: remain contractor, distributor and industrial focused
Homeowner/DIY proposition through existing retail and hardware channels, using existing products in homeowner-friendly packaging
Product redesign for a specific use case (for example ready-to-use repair or waterproofing kits) sold through existing distributors
Direct-to-consumer or online channel for a niche use case
Partnership or licensing with a consumer brand or retailer instead of an in-house consumer brand
Pro-sumer segment: serve skilled renovators and small trades who buy at retail, or adjacent customers such as vehicle aftermarket

T1.claim: Sika can extend its existing products to homeowners mainly through the retail channels it already uses in North America, because homeowners buy simple sealing and patching products at hardware retail when the packaging and brand signal trade-grade performance without requiring a professional applicator.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners who want a trusted trade-grade product for small repairs; hardware retailers that gain a premium SKU; Sika, which earns retail margin on existing formulations with little redesign.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners who face a small leak, crack or gap but do not hire a contractor for it choose the product on the shelf. A brand that says 'pro quality' and gives clear instructions shifts their choice from generic products to the premium one.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika sells existing formulations, repackaged and labelled for retail, through partners such as Sakrete in Canada and Pro Select in the US. Value is captured as a retail price premium over generic products, at a retailer margin, with limited new R&D.
assumptions: Homeowners buy small-job sealants and patchers at hardware retail and notice brand and packaging
Retail margin and shelf space are available on acceptable terms
Existing formulations need little change for retail use
Sika's retail partners already carry the products in the target markets
predictions: Pro-select SKUs sell through in hardware retail at a price premium over comparable generic products
Sales growth comes from small-job SKUs, not from full roofing or flooring systems
Retail sell-through rises after in-store instructions and pack-size changes
Growth is concentrated in markets where Sika already has a retail partner
T1.first_claim: Sika can extend its existing products to homeowners mainly through the retail channels it already uses in North America, because homeowners buy simple sealing and patching products at hardware retail when the packaging and brand signal trade-grade performance without requiring a professional applicator.

T2.claim: Homeowners will not buy high-performance Sika systems for consequential jobs such as roofing or waterproofing unless the purchase comes with a guarantee of correct application, so value is captured by bundling applicator training, certification or a warranty with the product rather than by lowering the product's price or changing its packaging.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who fear a failed repair costing more than the job, and the small trades or certified applicators who can deliver the work; Sika, which captures value by selling the warranted system and the training.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A homeowner who sees that a failed repair would cost far more than a professional visit will pay for certainty. A warranty backed by a trained applicator removes that risk, so the buyer chooses the system over a cheap generic repair.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika earns a premium on the system and the warranty, and may take a fee or share of revenue from a certified-applicator network or from the product sold through a installer-led channel. Training and certification build a moat that generic products cannot copy quickly.
assumptions: The main barrier for homeowners is fear of failed application rather than product price
A warranty or certified applicator changes the buyer's decision
Enough certified applicators exist or can be recruited in target areas
Sika's own annual report shows its specialised systems are kept away from DIY because of risk, which is consistent with this barrier
predictions: Homeowners buying a warranted system convert at a higher rate than those buying the same product without a warranty
Installer-led sales rise when a visible certification or warranty is offered
Claims and callbacks fall when applicators are trained
The premium is paid for the warranty, not the product's chemistry

X1.name: Retail pack and warranty pilot in one existing retail market
X1.method: Pick one market where Sika already has a retail partner (for example a Sakrete or Pro Select listing). Place existing product in three variants across matched stores: (A) current pack, (B) pack with clearer homeowner instructions and a 'pro quality' label, (C) pack with instructions plus a visible warranty or certified-applicator finder offer. Rotate store assignments to control for location, and record sell-through per store per week.
X1.sample: About 30 matched stores, 10 per arm (proposed), with the same product set, for 8 weeks after a 2-week set-up (proposed).
X1.measure: Units sold per store per week, price realised per unit against a generic comparator in the same aisle, and conversion of shoppers buying the small-job SKU (estimated from store till data where available).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm B sells more than Arm A at a price premium over the generic comparator, because pack and labelling signal trade grade. Arm C adds little over Arm B, since the warranty is not what drives choice.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm C sells clearly more than Arms A and B and holds its price premium, because buyers pay for the warranty or applicator assurance, not the pack. Arm B gains little over Arm A.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if Arm C beats Arm B by at least 15 percent in units per store-week and holds at least a 10 percent price premium over the generic comparator, favour T2 and scope a warranty-backed offer. If Arm B beats Arm A by at least 15 percent with no meaningful gap to Arm C, favour T1 and scope a retail pack extension. If neither arm beats A by 15 percent, reject both and do not invest beyond the pilot.

revisions.reason: The new result is SIMULATED and concerns warehouse packing errors from a label printer. It measures no buyers, shelves or prices, so it bears on neither T1 nor T2 and changes nothing. I do not cite it. T1 stays kept on the real sources only (retail DIY listings, the market growth figure and the Everbuild acquisition), and remains unproven until the retail pilot is run.

The simulated result SYN-D concerns warehouse packing errors and says nothing about warranties, applicator assurance or buyer behaviour, so it does not bear on T2 and changes nothing. T2 stays kept but untested. Its only real support is Sika's own statement that specialised systems are not sold for DIY because of performance and safety risk. Nothing found shows homeowners would pay for a warranty or certified applicator, so T2 remains uncertain until the warranty arm of the pilot runs.

Supposing SYN-D were real: it reports a slight drop in warehouse packing errors from a label printer and measures nothing about wearers, buyers, shelves or prices. Taken at face value it would bear on warehouse operations, not on whether homeowners buy Sika products at a premium, so it changes nothing for T1. It is SIMULATED and is recorded here only for the update step. It is excluded from the finish evidence.

final.recommendation: Do not build a new consumer brand, direct-to-consumer channel or homeowner product line yet. Sika already reaches individual buyers in some markets through retail partners: Pro Select in the US and Sakrete in Canada. The open question is whether that retail presence can be extended into a differentiated homeowner proposition. The cheapest test is a retail pack and labelling pilot on existing formulations in one market with a retail partner, with a warranty arm to separate pack effect from warranty effect. Scale only if the pilot shows clear sell-through and price premium.
final.target_customer: Homeowners doing small sealing, patching and waterproofing repairs who buy at hardware retail and do not hire a contractor. Roofing and flooring are not the target, since Sika's annual report keeps those away from general retail.
final.value_proposition: Trade-grade performance on existing products, in homeowner-friendly packaging with clear instructions, sold at a retail price premium over generic repair products. A warranty or applicator-finder offer is tested as a second layer, not assumed.
final.next_action: Run the retail pack and warranty pilot (X1) in one existing retail market: three store arms, about 30 matched stores, 8 weeks after a 2-week set-up, EUR 20,000 and 12 weeks (all proposed). Proposed threshold: 15 percent unit lift and 10 percent price premium over the generic comparator. Before the pilot, request Sika's retail sell-through and margin data for Pro Select and Sakrete, which are not public.
final.uncertainty: Evidence is almost all company marketing or corporate statements. No public sell-through, shelf-share, price-premium or margin data was found. Everbuild acquisition (2013) concerns the trade merchant channel. Market growth figure covers overall home improvement, not sealants or Sika's consumer lines. Nothing contradicts T1; nothing confirms homeowners pay a premium. T2 is untested. SYN-D (simulated, packing errors) was not used as evidence.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product build yet. Favour the collection-service route (T1), since the only sourced evidence points to bulk and convenience collection as an established complement that operators and retailers buy. Test it first with a matched-store pilot before any investment. Treat the home-appliance idea (T2) as unlikely on current evidence, because the only sourced evidence on it is a different company's analogy.

frame.objective: Decide whether TOMRA should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case (beyond its B2B reverse vending and sensor sorting business), and identify what evidence would justify that investment, starting from how far it already reaches individual buyers.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with company and no knowledge of its intentions
Financial and contractual detail (customer contracts, margins, consumer-facing revenue) may be non-public and must be flagged as unknown
Test budget assumed at 20000 EUR and 12-week limit (analyst assumptions, not company figures)
Search budget limited to 8 searches (7 remaining); tool use must be economical
No simulated results may be cited as evidence
alternatives: No expansion: keep B2B focus on deposit return, retailer, recycling, mining and food sorting customers
Consumer-facing product redesign: adapt existing reverse vending or sorting hardware into a smaller consumer-friendly device for a specific use case (e.g., home or office recycling)
Different route to buyers: sell through existing retailer or deposit-system channels to reach consumers indirectly, or via subscription/service model
Different customer group: target a non-consumer segment not yet served (e.g., food processors or mining) rather than individuals
Partnership or licensing: supply sensing/sorting technology to consumer brands or appliance makers rather than selling direct
Targeted consumer use case inside existing deposit systems: improve the consumer experience (e.g., app, loyalty, refunds) to lift return rates, monetised through operators

T1.claim: Consumers return deposit containers more when collection is convenient (bulk bag drop or nearby automated return), so a consumer collection service raises return rates and is paid for by deposit system operators and retailers rather than by consumers.
T1.who_benefits: Deposit system operators and retailers, who need higher return rates to meet targets and reduce unredeemed deposits; consumers with bulk volumes or limited time.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Returning containers is a chore. Consumers with large volumes, or who lack a nearby machine, skip returns. A bag drop removes sorting and queueing, so more containers come back.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA earns machine, service and handling fees from operators and retailers under contract, not from consumer purchases. Consumer-facing revenue would be small or zero.
assumptions: Return rates are limited mainly by convenience rather than by deposit value
Operators will pay for collection services that lift return rates
Bag drop is already an established service in North America, per company claim
predictions: Regions with bag drop or extra collection points show higher return rates than comparable regions without them
Operators renew or expand contracts that include collection services
Consumer willingness to pay directly for the service is low
T1.first_claim: Consumers return deposit containers more when collection is convenient (bulk bag drop or nearby automated return), so a consumer collection service raises return rates and is paid for by deposit system operators and retailers rather than by consumers.

T2.claim: Households buy a home sorting or composting appliance when it solves a daily nuisance (smell, storage, separating food waste), so a consumer device sold directly to households could earn a premium price, provided it is demonstrated in the home.
T2.who_benefits: Households with food waste or recycling storage problems, and retailers wanting a differentiated appliance category.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A visible, daily problem makes a device worth paying for. Buyers need to see and try it, because the category is unfamiliar and the price is high.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA would sell hardware direct or through retail, earning margin per unit plus consumables or service. This requires a consumer brand, distribution and after-sales support that TOMRA does not currently run for households.
assumptions: Households will pay a premium for a solved daily nuisance
Demonstration in store or at home is needed to close the sale, as the Lomi case suggests
Sorting or composting hardware can be shrunk and made affordable for homes
predictions: Demo-led trials convert to purchases at a rate that supports a viable unit margin
Sales concentrate in households with high food waste volumes or storage problems
Price sensitivity is high above a few hundred euros
T2.first_claim: Households buy a home sorting or composting appliance when it solves a daily nuisance (smell, storage, separating food waste), so a consumer device sold directly to households could earn a premium price, provided it is demonstrated in the home.

assessments.quote: Bag drop is a convenient collection method whereby consumers can drop off entire bags of empty beverage containers at collection points and have their deposit refunded. It is a well-established and popular complement to reverse vending machines and redemption centers in North America, with strong growth potential.
assessments.does_not_show: It is the company's own description, so it does not show that bag drop raises return rates, that operators pay for it, or how large the fees are. It does not give volumes, prices or contract terms, and it covers North America only.

assessments.quote: None of these are cheap, especially for a fairly new product category like smart composters, which is probably why Lomi felt the need to start sending demo teams into markets in California and Washington to show people what these products are all about.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a different company's composter, not a TOMRA product, so it shows nothing about TOMRA's costs, margins or sales. It does not show that households will pay a premium, nor the conversion rate of demonstrations. It is a 2023 US news item with no sales data.

X1.name: Matched-store bag-drop pilot
X1.method: Partner with one retailer or deposit operator in one region (no company contact has occurred, so this is a proposal). Place a bag-drop collection point in about 12 treatment stores and match them to 12 control stores on size, footfall and existing machine uptime. Run for 12 weeks, measuring containers returned per store per week. Separately, run a 2-week in-store demonstration of a home sorting unit at 3 stores to record demo-to-purchase conversion (proposed sample, estimated).
X1.sample: 24 stores (12 treatment, 12 control), plus 3 demo stores (proposed, not from any source)
X1.measure: Weekly containers returned per store, change against matched controls, bag-drop volume, machine downtime logged; for the demo arm, conversion of visitors to purchase intent

prediction_by_theory.T1: Treatment stores return measurably more containers than matched controls, and the gain holds after adjusting for machine uptime, so the bottleneck is convenience.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Demo visitors convert to purchases at a rate that supports a unit margin; without demos, sales are near zero.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a commercial pilot for T1 only if treatment stores show at least 10% more containers returned than control over 12 weeks, and the gap is larger than the control stores' week-to-week variation. Reject T1 if the gap is below 5% or disappears when machine downtime is controlled. For T2, proceed only if demo conversion is at least 5% of visitors (estimated threshold); otherwise reject.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer product yet. Investigate the collection-service route (T1) with a low-cost matched-store pilot. Do not invest in a household sorting or composting appliance (T2) on current evidence. TOMRA's consumer-facing reach is unknown from public sources; it appears to reach individuals only indirectly, through deposit systems and retailers.
final.target_customer: Deposit system operators and retailers (B2B2C), with bulk-volume and time-poor households as end users of a collection service. Not direct household consumers for now.
final.value_proposition: A convenient bulk or bag-drop collection option that raises container return rates, paid for by operators or retailers through machine, service and handling fees.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 12-week matched-store bag-drop pilot (about 18,000 EUR, estimated) with a willing partner in one region. Check whether treatment stores return at least 10% more containers than matched controls after controlling for machine uptime.
final.uncertainty: Commercial detail is unknown: consumer revenue, contract terms, margins, fee levels, and European bag-drop return effects. The only bag-drop evidence is a TOMRA press release about North America. The RTÉ report shows reliability and supplier switching can limit returns, a rival cause. The appliance evidence is from another company. Only 3 sources read.
would_change_if: Pilot shows no return gain over matched controls once machine uptime is controlled, rejecting T1
Operators or retailers will not pay separately for collection services
Evidence that TOMRA already sells bag-drop or household collection in Europe at scale
Independent data showing households buy home sorting appliances at a viable price and margin, promoting T2

assessments.quote: With no retailer obligation in the New South Wales’ DRS, TOMRA saw value in a consumer app that could instead offer digital payout of refunds, and a map to show recyclers where to return their containers.

It does suggest the retailer, not a collection contractor, captures the footfall value, which weakens the claim that a paid collection service is the main route.

X1.name: Digital-redemption and collection-point pilot in one deposit market
X1.method: Pilot in one city or region with an existing deposit scheme. Randomise a set of comparable retail or community sites into three arms: (a) machine only, (b) machine plus app with digital payout and map, (c) machine plus a bag-drop collection point run by a paying partner. Track returns per site and per household panel.
X1.sample: Proposed: 30 sites, about 10 per arm, plus a household panel of about 300 registered app users across arms, over 12 weeks.
X1.measure: Containers returned per site per week; share of returns by bag drop; number of households returning more than once; operator or brand willingness to pay, tested with a signed pilot fee.

prediction_by_theory.T1: App arm shows the largest rise in returns over machine-only; bag drop shows little extra volume once the app is present; a paying operator agrees to fund the app.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Bag-drop arm shows the largest rise in returns and the highest volume per site; paying partner (retailer or brand) agrees to fund bag-drop; app adds little.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a commercial offer only if the winning arm lifts returns by at least 15 percent over machine-only and a paying party signs a pilot fee covering at least 50 percent of pilot cost. If neither arm reaches 15 percent, or no party pays, do not invest in a consumer proposition and keep the B2B focus.

result.title: Simulated parking-heater installation offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters.
