position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Nothing read shows that Gühring sells to individual buyers at all: its public channel is a B2B procurement shop, and its customer base is described as automotive, aerospace and mechanical engineering. Neither the home-workshop segment (Tormach blog, a vendor's own marketing) nor the Heller rebranding tests whether hobbyists pay for industrial origin. Before any redesign or new channel spend, run the low-cost listing test X1 and invest only if it clears its threshold.

frame.objective: Determine whether Gühring's precision metal-cutting know-how could support a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific individual-buyer use case (for example hobbyist or home-workshop machinists) that is worth investing in, compared with remaining a B2B industrial toolmaker. Establish whether Gühring already sells to individual buyers, and identify what evidence would justify the investment.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked this question and nothing here describes its intentions
Search budget of 8 searches (7 remaining); test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state what could not be found
Theories are hypotheses, not recommendations about what the company should do
Observed numbers must come from sources read; proposed numbers must be labelled as proposed or estimated
alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B precision tool maker for automotive, aerospace, mechanical engineering and medical customers
Product redesign: adapt existing precision tools into a simpler or lower-cost variant for the same industrial customers such as job shops and SMEs
Different route to buyers: sell existing tools to individual buyers through online retail or distributors, with no new product
Different customer group: a hobbyist or home-workshop segment with a dedicated proposition
Service or training proposition: tooling advice, machining courses or content that builds demand for the existing range
Partnership or licensing: supply a consumer-facing machine-tool or kit brand that owns the buyer relationship

T1.claim: Gühring's industrial quality reputation can act as a quality signal that hobbyist machinists pay a premium for, so a simplified precision range sold through online retail to home-workshop users could earn margin without the sales cost of B2B.
T1.who_benefits: Gühring, if it owns the online buyer relationship and sells a branded precision range; hobbyist machinists who want industrial-grade tools.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists who buy cheap tools often face breakage and poor finish. They look for a trusted brand signal and will pay more when the brand is credibly industrial and the product is easy to choose.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Price premium on a branded, simplified range sold direct or through a retailer, with margin higher than the industrial OEM price after accounting for the small-order channel cost.
assumptions: Hobbyists recognise and value the Gühring brand or industrial origin
Hobbyists will pay a premium of at least 20 percent over generic tools (proposed threshold)
Retail and fulfilment costs for small orders can be covered by the premium
predictions: A listing of a simplified range on a consumer marketplace would sell at a price above comparable generic tools
Repeat purchase among hobbyists would be higher for branded than for unbranded tools
Hobbyist buyers would cite quality or industrial origin as their reason to choose the brand in reviews or surveys
T1.first_claim: Gühring's industrial quality reputation can act as a quality signal that hobbyist machinists pay a premium for, so a simplified precision range sold through online retail to home-workshop users could earn margin without the sales cost of B2B.

T2.claim: Individual buyers of precision cutting tools choose mainly on price and availability, so an industrial toolmaker's brand adds little, and a consumer range would be a low-margin, high-service business that leaves the core B2B value chain where it is.
T2.who_benefits: Online retailers and generic tool brands that already own the hobbyist channel and price-sensitive buyers.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists buy infrequently, compare prices across marketplaces and treat cutting tools as commodity consumables, so they do not reward a manufacturer's industrial reputation with a premium.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Gühring would capture value only through B2B volume; a consumer range would carry marketing, returns and small-order costs that erode margin, so the manufacturer gains little from entering this segment.
assumptions: Hobbyist purchase decisions are driven mainly by price and delivery time
Gühring's brand does not transfer to individual buyers without heavy marketing spend
Small-order handling costs exceed the premium achievable
predictions: Hobbyist buyers would switch to a cheaper generic tool when price differences of about 20 percent appear (proposed)
A consumer listing would show high return or support rates per euro of revenue compared with B2B
Surveys would rank price above brand origin as the purchase reason
T2.first_claim: Individual buyers of precision cutting tools choose mainly on price and availability, so an industrial toolmaker's brand adds little, and a consumer range would be a low-margin, high-service business that leaves the core B2B value chain where it is.

assessments.quote: With a PunchOut interface, the Gühring online shop and your ERP system merge: you place the desired products in the shopping basket in our shop and transfer the relevant product data to your procurement system
assessments.does_not_show: Whether any individual buyer uses the shop, what the consumer demand or price sensitivity is, or whether hobbyists would pay a premium. It shows the online channel is built for business procurement systems, which is consistent with the core route staying B2B, but it does not test T2's causal claim about hobbyist behaviour.

assessments.quote: customers from the automotive industry, aerospace, and mechanical engineering rely on its leading-edge tool, which is manufactured worldwide to the highest quality standards
assessments.does_not_show: Any hobbyist or home-workshop buyer, any premium that individual buyers pay for an industrial origin, or any consumer brand recognition. assessments.quote: Most of our customers are hobbyists working from home or small workshops tight on space but in need of a reliable, affordable CNC mill.
assessments.does_not_show: Any premium that hobbyists pay for industrial origin, or how they choose cutting tools. It shows a home-workshop segment exists and uses demanding materials, which is a precondition for T1, but it says nothing about tool brand choice or price sensitivity, so it is neutral on both T1 and T2.

It shows a tool maker choosing a professional-brand position rather than a consumer one, which is consistent with T2 but does not test it.

X1.name: Hobbyist brand-premium listing test
X1.method: List an identical small range of drills and end mills on a consumer marketplace under two conditions: a plain-label version and a version carrying the industrial origin statement. Compare conversion, price realised and repeat purchase. Use only tools and dimensions the company already makes, with no product redesign.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 2,000 site visitors per arm from home-workshop search terms, and about 300 orders in total (estimated)
X1.measure: Conversion rate per arm; average realised price relative to the generic benchmark; share of buyers who return within 90 days (proposed measures)

prediction_by_theory.T1: The industrial-origin arm converts at a higher rate and realises at least 20 percent more than the plain-label arm, with repeat purchase higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Conversion and realised price do not differ between arms by more than 5 percent; buyers choose on price and delivery time.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a further test only if the origin arm shows at least a 20 percent price premium and at least a 15 percent higher conversion rate at 95 percent confidence (proposed threshold). Otherwise treat T2 as the better-supported explanation and do not invest in a consumer range.

The SIMULATED printer-nozzle test is not real data and I do not cite it. Its bearing is on T1's quality-signal idea more than on T2. tool_result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer business now. Treat the consumer proposition as an open question worth a small, reversible test (proposed X1, about 15,000 EUR over 12 weeks) before any product redesign or channel investment. Keep the industrial and semi-professional B2B focus as the default. The evidence so far shows that some hobbyists know and rate Gühring quality, but it does not show that they will pay a premium or buy repeatedly.

frame.objective: Decide whether Gühring KG should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its industrial precision rotary cutting tools, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The objective is to find out whether individual buyers represent a real, reachable and profitable value pool for Gühring, not to assume it does.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions.
Financial and contractual detail (margins, distributor agreements, channel economics, customer contracts) may not be public and must be flagged as unknown.
Search budget of 8 searches (7 remaining) and a 20,000 EUR test budget over at most 12 weeks, both analyst assumptions, not company figures.

Gühring's core business is B2B for automotive, aerospace, mechanical engineering and medical technology, across production sites in 48 countries; any consumer move must not damage its industrial reputation or channel relationships.
Family-owned, owner-managed in the fourth generation: decisions may weigh long-term stability and brand over short-term revenue.
Any consumer proposition must be credible against precision-tool quality expectations and reachable through channels Gühring can actually operate.
alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the industrial focus and do not invest in individual buyers.

B. Existing products through existing or retail channels to individual buyers: check whether Gühring already sells to hobbyists, workshops or retailers, and whether that can be served better without redesign.
C. Product redesign for a specific use case, or a different customer group such as semi-professional job shops, vocational training or repair workshops, with simpler specification and packaging.
D. Different route to buyers: distributor, marketplace or online partnerships reaching individual buyers without changing the product.

E. Non-tool offering: knowledge products (machining guides, tool-selection tools, training) or licensing the brand or technology to consumer toolmakers, capturing value without building a consumer channel.
F. Monitor only: track whether consumer demand emerges (e.g. e-commerce signals or inbound requests) before committing budget.

T1.claim: Hobbyists who know a precision brand's quality may buy a use-case kit more readily if reassurance (guidance, a simple guarantee) is added, but whether they will pay a premium over hobby brands is unknown and is the question a test must answer.
T1.who_benefits: Home-workshop and hobby metal machinists who want industrial-grade reliability without paying for professional procurement; Gühring, which would earn a price premium on a brand known for precision.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Forum and review culture shows hobbyists are divided on quality and rely on recommended brands (Proxxon, Alpen, S&R are named as popular). A recognised precision name with a clear use-case range reduces the uncertainty that makes them stay with familiar budget brands.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Gühring sells a branded, simplified range at a premium through retail or marketplace partners, using its existing manufacturing and brand, with the consumer range priced above hobby brands.
assumptions: Hobbyists would pay a premium for a recognised precision brand when quality is explained.
Retail or marketplace listings can be reached without damaging industrial channel relationships.
Gühring's brand is not already known to hobbyists, so a consumer range would create new awareness.
The product does not need heavy redesign beyond packaging, specification and guidance.
predictions: In a small retail or marketplace test, a branded use-case range shows higher conversion at a premium price than unbranded equivalents from the same channel.
Buyers who review the range cite quality and reassurance, not price, as the main reason to buy.
Repeat purchase rate is measurable within 12 weeks, which would show value beyond one-off purchase.
T1.first_claim: Hobbyist and home-workshop buyers judge metal drills mainly on brand trust and price, not on precision. A precision-industrial brand can earn a premium with this group only if it lowers the perceived risk of buying (clear use-case range, simple guidance, reliable retail availability), so a packaged, differentiated range sold through retail or marketplaces would capture value that the industrial product alone cannot.

T2.claim: Individual buyers rarely buy precision metal-cutting tools often enough to make a consumer proposition pay. Hobbyists use drills occasionally, buy on price, and replace tools infrequently, so the demand that would justify a premium consumer range is thin and fragmented. Gühring's value sits with B2B customers and semi-professional buyers already reached through its online shop and distributors, and entering retail would add cost and channel conflict without enough return.
T2.who_benefits: Gühring, which keeps its focus, avoids channel conflict with distributors and industrial customers, and protects its brand from being diluted in a low-frequency consumer market.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists have low use frequency and price sensitivity, so a premium brand gains little extra purchase volume. Those who need precision tools regularly already buy through professional or semi-professional channels, where Gühring's existing reach is sufficient.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Gühring keeps capturing value through its existing industrial and semi-professional channels, selling premium products to business customers rather than building a consumer brand.
assumptions: Hobbyist purchase frequency for precision metal drills is low, so lifetime value per consumer is small.
Price sensitivity among hobbyists is high enough that a premium consumer range would not sell at scale.
Consumer retail entry would strain distributor and industrial customer relationships.
Semi-professional buyers already find Gühring through its existing online shop and distributors.
predictions: A consumer test shows low repeat purchase and low volume per buyer, well below what B2B accounts generate per euro of marketing.
Hobbyist reviews emphasise price and familiar brands rather than precision specifications.
Distributors or industrial customers react negatively to a retail listing or consumer range.
T2.first_claim: Individual buyers rarely buy precision metal-cutting tools often enough to make a consumer proposition pay. Hobbyists use drills occasionally, buy on price, and replace tools infrequently, so the demand that would justify a premium consumer range is thin and fragmented. Gühring's value sits with B2B customers and semi-professional buyers already reached through its online shop and distributors, and entering retail would add cost and channel conflict without enough return.

X1.name: Use-case kit price test in a home-workshop channel

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers judge drill quality on durability and sharpness, and a visible industrial reputation signals that quality. Forum posts show hobbyists already disagree about brand quality, which means they are searching for a trusted reference.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Direct online sales of a smaller, lower-priced range, using the existing online shop and product know-how, so Gühring keeps the retail margin rather than passing it to a retailer.

T1.first_claim: Hobby and small-workshop machinists would pay a premium for professional-grade metal cutting tools if they were sold in a simplified range under a recognised industrial brand, so Gühring could earn margin by selling directly to them.

T2.claim: Hobbyists buy metal drills on shelf price and familiarity, not on tool quality, so a manufacturer without consumer brand awareness cannot earn a premium through individual buyers, and retailers capture most of the value.
T2.who_benefits: Retailers and established consumer brands such as Proxxon, Alpen and S&R, which already hold shelf space and trust with hobbyists.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists buy rarely, have limited technical knowledge, and choose from familiar brands in store or in a shop listing. Forum disagreement about brand quality suggests they lack a reliable quality signal, so they fall back on familiarity and price.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Retail distribution and brand familiarity: the shop or consumer brand owns the customer relationship and sets the price, so a manufacturer selling to individuals would need heavy marketing spend that the margin does not cover.

X1.name: Premium hobby drill-set price test via online pre-order
X1.method: Offer a small, clearly labelled premium drill set (proposed: HSS-Co cobalt metal drills, 10 sizes) on a landing page, using paid search and maker-forum ads, at a proposed price 40% above a comparable mid-range consumer brand. Run a parallel arm that shows the same product with and without the Gühring name, plus a control listing of an established consumer brand at the same price point. Measure click-through, pre-order conversion and stated reasons. Gate sales on a refundable deposit.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 6,000 unique visitors across the test arms over 4 weeks, drawn from German-speaking hobby and DIY audiences, with an estimated 1 to 2 percent interest rate.
X1.measure: Pre-order conversion rate per arm; share of buyers who cite quality versus price or brand familiarity in a one-question exit survey; click-through rate per arm.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium pricing converts at a reasonable rate, and the Gühring-named arm converts at least as well as the unnamed arm, because the industrial reputation works as a quality signal.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Conversion is driven by familiarity: the consumer-brand control converts clearly better than the Gühring-named premium arm, and buyers cite brand or price more than quality.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a larger test only if the Gühring-named arm reaches at least 2 percent pre-order conversion and matches or beats the unnamed arm (T1 supported). Abandon consumer expansion if the named arm converts below 0.5 percent or the consumer-brand control converts at least 2x the named arm (T2 supported).

revisions.reason: The simulated SYN-GUEHRING-UPDATE is not real evidence and I do not cite it. Taken as a what-if, a durability guarantee on a 3D-printer nozzle tests a different mechanism from a manufacturer's brand premium on metal drills, so it changes nothing for T1. T1 stays as stated: the premium and brand-signal mechanisms remain untested, and the real forum observation is still neutral on Gühring specifically.

The simulated SYN-GUEHRING-UPDATE is not real evidence and I do not cite it. Taken as a what-if, a durability guarantee on a 3D-printer nozzle would not show whether brand familiarity beats quality for metal drills, so it does not change T2. T2 remains likely on the real evidence: consumer brands are named as popular, Gühring is not mentioned, and I found no consumer channel. Its main weakness is that it rests on one indirect observation.

Taken only as a what-if, SYN-GUEHRING-UPDATE would show that a written durability guarantee changed purchase choice for 3D-printer nozzle buyers. If it were real, it would hint that assurances can shift hobbyist choice, which is compatible with T1's trust-signal mechanism. It does not test a manufacturer brand premium on metal drills, and it is simulated, so it changes my belief about T1 by nothing. T1 is kept as an untested hypothesis, and I do not cite the result in the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The public evidence shows Gühring as an industrial, B2B-only supplier. I found no consumer product line or consumer channel. The one consumer-facing source is a hobby retail page that names other brands as popular and does not mention Gühring. The hardware-store origin is company history, not current consumer reach. Before any investment, run a small, gated premium pre-order test to see whether brand familiarity or quality drives hobbyist purchase.
final.target_customer: Hobbyist and small-workshop metal machinists in German-speaking markets. This is a hypothesis only and has not been validated.
final.value_proposition: A small, clearly labelled premium drill set that uses Gühring's industrial reputation as a quality signal. Unproven: it holds only if quality, not brand familiarity, drives purchase.
final.next_action: Run the premium pre-order test X1 as proposed (estimated EUR 12,000, 6 weeks). Fix its decision threshold before seeing results. Also check whether any distributor or retailer already sells Gühring tools to individuals, since public sources did not show it.
final.uncertainty: High. I could not find Gühring's sales split by customer type, distributor volumes, retail presence or financials; these may not be public. Evidence on hobbyist behaviour is one retail page that does not mention Gühring. The test has not been run. The simulated printer-nozzle result is not evidence and is excluded from this conclusion.

arguments.name: Premium hobby drill-set price test via online pre-order
arguments.method: Offer a small, clearly labelled premium drill set (proposed: HSS-Co cobalt metal drills, 10 sizes) on a landing page, using paid search and maker-forum ads, at a proposed price 40% above a comparable mid-range consumer brand. Run a parallel arm that shows the same product with and without the Gühring name, plus a control listing of an established consumer brand at the same price point. Measure click-through, pre-order conversion and stated reasons. Gate sales on a refundable deposit.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 6,000 unique visitors across the test arms over 4 weeks, drawn from German-speaking hobby and DIY audiences, with an estimated 1 to 2 percent interest rate.
arguments.measure: Pre-order conversion rate per arm; share of buyers who cite quality versus price or brand familiarity in a one-question exit survey; click-through rate per arm.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium pricing converts at a reasonable rate, and the Gühring-named arm converts at least as well as the unnamed arm, because the industrial reputation works as a quality signal.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Conversion is driven by familiarity: the consumer-brand control converts clearly better than the Gühring-named premium arm, and buyers cite brand or price more than quality.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed to a larger test only if the Gühring-named arm reaches at least 2 percent pre-order conversion and matches or beats the unnamed arm (T1 supported). Abandon consumer expansion if the named arm converts below 0.5 percent or the consumer-brand control converts at least 2x the named arm (T2 supported).

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Gühring's public record shows B2B and distributor reach and no consumer line; the only consumer-facing evidence is a hobby forum-style retail page naming other brands. Before any investment, run the small premium pre-order test (X1) to see whether brand or quality drives hobbyist purchase.

result.title: Simulated printer-nozzle durability offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not launch a new consumer appliance. Treat the question as a small-producer segment question: test whether a compact machine with a bundled service contract converts small craft brewers and small venues at a premium, before any consumer-facing build-out. Keep consumables and service (T2) as the fallback if the machine arm fails. Keep no-expansion as the default if neither arm clears the threshold.

frame.objective: Determine whether Krones AG should invest in a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, beyond its B2B filling, packaging and process-technology lines, and what evidence would justify that investment. The real objective is the highest-value way for a machine maker to capture value from end consumers or small buyers, not a consumer product for its own sake.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with Krones and no knowledge of its intentions
Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining; evidence is read-only
Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; gaps must be stated
Company sells about 90 percent abroad and serves beverage and liquid-food producers plus adjacent industries on a B2B machine model
Existing consumer reach must be verified, not assumed
alternatives: A. No expansion: stay a pure B2B machine and line supplier and improve service within the current model
B. Product redesign: a smaller prosumer or small-venue machine sold through existing B2B channels
C. Different route to buyers: direct-to-consumer, retail or subscription consumables (capsules, kegs, cleaning or refill services) linked to machines
D. Different customer group: microbreweries, cafes or hospitality venues as a new mid-size segment
E. Platform or licensing: license brewing, filling or process know-how or the Steinecker brand to consumer-brand partners for royalties
F. Aftermarket and digital services sold to existing customers: spare parts, cleaning chemicals, remote monitoring subscriptions

T1.claim: Small craft brewers and small-venue operators will pay a premium for compact, easy-to-run filling or brewing equipment that a large machine maker can build with its existing engineering, so a smaller product line can be sold profitably to a segment that big-machine buyers ignore.
T1.who_benefits: Krones (new revenue from a segment it already serves in part), and small brewers who lack access to scaled, service-backed equipment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Small producers cannot justify large fillers and depend on flexibility and service; a compact machine with reliable support lowers their entry cost and risk, so they buy from a known supplier rather than improvised or second-hand equipment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Machine sales at a higher margin per unit than bulk lines, plus spare parts and service contracts over the machine's life.
assumptions: Small producers want and can afford a machine priced well above used equipment but well below a Krones line
Krones's existing product range already covers a sub-250 bottles-per-minute tier
Demand is large enough in target markets to justify a dedicated sales channel
predictions: Enquiries or orders for compact machines rise when the offer includes service and financing terms
Small buyers choose a compact machine over used equipment at a stated price premium
Margin on compact units is higher than on large lines once service is included
T1.first_claim: Small craft brewers and small-venue operators will pay a premium for compact, easy-to-run filling or brewing equipment that a large machine maker can build with its existing engineering, so a smaller product line can be sold profitably to a segment that big-machine buyers ignore.

T2.claim: Consumables and service tied to installed machines, not the machines themselves, are where a machine maker can capture recurring value, so a consumer-facing consumables or subscription model linked to its equipment would earn more than selling a new consumer appliance.
T2.who_benefits: Krones (recurring revenue from installed base) and small or home producers who get reliable supply and cleaning or refill services without buying a full machine.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Once a machine is installed, operators prefer buying matched consumables and service from the same supplier to avoid compatibility and warranty risk, so switching cost and convenience keep them on the platform.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Recurring sales of parts, cleaning chemicals, refill or capsule consumables, and monitoring subscriptions over the installed base's life.
assumptions: Krones already has an installed base in the target segment that can be reached
Customers accept proprietary consumables if they are priced below alternatives
Aftermarket margins exceed the margin on new machine sales
predictions: Aftermarket revenue per installed unit grows over time for compact-class customers
Customers with service contracts renew at higher rates than those without
A consumables-only offer attracts buyers who would not buy a machine outright

assessments.does_not_show: Shows only that a small-scale filler tier was offered in 2010 in the United States, as reported by trade press. It does not show demand, price premium, margins or whether the product is still sold, so it cannot confirm the predictions of T1.

assessments.quote: Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.
assessments.does_not_show: The press release says nothing about consumables, spare parts, service contracts or installed-base revenue, so it neither supports nor contradicts T2. It is a company claim of profitability with no figures, and it does not show the aftermarket share of sales.

assessments.quote: Thanks to the major success of the compact can filler, Krones has now also developed a dedicated filler for the low output range for glass applications: the Craftmate G.
assessments.does_not_show: This is Krones's own claim of success with no sales volumes, prices, customer count or margin. It shows the company has built a second small-output product, not that small buyers pay a premium or that the segment is profitable. Challenge search found no source that contradicts T1, but it also found only company claims.

X1.name: Compact-machine versus consumables-only offer to small brewers
X1.method: Two-arm landing-page and sales-call test in one or two regions. Arm A offers a compact filler or brewing unit with a service contract at a stated price. Arm B offers only cleaning chemicals, spare parts and refill consumables on a subscription, with no machine. Both arms are offered to the same pool of small brewers and venues, with a deposit or letter of intent as the measured action. Labels and sample sizes are proposed estimates.
X1.sample: Proposed: 150 to 200 small brewers and small hospitality venues identified from public craft-brewery directories in one region, split randomly between the two arms.
X1.measure: Share of contacted prospects who pay a refundable deposit or sign a letter of intent within 6 weeks, and the average stated price accepted for each arm.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A converts at a meaningful rate and accepts a price above a used-equipment benchmark, with service bundled, so the compact machine is the value driver.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B converts at least as well as Arm A, and buyers reject a machine purchase but accept consumables, so the installed-base consumable model is the value driver.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if Arm A deposit or letter-of-intent rate is at least 10 percent and at least 1.5 times Arm B's rate, keep T1 and pursue a compact product line. If Arm B rate is at least 10 percent and at least Arm A's rate, keep T2 and pursue consumables or service first. If both are below 5 percent, reject both as a consumer-facing offer and stop.

revisions.reason: No real new evidence arrived. The simulated result is not counted, since it is not real data. As a what-if it would suggest that reducing the cleaning burden changes choice among small brewers, which is consistent with T1's claim that small buyers value ease of running and service. It does not test price premium, market size or profitability, so T1 stays uncertain until the real two-arm test runs.

SYN-KRONES-UPDATE is SIMULATED and not real data, so it does not change my belief. As a what-if, a cleaning-service feature that changes choice among small buyers would be consistent with T2's idea that recurring cleaning and service can drive value. It says nothing about consumables revenue, installed-base size or price, so T2 stays uncertain. The recommendation does not change.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer-facing appliance or direct-to-consumer channel on current evidence. Krones already sells small-output B2B equipment to craft brewers (Craftmate filling units, MicroCube brewing systems, and a Compact Class business it calls profitable and growing). The open question is whether a compact machine bundled with service earns a premium from small producers. Test that first with a small, cheap experiment. Keep no-expansion as the default if the test fails.
final.target_customer: Small craft breweries and small hospitality venues that need compact filling or brewing equipment, not private consumers.
final.value_proposition: A compact filler or brewing unit with service and maintenance bundled, sold through Krones's existing B2B and trade-fair channels. Consumables and service are the fallback if the machine offer does not convert.
final.next_action: Run the proposed two-arm test X1 (about EUR 18,000 over 10 weeks; proposed, not yet run): compact machine with service versus a consumables-only subscription, measured by refundable deposits or letters of intent among 150 to 200 small brewers and venues in one region. Pursue a compact product line if the machine arm reaches at least 10 percent and at least 1.5 times the consumables arm. Pursue consumables or service first if consumables reach at least 10 percent and at least the machine arm. Stop if both fall below 5 percent.
final.uncertainty: High. I did not verify whether Krones already sells consumables or service to individual buyers; the sources read say nothing on aftermarket revenue. The sources are company press releases and a 2010 trade-press report, with no sales volumes, prices, margins or customer counts. Financial and contractual detail is not public in what I could find. The only simulated result is excluded from evidence. Both theories are rated uncertain.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

T1 stays as the working hypothesis, still uncertain, pending the real two-arm test.

It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. frame.objective: Decide whether Krones AG should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, beyond its B2B filling, packaging and process-technology lines, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Judge by whether individual buyers would pay for it and whether Krones can capture that value without damaging its core B2B business.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions
Company's direct reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be established from sources, not assumed

alternatives: No expansion: keep the current B2B line-equipment model and do not pursue consumer-facing offers
Product redesign: a smaller or modular machine for a specific use case, sold through the existing B2B channel
Different route to buyers: a direct-to-consumer or prosumer offer (e.g. home or craft brewing equipment sold online or via retail)
Different customer group: a focused B2B segment such as craft or microbreweries or small-scale producers, using existing technology
Service or aftermarket layer: consumables, data or maintenance subscriptions sold to existing B2B customers, with no consumer product

T1.claim: Individual buyers will pay a premium for fresh, home-made beer from a machine that handles brewing end to end, so a consumer product built on Krones' automation know-how can earn premium margins through recurring capsule or consumable sales.
T1.who_benefits: Households who want fresh craft beer without brewing skill, and the manufacturer that owns the machine and the consumable supply.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Convenience and novelty: the machine removes the skill and time of brewing, and a sealed capsule system makes each batch predictable. Buyers accept a high up-front price because the result is fresh beer they could not otherwise get at home.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Krones sells the appliance at a premium and earns repeat revenue from proprietary capsules or ingredient sets, which only its machine can use.
assumptions: Enough households will pay a premium for the appliance and then keep buying capsules
Capsule lock-in can be maintained against third-party ingredient makers
Krones can sell direct or through retail to consumers, which is not yet shown
The appliance can be made and supported at consumer prices using Krones' industrial design capability
predictions: Pre-orders or waitlist sign-ups at a premium price point (for example above 2000 EUR) will show repeat-purchase intent among a defined buyer panel
Capsule repeat purchase rate of at least 2 refills per owner in 6 months would indicate recurring revenue
A consumer price test will show demand falls sharply when the appliance price rises above a threshold
T1.first_claim: Individual buyers will pay a premium for fresh, home-made beer from a machine that handles brewing end to end, so a consumer product built on Krones' automation know-how can earn premium margins through recurring capsule or consumable sales.

T2.claim: Individual home-brewing is a stepping stone: hobbyists who graduate to small commercial brewing (caterers, micro-breweries) buy equipment that scales up, so value sits in the upgrade path to small B2B customers rather than in consumer hardware sales.
T2.who_benefits: Hobbyists turning into small commercial producers, and the equipment maker that supplies the next step up.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who want to sell beer need equipment that does not have to be replaced when volume grows. A brand that offers a home unit and a compatible small-batch commercial system keeps the customer through the transition.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Krones earns revenue from the commercial small-batch systems (Compact Class, MicroCube-type lines) sold to graduates, and the consumer unit is a low-margin entry point, not the profit source.
assumptions: A meaningful share of home brewers want to sell commercially
Upgrade decisions are driven by equipment compatibility and scale, not only by brand
Krones' small-scale business can serve buyers this small and at this price
predictions: Surveys or sales data show that a material share of home-equipment buyers later buy or plan to buy commercial equipment
Customers of small-batch commercial brewing systems have a home-brewing history at above-average rates
The B2B small-scale segment grows faster than the consumer segment
T2.first_claim: Individual home-brewing is a stepping stone: hobbyists who graduate to small commercial brewing (caterers, micro-breweries) buy equipment that scales up, so value sits in the upgrade path to small B2B customers rather than in consumer hardware sales.

assessments.quote: Each set of capsules - different capsules contain different ingredients - can make 5 liters, or about 10.5 pints, of beer after roughly two weeks of brewing.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a 2019 LG product in South Korea, not Krones. It shows a capsule-based premium home machine existed and was priced at 3.99 million won, but not that buyers repeat-purchased capsules, that Krones could make or sell such a product, or that demand exists outside Korea.

assessments.quote: It is the ideal brewing device for switching from hobby to commercial brewing, for example as an introduction for caterers who want to offer their own beer to their guests.
assessments.does_not_show: This is marketing from Speidel, a different company, not Krones. It shows that at least one maker positions home equipment as an entry to commercial brewing, but not that many hobbyists upgrade, that upgrade drives purchases of commercial equipment, or that Krones captures that value.

X1.name: Pre-order and upgrade-intent test for a consumer capsule brewer versus a small-commercial path
X1.method: Run two parallel online offers in Germany for 10 weeks (proposed): (a) a landing page for a home capsule brewing appliance at three price points, with a refundable deposit (pre-order) and a repeat-capsule pricing option; (b) a survey and deposit offer for a small-batch commercial brewing unit, aimed at hobby brewers who say they might sell beer. Traffic from home-brewing forums and paid search. Stop-loss if unit cost estimate cannot support the price points.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 1,500 landing-page visitors per arm, targeted at home brewers and people searching for home beer machines; about 300 survey respondents among hobby brewers.
X1.measure: Deposit conversion rate at each price point for the consumer arm; share of respondents with stated plans to sell beer commercially who would deposit for the commercial unit; stated repeat-capsule intent among deposit-holders.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Deposit conversion is meaningful (for example at least 2% at a price around 2,000 EUR) and holds up at the middle price point, with stated capsule repeat intent at least 2 refills per owner per 6 months.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Deposit conversion for the consumer unit is weak; interest concentrates among respondents with commercial plans, who deposit for the small-batch commercial unit at a higher rate than general hobbyists.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a prototype only if the consumer arm reaches at least 2% deposit conversion at the middle price AND stated repeat-capsule intent is at least 2 refills per owner per 6 months. If the consumer arm fails but commercial-plan respondents deposit at 5% or more, pursue the B2B small-batch route instead. If neither passes, do not invest.

revisions.reason: SYN-KRONES-UPDATE is SIMULATED, so it cannot justify a change. If real, it would bear on T2 not T1: among small craft buyers an automated clean-in-place option drew 72 reservations versus 32 for manual cleaning, hinting that cleaning burden shapes choice in the small commercial segment. It does not show a buildable product at a price buyers pay, market size, or fit with Krones' industrial business. T2 stays uncertain pending real evidence.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer-facing Krones product on current evidence. Before any product investment, run the proposed low-cost pre-order and upgrade-intent test (X1: about 20000 EUR over 10 weeks; all figures are my proposals, not observations). Keep the small-batch B2B route (Compact Class and similar lines) as the fallback. arguments.name: Pre-order and upgrade-intent test for a consumer capsule brewer versus a small-commercial path
arguments.method: Run two parallel online offers in Germany for 10 weeks (proposed): (a) a landing page for a home capsule brewing appliance at three price points, with a refundable deposit (pre-order) and a repeat-capsule pricing option; (b) a survey and deposit offer for a small-batch commercial brewing unit, aimed at hobby brewers who say they might sell beer. Traffic from home-brewing forums and paid search. Stop-loss if unit cost estimate cannot support the price points.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 1,500 landing-page visitors per arm, targeted at home brewers and people searching for home beer machines; about 300 survey respondents among hobby brewers.
arguments.measure: Deposit conversion rate at each price point for the consumer arm; share of respondents with stated plans to sell beer commercially who would deposit for the commercial unit; stated repeat-capsule intent among deposit-holders.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Deposit conversion is meaningful (for example at least 2% at a price around 2,000 EUR) and holds up at the middle price point, with stated capsule repeat intent at least 2 refills per owner per 6 months.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Deposit conversion for the consumer unit is weak; interest concentrates among respondents with commercial plans, who deposit for the small-batch commercial unit at a higher rate than general hobbyists.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed to a prototype only if the consumer arm reaches at least 2% deposit conversion at the middle price AND stated repeat-capsule intent is at least 2 refills per owner per 6 months. If the consumer arm fails but commercial-plan respondents deposit at 5% or more, pursue the B2B small-batch route instead. If neither passes, do not invest.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer-facing Krones product on current evidence. Run the proposed low-cost pre-order and upgrade-intent test (X1, about 20000 EUR over 10 weeks, all figures proposed) before any product investment. Keep the small-batch B2B route (Compact Class and similar) as the fallback if the consumer arm fails.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

X1.name: Small-brewer quote-request and consumer pre-order split test
X1.method: Two parallel low-cost probes over 12 weeks. (a) B2B: a landing page and outreach to craft and contract brewers in Germany and the EU offering a compact 5 to 17 hl system with an indicative price range, measuring qualified quote requests and whether prospects will book a call with a sales engineer. (b) Consumer: a pre-order page for a home beer machine with a capsule refill plan, measuring pre-orders with a refundable deposit and the share of buyers who accept a recurring capsule plan. Both use a neutral brand test, not Krones-branded, to avoid the company's own reputation distorting results.
X1.sample: B2B: about 60 craft or contract brewers contacted (proposed). Consumer: about 2,000 paid-traffic impressions to home-brewing enthusiasts in Germany, Austria and Switzerland (proposed, estimated).
X1.measure: B2B: qualified quote requests per 60 contacts and call-booking rate. Consumer: pre-order rate with deposit and acceptance rate of recurring capsule plan.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Several qualified quote requests and calls from small brewers (roughly 10% or more of contacts), with consumer pre-orders low and the capsule plan rejected by most who pre-order.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Consumer pre-orders accepted at a meaningful rate and most pre-orders accepting a capsule plan, with few B2B requests from small brewers, because a machine-plus-consumables offer would be the attractive route.

X1.decision_rule: Pursue the B2B small-brewer route (T1) if at least 6 of 60 contacts (10%) give a qualified quote request and consumer pre-order rate stays below 1% of impressions. Pursue a consumer proposition (T2) only if consumer deposits exceed 1% of impressions and at least half of pre-orders accept a recurring capsule plan. If neither threshold is met, do not invest beyond the test.

(a) B2B: a landing page and outreach to craft and contract brewers in Germany and the EU offering a compact 5 to 17 hl system with an indicative price range, measuring qualified quote requests and whether prospects will book a call with a sales engineer. (b) Consumer: a pre-order page for a home beer machine with a capsule refill plan, measuring pre-orders with a refundable deposit and the share of buyers who accept a recurring capsule plan. Both use a neutral brand test, not Krones-branded, to avoid the company's own reputation distorting results.
arguments.sample: B2B: about 60 craft or contract brewers contacted (proposed). Consumer: about 2,000 paid-traffic impressions to home-brewing enthusiasts in Germany, Austria and Switzerland (proposed, estimated).
arguments.measure: B2B: qualified quote requests per 60 contacts and call-booking rate. Consumer: pre-order rate with deposit and acceptance rate of recurring capsule plan.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Several qualified quote requests and calls from small brewers (roughly 10% or more of contacts), with consumer pre-orders low and the capsule plan rejected by most who pre-order.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Consumer pre-orders accepted at a meaningful rate and most pre-orders accepting a capsule plan, with few B2B requests from small brewers, because a machine-plus-consumables offer would be the attractive route.

arguments.decision_rule: Pursue the B2B small-brewer route (T1) if at least 6 of 60 contacts (10%) give a qualified quote request and consumer pre-order rate stays below 1% of impressions. Pursue a consumer proposition (T2) only if consumer deposits exceed 1% of impressions and at least half of pre-orders accept a recurring capsule plan. If neither threshold is met, do not invest beyond the test.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-facing product now. If Krones pursues anything beyond its B2B lines, the evidence so far points to a small-batch offer for craft and contract brewers, sold through existing channels, and only after the proposed test confirms qualified demand. The consumer route rests on one 2019 Korean product example and an unverified market size.

result.title: Simulated compact-brewing-system cleaning offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

X1.name: Parallel channel pilot: installer kit vs direct consumer price premium
X1.method: Two-arm pilot run over 12 weeks. Arm A: a Lapp-branded EV-charging accessory bundle offered at a list price premium (+15 percent over comparable generic bundle) through the existing Lapp Mobility consumer shop, with the same product listed at standard price on a separate page to measure conversion difference. Arm B: the same bundle offered as a configured kit to a set of installer accounts (for example 20 to 30 electricians recruited via trade contacts or a trade-show list), measuring units ordered per account. Price and conversion data come from the shop; order data from trade accounts. Analyst-proposed design; not yet approved by any company.
X1.sample: Consumer arm: traffic from the existing shop, estimated 2,000 to 4,000 visitors over 12 weeks (estimated). Trade arm: 20 to 30 installer accounts (proposed).
X1.measure: Consumer arm: conversion rate at premium price vs standard price, and share of buyers citing safety or certification in a post-purchase question. Trade arm: units ordered per account in weeks 1 to 12, and share of orders that are configured kits vs loose components.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium-priced bundle converts at no more than a 10 percent relative drop versus standard price, and safety or certification is cited by a large share of buyers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trade accounts order more units per account for the configured kit than the consumer arm sells per visitor, and private conversion at premium price falls sharply, showing installers rather than homeowners drive the volume.

X1.decision_rule: Keep T1 (direct premium) as the lead if the premium arm's conversion drops by less than 10 percent relative to standard and at least 25 percent of buyers cite safety or certification. Keep T2 (trade-led) if trade accounts average at least 3 kit orders each over the 12 weeks and the consumer premium arm drops conversion by more than 30 percent. If neither threshold is met, do not invest; treat both theories as unsupported.

The real evidence I rely on is the trade-press article, which points to price sensitivity and cuts against T1's premium claim. The simulated result changes nothing in my recommendation.

SYN-LAPP-UPDATE is SIMULATED and I do not cite it. Had it been real, it would concern consumer trust in compatibility assurance, which bears on private buyers rather than on who chooses components. It therefore does not test T2 (installers and electricians specify home-charging kits), and it cannot confirm or undercut that theory. T2 remains unconfirmed; the trade-press article and company pages say nothing about installer decision-making.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who cannot judge electrical safety by themselves defer to visibly certified, engineering-grade brands, which lifts willingness to pay over generic cheap cables.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Lapp sells a branded, certified cable or wallbox accessory through online or retail channels and keeps the margin that a distributor or electrician would otherwise take.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Lapp earns OEM or wholesale margin by supplying cables and assemblies to wallbox makers and installers, without owning the consumer relationship.

X1.name: Private buyer channel test for home EV cable
X1.method: Run two paid online listings for a certified home charging cable under a Lapp-branded product, and a no-brand listing of the same cable through a wallbox or installer partner. Compare conversion and stated cable-brand reasons for buying.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors to EV-owner or wallbox search ads in Germany over 8 weeks, split across the two offers.
X1.measure: Conversion rate to an order or waitlist sign-up per 1,000 exposures; share of buyers who name brand or certification as a reason; price acceptance at 10 and 20 percent premium.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Certified, branded listing converts at least as well as the unbranded one at a 10 to 20 percent premium, and buyers name safety or certification as a main reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Direct consumer listing converts poorly at any premium, and buyers name installer or car brand rather than cable brand as the decision factor.

X1.decision_rule: Pursue a direct consumer line only if the branded listing converts at least 50 percent as well as the installer-led route at a 10 percent premium, and at least 30 percent of buyers name certification or brand as a reason. Otherwise keep to component supply to wallbox makers and installers.

revisions.reason: No change. The simulated SYN-LAPP-UPDATE is excluded from the evidence, since it is not real data. As a what-if only: fewer completed purchases with the free compatibility check (32) than with self-check (72) would weaken the idea that a paid consumer service adds value, but it would not test whether installers or car makers choose the cable. T2 rests on the public sources, and its uncertainty is unchanged.

Kept as a rival, not favoured. The simulated SYN-LAPP-UPDATE is not real evidence and is not cited. As a what-if: a compatibility-assurance offer that converted less than a self-check offer would count against the idea that buyers pay for an added assurance, which is T1's premium mechanism. The public trade press already points that way, since it describes a price-sensitive, fiercely contested market. T1 is kept only because no public source tests a safety premium directly.

SIMULATED what-if, not evidence: if SYN-LAPP-UPDATE were real, the offer with a free compatibility check (32 purchases from 400) would have converted less than the self-check offer (72 from 400). That would count against T1's premium mechanism, since it suggests buyers do not pay for added assurance. It would not show anything about installers or car makers, which is T2's claim. The recommendation is unchanged, and T1 stays unlikely on public sources.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the main effort in B2B supply of cables and assemblies to wallbox makers, charging-station makers and installers, which the public sources show Lapp already serves. Before any direct consumer line, run a small channel test to see whether private buyers choose cable brands at all.
final.target_customer: Wallbox makers, charging-station makers and infrastructure operators as primary; private EV owners only as a later, tested segment.
final.value_proposition: Certified, engineering-grade charging cables and assemblies that wallbox and installer partners can specify, so the consumer buys the partner's product and Lapp earns component margin.
final.next_action: Run proposed test X1 (two paid online listings plus an installer-led route, about EUR 18,000 over 10 weeks; budget and duration are estimates). Pursue direct consumer sales only if the branded listing converts at least half as well as the installer route at a 10 percent premium, and at least 30 percent of buyers name certification or brand as a reason.
final.uncertainty: Lapp's actual consumer sales, margins and channel costs are not public, and I did not find them. Trade-press sources show Lapp Mobility offers products to private EV drivers, but not how large that business is. Public evidence on whether private buyers choose a cable brand is thin. A trade article says the consumer market is price-sensitive and fiercely contested, which weakens T1's premium assumption without proving it wrong. I read 3 sources and ran 1 challenge search, so the picture is partial.

arguments.name: Private buyer channel test for home EV cable
arguments.method: Run two paid online listings for a certified home charging cable under a Lapp-branded product, and a no-brand listing of the same cable through a wallbox or installer partner. Compare conversion and stated cable-brand reasons for buying.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors to EV-owner or wallbox search ads in Germany over 8 weeks, split across the two offers.
arguments.measure: Conversion rate to an order or waitlist sign-up per 1,000 exposures; share of buyers who name brand or certification as a reason; price acceptance at 10 and 20 percent premium.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Certified, branded listing converts at least as well as the unbranded one at a 10 to 20 percent premium, and buyers name safety or certification as a main reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Direct consumer listing converts poorly at any premium, and buyers name installer or car brand rather than cable brand as the decision factor.

arguments.decision_rule: Pursue a direct consumer line only if the branded listing converts at least 50 percent as well as the installer-led route at a 10 percent premium, and at least 30 percent of buyers name certification or brand as a reason. Otherwise keep to component supply to wallbox makers and installers.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The SIMULATED result (not real data, not cited) concerns how compatibility assurance changes purchase in a recruited group. Even if real, its offer added an installer-like check, which if anything hints that buyers value trade-style assurance, a point for T2 rather than T1. I keep T1 as a hypothesis, unchanged, and treat the result as a what-if only.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-charging compatibility offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
