X1.name: Dealer price-point pilot with a compact tabletop variant versus a consumer-retail listing
X1.method: Two-arm, 10-week pilot. Arm A: two UK/Ireland catering dealers offer a discounted tabletop chamber bundle (existing C 70 or a proposed lower-priced variant) to small food businesses, with a price-tested quote and follow-up. Arm B: one specialist online retailer lists a consumer-positioned chamber sealer at a premium price with sous vide and liquid-sealing messaging. Both arms record inquiries, quotes and conversions.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 40 small food businesses (craft butchers, cheese dairies, farm shops) reached through the two dealers, and about 300 retail page visitors in Arm B. Sample sizes are estimated, not sourced.
X1.measure: Conversion from inquiry to quote and from quote to order in Arm A, with the reason for lost sales recorded (price versus function). In Arm B, conversion from page view to purchase and the share of buyers citing liquid or sous vide sealing in reviews.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A conversion rises clearly when the price is lowered, and lost sales cite price, not function. Arm B sales stay weak.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B converts at a premium price, with buyers citing liquid or sous vide sealing. Arm A conversion does not depend much on price.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed with a compact dealer variant if the lower-priced quote converts at least 1.5 times the current conversion in Arm A, and at least half of lost sales cite price. Treat T2 as worth a retail pilot only if Arm B reaches at least 2 percent page-to-purchase conversion with at least 30 percent of buyers citing liquid or sous vide sealing. Otherwise keep the status quo and do not build either product.

revisions.reason: SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE is a SIMULATED what-if, not evidence. If it were real, it would be a narrow test of running-cost framing in a recruited household group, with 32 reservations for the running-cost offer against 72 for the standard offer. That counts against the idea that a cost message helps household demand, but it does not test T2's premium or sous vide mechanism, and it says nothing about price or market size. T2 stays as an untested hypothesis, and I do not change my belief on that basis.

final.recommendation: Do not build a consumer product now. MULTIVAC already reaches small food businesses through catering dealers with its tabletop chamber range, so the first step is to test whether a lower-priced compact variant converts better through those dealers. Hold any household-branded SKU until a separate retail pilot shows premium demand. The evidence I could read supports the existence of the dealer channel, not a price gap or a household market worth a new product line.
final.target_customer: Small food businesses served through existing catering dealers, such as craft butchers, cheese dairies and farm shops. Household enthusiasts are a secondary and unproven segment.
final.value_proposition: A lower-priced tabletop chamber machine with consumables, sold through the existing dealer network, offering professional seal quality to buyers who cannot justify a full industrial thermoformer.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 10-week dealer price-point pilot (X1, estimated 18000 EUR) comparing a discounted tabletop quote with the current price across two dealers, and a retail listing for the household hypothesis. Check dealer sales and pricing data first if it can be obtained.
final.uncertainty: Much is unknown. I could not find MULTIVAC's dealer sales, pricing, margins, channel contracts or financials; these are likely non-public. The dealer and marketing sources are company or dealer claims, one undated, with no sales or price data. The household market source is an undated commercial report summary, and it describes chamber sealers as a smaller share of the market. I found no evidence of MULTIVAC selling directly to households, so I cannot say how far it reaches individual buyers beyond dealer-led small business. No demand, price or margin figure for either route was verified.

arguments.name: Dealer price-point pilot with a compact tabletop variant versus a consumer-retail listing
arguments.method: Two-arm, 10-week pilot. Arm A: two UK/Ireland catering dealers offer a discounted tabletop chamber bundle (existing C 70 or a proposed lower-priced variant) to small food businesses, with a price-tested quote and follow-up. Arm B: one specialist online retailer lists a consumer-positioned chamber sealer at a premium price with sous vide and liquid-sealing messaging. Both arms record inquiries, quotes and conversions.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 40 small food businesses (craft butchers, cheese dairies, farm shops) reached through the two dealers, and about 300 retail page visitors in Arm B. Sample sizes are estimated, not sourced.
arguments.measure: Conversion from inquiry to quote and from quote to order in Arm A, with the reason for lost sales recorded (price versus function). In Arm B, conversion from page view to purchase and the share of buyers citing liquid or sous vide sealing in reviews.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A conversion rises clearly when the price is lowered, and lost sales cite price, not function. Arm B sales stay weak.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B converts at a premium price, with buyers citing liquid or sous vide sealing. Arm A conversion does not depend much on price.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed with a compact dealer variant if the lower-priced quote converts at least 1.5 times the current conversion in Arm A, and at least half of lost sales cite price. Treat T2 as worth a retail pilot only if Arm B reaches at least 2 percent page-to-purchase conversion with at least 30 percent of buyers citing liquid or sous vide sealing. Otherwise keep the status quo and do not build either product.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated household chamber-sealer running-cost offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. frame.objective: Decide whether Rieter should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case beyond its industrial spinning-mill business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The test is whether individual buyers (e.g. home sewing, small makers, textile hobbyists, or yarn-based craft users) would pay for something Rieter can uniquely supply, versus whether the effort is better spent on its core mill customers.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions
Rieter's contractual and detailed financial data may not be public, so some conclusions will rest on incomplete information
Search budget of 8 searches (7 left after the brief); the 20,000 EUR and 12-week test limits are analyst assumptions
Rieter's core market is industrial spinning mills with long sales cycles, high-value machines and after-sales service revenue; any consumer move must not endanger that base
Rieter's machines and components are not designed for individual buyers and may not transfer to them; a consumer product may need a different manufacturing and distribution model
Barmag (man-made fibre equipment, acquired February 2026) adds a second industrial customer group and may change the scope of options
alternatives: A. No expansion: stay with industrial spinning machines, components and after-sales services for mills, including Barmag integration
B. Product redesign for an adjacent industrial niche (e.g. smaller-scale spinning units for technical or artisan yarn producers) sold through existing channels
C. Differentiated consumer proposition via a new route to buyers: a branded product or kit for a specific home or craft use case, sold directly or via retailers
D. Different industrial customer group: serve new mill segments such as recycled or technical fibre producers using the existing platform, or Barmag's man-made fibre customers

E. Service-led or licensing model: monetise know-how, digital monitoring or training for small producers, or license technology to a consumer appliance or craft-supply brand, keeping Rieter out of direct consumer sales
F. Acquisition or partnership with a consumer-facing yarn or craft business to gain brand and distribution instead of building internally

frame.objective: Decide whether Rieter Holding AG should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its industrial business of selling short-staple spinning machines, components and after-sales services to spinning mills. The decision turns on whether individual buyers would pay for, and Rieter could capture value from, a consumer-facing offer, and what evidence would justify the investment.
constraints: Outside analyst using only public sources; the company has not asked this question and its intentions are unknown; financial and contractual detail may be non-public, so state what could not be found

B. Product redesign for an existing industrial use case: a differentiated machine or component line for a specific fibre or yarn segment sold to mills
C. Different route to existing buyers: sell service, digital monitoring or consumables to mill operators on subscription, with no consumer product
D. Consumer proposition for a specific use case: a branded or direct-to-consumer product (for example yarn, textiles or home-spinning equipment) sold to individual buyers
E. Different customer group: serve independent or small-scale yarn producers, makers or craft spinners as a distinct segment with a simplified machine

T1.claim: Individual buyers of craft and hobby yarn will pay a premium for yarn with verified recycled or traceable content, and that premium is captured by a certified-provenance licence that Rieter already operates for mills, not by Rieter selling to consumers directly.
T1.who_benefits: Mills and yarn brands that sell certified recycled yarn; craft buyers who want provenance; Rieter, if it earns licence fees and machine or component sales from licensees
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Crafters who have recently started a hobby are a large, growing group (the CYC survey reports many started crocheting within two years). Their purchasing may respond to visible sustainability claims, so a certified label can shift which yarn they choose.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rieter licenses the Com4recycling process to spinning mills that run Rieter machines and hold GRS certification, earning licence and machine or component revenue; consumer premium flows to the mill or brand, with Rieter sharing it through the licence
assumptions: A certified recycled label changes craft buyers' yarn choice and price tolerance
Mills and brands will pay a licence fee rather than build their own certification
The CYC consumer segment is large enough and reachable through brands, not through Rieter
Licence revenue is material relative to Rieter's industrial business
predictions: Craft yarn sold with a recycled/GRS label carries a measurable price premium over comparable unlabelled yarn
Mills that hold a Rieter licence can show more licensed yarn sold to consumers than unlicensed mills

T1.first_claim: Individual buyers of craft and hobby yarn will pay a premium for yarn with verified recycled or traceable content, and that premium is captured by a certified-provenance licence that Rieter already operates for mills, not by Rieter selling to consumers directly.

T2.claim: Consumers do not choose yarn by the spinning machine behind it, so a machine maker that sells to individual buyers would have no brand pull; value stays with the mills and yarn brands that own the buyer relationship, and Rieter's economic position is to keep selling machines, components and services to those mills.
T2.who_benefits: Spinning mills and yarn brands, which own the retail and brand relationship; Rieter keeps its industrial customers
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Mills and brands change what they buy from machine suppliers when cost, quality or certification pressure rises, not when end consumers ask for a machine, so the purchasing decision sits upstream of the consumer
T2.how_value_is_captured: Rieter sells machines, components and after-sales services to mills that serve the consumer market; it earns no consumer premium and only captures value where mills buy more equipment or service
assumptions: Individual buyers do not know or care which machine maker produced the yarn
Brands, not machine makers, control the consumer relationship and marketing
Mill demand for Rieter equipment rises with consumer demand for the mill's yarn, not with a Rieter brand
predictions: Consumers in a yarn-choice test rate brand and fibre content far above machine maker name
Yarn labels that name Rieter machines do not move craft-buyer choice
Mills that add Rieter equipment grow capacity in line with their own yarn sales, not with any consumer premium attributable to Rieter
T2.first_claim: Consumers do not choose yarn by the spinning machine behind it, so a machine maker that sells to individual buyers would have no brand pull; value stays with the mills and yarn brands that own the buyer relationship, and Rieter's economic position is to keep selling machines, components and services to those mills.

assessments.quote: To apply for a license, spinning mills must produce their recycled yarn on a Rieter card, draw frame and end-spinning machine. In addition, a Global Recycled Standard (GRS) certification is required.
assessments.does_not_show: It shows that a licence mechanism exists and ties licensees to Rieter machines plus GRS certification. It does not show any licence fee, licence revenue, the number of licensees, or that craft or consumer buyers pay any premium for licensed yarn.

assessments.quote: As market leader, more than 3 000 customers rely on Rieter technology every day to achieve more with less.
assessments.does_not_show: It shows Rieter's own claim of a customer base of more than 3,000, consistent with an industrial business. It does not show who those customers are, whether they are mills or consumer-facing brands, how much equipment they buy, or any consumer brand pull for Rieter.

assessments.quote: It uses equipment designed for large quantities of wool, running 240 spindles for yarn production while a mini mill uses from six to 12.
assessments.does_not_show: It describes small Maine fibre mills and their spindle counts. It says nothing about whether craft buyers pay a premium for recycled or certified yarn, nor about any Rieter equipment or licence in use there. It does not contradict T1 and does not support it.

X1.name: Certified-provenance yarn choice and premium test (craft buyers, proposed)
X1.method: Online and in-store choice experiment with craft yarn buyers. Each participant sees paired skeins of matched yarn (same fibre, weight and colour), one labelled as recycled with GRS certification and one unlabelled, with a price shown. Measure choice share and the highest price the buyer would pay for the labelled skein. Brand and machine maker names are kept off all labels to test whether provenance, not machine identity, moves buyers. A parallel arm shows machine maker name on a subset to test whether naming Rieter adds any pull. Yarn is sourced through an existing licensed mill partner, or through a non-licensed mill if no licensee will take part.
X1.sample: Proposed: 300 craft buyers recruited online (crocheting and knitting hobbyists who started within two years), plus 2 in-store sessions at 2 craft retailers, about 60 participants each.
X1.measure: Share of participants choosing the labelled skein over the unlabelled one; willingness to pay premium in percent; share who choose the Rieter-named skein over unnamed when machine name is shown.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Labelled recycled/GRS yarn is chosen clearly more often than the unlabelled match, at a measurable price premium of at least 10 percent, and machine name adds little or nothing beyond provenance.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Provenance label moves choice little or not at all once fibre content and brand are matched; machine maker name adds no pull; buyers rate the mill or brand as the decision point, not the machine supplier.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: support T1 over T2 only if the labelled skein is chosen in at least 10 percentage points more often than the unlabelled match (with a 95 percent interval excluding zero) and median stated premium is at least 10 percent. If the choice gap is under 5 points, or the premium is under 5 percent, keep T2 as the working view and do not pursue a consumer proposition. Between these, extend the test before deciding.

revisions.reason: The simulated update (SYN-RIETER-UPDATE) is not real evidence and I do not cite it. It concerns a skill barrier in a hobby machine offer, not a premium on certified-provenance yarn, so it does not bear on T1. T1 stays uncertain: the licence source shows a mechanism (licence tied to Rieter machines plus GRS) but no revenue or premium, and the craft survey shows a recent-entrant segment but not willingness to pay for provenance. The proposed test X1 remains the next step.

Treated as a what-if only: the simulated onboarding result is not real evidence and bears on a skill-barrier mechanism, not on whether consumers choose yarn by brand over machine maker. Even if it were real, it would not move T2, which rests on the industrial customer base and the upstream purchase decision. T2 stays uncertain; the real test of it is X1.

What-if only. Had SYN-RIETER-UPDATE been real, it would show a skill barrier (instructor onboarding) changing deposits in a hobby machine offer. That bears on a machine-buying mechanism, not on T1's claim that buyers pay a premium for certified-provenance yarn captured through a licence. It would therefore leave T1 unchanged. The simulated result is not evidence and is not cited in the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Keep the industrial model (machines, components, after-sales service, and licences to mills) as the base. Test the one consumer-adjacent idea, certified-provenance yarn, before any larger commitment. The evidence read so far does not show individual buyers paying for Rieter-linked provenance. The only consumer-facing item found is a B2B licence for mills.
final.target_customer: Craft and hobby yarn buyers, reached through spinning mills and yarn brands rather than directly by Rieter. Rieter's own customers remain the more than 3,000 industrial mills.
final.value_proposition: Certified recycled yarn (Com4recycling licence tied to Rieter machines plus GRS certification), giving mills and brands a provenance claim that could earn a consumer premium. Rieter's share would come from licence and machine or component revenue. The consumer premium is unproven.
final.next_action: Run the proposed choice and premium test X1 (proposed, about EUR 14,000 and 8 weeks, within the EUR 20,000 and 12-week limits). Separately, seek non-public licence terms and revenue, which this analysis could not find.
final.uncertainty: High. Three real sources plus one Maine mini-mill report. The CYC excerpt is internally inconsistent (two of five is 40 percent, stated as about 50 percent) and covers US crocheters only. Licence revenue, contract terms, Barmag effects and craft premium market size were not found. No test has been run.
would_change_if: X1 shows a choice gap of at least 10 points (interval excluding zero) and a premium of at least 10 percent: supports T1
X1 shows a gap under 5 points or a premium under 5 percent: keep T2 and drop the consumer proposition
Non-public data shows licence revenue is immaterial to Rieter
Licensed mills see no sales gain from the label, or brands will not pay licence fees
A larger, credible survey shows the craft segment is small or transient

arguments.name: Certified-provenance yarn choice and premium test (craft buyers, proposed)
arguments.method: Online and in-store choice experiment with craft yarn buyers. Each participant sees paired skeins of matched yarn (same fibre, weight and colour), one labelled as recycled with GRS certification and one unlabelled, with a price shown. Measure choice share and the highest price the buyer would pay for the labelled skein. Brand and machine maker names are kept off all labels to test whether provenance, not machine identity, moves buyers. A parallel arm shows machine maker name on a subset to test whether naming Rieter adds any pull. Yarn is sourced through an existing licensed mill partner, or through a non-licensed mill if no licensee will take part.
arguments.sample: Proposed: 300 craft buyers recruited online (crocheting and knitting hobbyists who started within two years), plus 2 in-store sessions at 2 craft retailers, about 60 participants each.
arguments.measure: Share of participants choosing the labelled skein over the unlabelled one; willingness to pay premium in percent; share who choose the Rieter-named skein over unnamed when machine name is shown.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Labelled recycled/GRS yarn is chosen clearly more often than the unlabelled match, at a measurable price premium of at least 10 percent, and machine name adds little or nothing beyond provenance.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Provenance label moves choice little or not at all once fibre content and brand are matched; machine maker name adds no pull; buyers rate the mill or brand as the decision point, not the machine supplier.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: support T1 over T2 only if the labelled skein is chosen in at least 10 percentage points more often than the unlabelled match (with a 95 percent interval excluding zero) and median stated premium is at least 10 percent. If the choice gap is under 5 points, or the premium is under 5 percent, keep T2 as the working view and do not pursue a consumer proposition. Between these, extend the test before deciding.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Keep the industrial model (machines, components, after-sales service and licences to mills) as the base, and test the one consumer-adjacent idea, certified-provenance yarn, cheaply before any larger commitment. The evidence read so far does not show individual buyers paying for Rieter-linked provenance, and the only consumer-facing item is a B2B licence for mills.

result.title: Simulated mini-spinning-machine onboarding offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Keep the core B2B business as it is. If pursued, test a leasing or pay-per-use offer for small organisations (T1) before investing, and treat the dealer-led route (T2) as a control arm in the same test. T1 is favoured only because it has a stated mechanism and a vendor's claim pointing its way. No independent evidence supports it yet.

frame.objective: Decide whether Kardex Holding AG should invest in a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case or buyer group, beyond its B2B automated storage and retrieval systems, and identify the evidence that would justify that investment. Core aim: find the highest-value route to growth without putting the core B2B business at risk.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only. The company has not asked this question and nothing here describes its intentions.
Financial and contractual detail (AutoStore partner terms, margins, consumer channel data) may not be public.
Search budget is 8 in total, 7 remaining. No direct contact with the company.
Test budget of EUR 20,000 and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
Must first establish how far Kardex already reaches individual buyers before assuming it does not.
Company materials are assertions, not demand evidence.
alternatives: No expansion: keep focus on B2B warehouse, factory and organisation automation.
Product redesign: adapt existing compact storage (for example AutoStore-based cube or carousel units) into smaller, simpler configurations for one use case.
Different route to buyers: sell through dealers, e-commerce or retail channels to small businesses or home users.
Different customer group: target small workshops, pharmacies, clinics or home-office users with a packaged storage offer.
Service or subscription model: leasing or managed storage for smaller organisations.
Partner-led: expand through AutoStore or other integrators rather than owning a consumer proposition.

T1.claim: Small organisations (independent workshops, small parts counters, clinics) would adopt compact automated storage if it were leased or sold as a pay-per-use subscription, because the capital cost, not the need, is what stops them. A manufacturer that offers the leasing and service package would capture recurring revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Small organisations with lumpy storage needs and limited capital, and the manufacturer, which earns recurring fees and locks in service contracts.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A monthly fee turns a large upfront purchase into an operating cost that a small business can approve without a capital budget. The Pio example shows a vendor using exactly this lever for SMB warehouse automation.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Subscription or lease fees plus maintenance and software contracts, billed monthly, rather than a one-off equipment sale.
assumptions: Capital cost is the main barrier for small buyers, not lack of need or space.
Small buyers will accept a fixed monthly fee and a multi-year commitment.
Kardex can deliver installation and service at a per-unit cost that keeps the subscription margin positive.
The subscription can be sold through a channel that reaches small buyers at acceptable cost.
predictions: Lead conversion from a leasing offer will be materially higher among small buyers than from a purchase-only offer at the same list price.
Small buyers who lease will show a higher share of recurring revenue per unit than buyers of the equivalent purchase model.
Churn will be low once installed, because switching means losing stored inventory and workflow.
T1.first_claim: Small organisations (independent workshops, small parts counters, clinics) would adopt compact automated storage if it were leased or sold as a pay-per-use subscription, because the capital cost, not the need, is what stops them. A manufacturer that offers the leasing and service package would capture recurring revenue.

T2.claim: Small organisations do not buy compact automated storage mainly because of capital cost. They buy only when a dealer or integrator already serves them with a finished solution, so the binding constraint is the route to buyers and installation support, not the price structure. A manufacturer would gain by partnering with existing dealers rather than building a consumer proposition.
T2.who_benefits: Local dealers and integrators that already hold the customer relationship, and the manufacturer, which avoids building a new sales channel.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A small buyer trusts a local firm that can survey the space, install, train staff and service the unit. Without that, even a cheap offer is not bought, because the buyer cannot judge fit or risk.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Equipment sales and service margin through dealer partners, with the manufacturer supplying product, configuration tools and training to the dealer network.
assumptions: Dealers or integrators exist who already sell to small businesses and would take on compact storage as an add-on.
Installation and service costs, not the equipment price, dominate the buyer's decision.
Dealer margins leave enough for Kardex after support costs.
predictions: In regions with an active dealer network, small-buyer adoption will be higher than in regions served only by direct online sales, even at equal prices.
Buyers who buy through a dealer will cite installation and service as the reason, not price.
Offering a leasing plan without a dealer will produce less uptake than a dealer-led sale at the same price.
T2.first_claim: Small organisations do not buy compact automated storage mainly because of capital cost. They buy only when a dealer or integrator already serves them with a finished solution, so the binding constraint is the route to buyers and installation support, not the price structure. A manufacturer would gain by partnering with existing dealers rather than building a consumer proposition.

assessments.quote: Pio said its pay-per-pick model reduces initial capital expense, so SMBs can adopt automation earlier in their life cycle.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a rival vendor's own claim about a different company's product, reported in a trade article. It does not show that small buyers actually adopted Pio, that capital cost is the binding barrier for small buyers, or that Kardex or AutoStore could offer a subscription at positive margin. The article gives no adoption numbers, and Pio is not Kardex.

assessments.quote: Kardex automated storage systems bring speed, structure, and visibility to dealership parts departments.
assessments.does_not_show: This is Kardex's own marketing for a US dealership use case. It shows a business customer segment that buys through a business sales process. It does not show that dealers or integrators sell to small buyers, that installation or service drives small-buyer decisions, or how much of Kardex's sales go through a dealer route. It is an assertion of fit, not measured adoption.

X1.name: Price structure versus route-to-buyer test with small organisations
X1.method: Run a two-by-two landing-page and outreach trial in one country with a compact storage configuration aimed at small parts counters, independent workshops and small clinics. Arm A: purchase price with direct online enquiry. Arm B: monthly lease with direct online enquiry. Arm C: purchase price offered through a partner dealer who installs and services. Arm D: monthly lease offered through the same dealer. Each arm gets equal paid reach and a qualified quote request form. Track enquiries, qualified quotes and signed letters of intent. Proposed, not run.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 400 small organisations across the four arms, roughly 100 per arm, drawn from paid search and trade-association mailings. Dealer arms need 2 to 3 partner dealers willing to take leads (proposed).
X1.measure: Qualified quote requests per 100 reached, and signed letters of intent or deposits within 6 weeks of quote. Secondary: stated reason for drop-off, from a short exit survey.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Lease arms (B and D) convert materially more than purchase arms (A and C) at equal list price, because the capital barrier is what stops small buyers. The lease effect should be present even without a dealer.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Dealer arms (C and D) convert more than direct arms (A and B) at equal price, and the gap is driven by installation and service reassurance. The lease effect should be small once a dealer is present.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if lease arms beat purchase arms by at least 1.5 times on signed letters of intent, and the dealer effect is under 1.2 times, favour T1 and pursue leasing. If dealer arms beat direct arms by at least 1.5 times and the lease effect is under 1.2 times, favour T2 and pursue dealer partnership. If neither threshold is met, or both are, do not invest further; decline a larger build.

revisions.reason: No real evidence has changed T1. SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not counted. Read as a what-if, a rental offer producing 72 letters of intent against 32 for purchase at identical total cost would support T1's mechanism, but it would not show that a small enough module can be built, that installation and service pay at scale, or that small buyers behave this way in the real market. T1 stays uncertain. The only real support is a rival vendor's own claim about its pay-per-pick model.

SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not counted. It compared rental against purchase with the dealer and service held equal, so it bears on T1 and says little about T2. T2 stays uncertain, with only one neutral company marketing source behind it.

Read as a what-if only. SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE is SIMULATED, and I do not count it as evidence. If real, a rental offer drawing 72 letters of intent against 32 for purchase at identical total cost would be the mechanism T1 predicts. It would not show that a small enough module can be built, that installation and service pay at scale, or that small buyers behave this way outside a recruited group. Real evidence for T1 is still limited to a rival vendor's press claim. T1 stays uncertain.

final.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Keep the core B2B business as it is. The public evidence I found shows Kardex selling to businesses: warehouses, factories, organisations and dealership parts departments. I found no sign of a consumer product, direct-to-home channel or small-buyer offer. If the company wants to explore small-organisation demand, run the proposed test X1 first (about EUR 18,500 over 10 weeks, proposed, not run), comparing rental against purchase with a dealer-led control. Do not commit development budget until that test has run.
final.target_customer: Small organisations with limited capital and space for storage, such as independent workshops, small parts counters and small clinics. This is a hypothesis to test, not a segment shown to be demanding.
final.value_proposition: A compact automated storage unit offered as a monthly rental with installation and service included, so the buyer faces an operating cost rather than a large upfront purchase. Untested.
final.next_action: Check public and investor sources for whether Kardex already offers leasing or subscription storage to smaller customers, and what share of sales go through dealers and partners. Then run test X1 if it can be funded, using the proposed decision threshold.
final.uncertainty: Large. Kardex's consumer reach, margins, AutoStore partner terms, lease financing terms and dealer economics were not found and may not be public. The main support for T1 is a rival vendor's own press claim about its pay-per-pick model, not independent evidence of small-buyer demand. T2 has only one neutral company marketing source. The SIMULATED update is not counted as evidence. The 20,000 euro budget and 12-week limit are assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.
would_change_if: Public or company data show Kardex already sells leasing or subscription storage to small customers at a positive margin.
Test X1 shows lease arms do not beat purchase arms by at least 1.5 times on signed letters of intent, which would reject T1's central mechanism.
Test X1 shows dealer arms beat direct arms by at least 1.5 times while the lease effect is under 1.2 times, which would favour T2.
Evidence that small buyers adopt automation mainly through dealers, with price a minor factor, would move belief from T1 to T2.
Evidence that a compact module cannot be built or serviced at a cost that keeps leasing margin positive would reject the proposition.

arguments.name: Price structure versus route-to-buyer test with small organisations
arguments.method: Run a two-by-two landing-page and outreach trial in one country with a compact storage configuration aimed at small parts counters, independent workshops and small clinics. Arm A: purchase price with direct online enquiry. Arm B: monthly lease with direct online enquiry. Arm C: purchase price offered through a partner dealer who installs and services. Arm D: monthly lease offered through the same dealer. Each arm gets equal paid reach and a qualified quote request form. Track enquiries, qualified quotes and signed letters of intent. Proposed, not run.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 400 small organisations across the four arms, roughly 100 per arm, drawn from paid search and trade-association mailings. Dealer arms need 2 to 3 partner dealers willing to take leads (proposed).
arguments.measure: Qualified quote requests per 100 reached, and signed letters of intent or deposits within 6 weeks of quote. Secondary: stated reason for drop-off, from a short exit survey.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Lease arms (B and D) convert materially more than purchase arms (A and C) at equal list price, because the capital barrier is what stops small buyers. The lease effect should be present even without a dealer.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Dealer arms (C and D) convert more than direct arms (A and B) at equal price, and the gap is driven by installation and service reassurance. The lease effect should be small once a dealer is present.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if lease arms beat purchase arms by at least 1.5 times on signed letters of intent, and the dealer effect is under 1.2 times, favour T1 and pursue leasing. If dealer arms beat direct arms by at least 1.5 times and the lease effect is under 1.2 times, favour T2 and pursue dealer partnership. If neither threshold is met, or both are, do not invest further; decline a larger build.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Keep the core B2B business as it is. If pursued, test a leasing or pay-per-use offer for small organisations (T1) before investing, and treat the dealer-led route (T2) as a control arm in the same test. T1 is favoured only because it has a stated mechanism and a vendor's claim pointing its way. No independent evidence supports it yet.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product. Treat the small-business, dealer-led and leased route (T2) as the only one worth testing, and run the two-arm probe (X1) before any product or channel build. The public evidence shows Kardex sells automated storage to industrial, office and dealership parts customers, and offers pre-owned entry units. It shows nothing about household demand, consumer prices or small-firm payback.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Space scarcity and the hassle of retrieving stored items create a felt need that a fast, tidy retrieval system addresses; the buyer compares the unit against a shelving or cabinet purchase, not against an industrial system
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex sells a shrunk product under its own brand at a retail price, earning hardware margin on a larger unit volume than its B2B business, and reuses its existing controls and engineering
assumptions: Consumers will pay a price that covers a far smaller unit cost than an industrial system, including retail margin

X1.name: Two-arm demand test: household retail offer vs small-business leased offer
X1.method: Run two paid-search and social landing pages in the same region for 8 weeks. Arm A (T1) offers a compact home storage unit with an indicative retail price and a 'request a quote' button. Arm B (T2) offers a dealer-led, monthly-lease system for small firms with a time-saving estimate calculator and a 'request a site visit' button. Both arms use the same page structure, budget and tracking; the offer is purely a demand probe, with no product sold and no contract taken.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 20,000 targeted impressions per arm across two regions, yielding roughly 1,500 to 2,500 landing-page visitors per arm. Arm B also targets sole traders, small workshops and small online sellers.
X1.measure: Qualified enquiries per 1,000 visitors (a quote or site-visit request with a contact detail), split by arm. For Arm B, also the share of enquiries choosing lease over purchase when that option is shown.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A produces at least 2 qualified enquiries per 1,000 visitors, and Arm B produces fewer qualified enquiries per 1,000 visitors than Arm A's household interest, because small firms do not see a payback without a dealer estimate.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B produces at least 10 qualified enquiries per 1,000 visitors, with a majority choosing the lease option, and Arm A produces well below that, because households do not value the compact unit enough to request a quote.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if Arm B reaches at least 10 qualified enquiries per 1,000 visitors and at least 50 percent of its enquiries choose the lease, keep T2 and move to a dealer pilot. If Arm A reaches at least 2 per 1,000 and Arm B does not reach 10, keep T1 under review and test price and fitting. If neither arm reaches its threshold, stop further investment in consumer or small-business offers.

revisions.reason: The new item is SIMULATED, so it is not counted as evidence. As a what-if, it bears on T2's lease assumption: 72 of 400 letters of intent for monthly rental versus 32 of 400 for purchase, same machine and total cost. Real, it would suggest upfront cost drives small-business choice. It would not show a small enough module can be built, or that installation and service pay at scale. T2 stays kept on public evidence; X1 must test the lease prediction directly.

No real evidence bears on T1. The one Kardex claim I read, that customers span industrial and office environments, says nothing about households. The SIMULATED result concerns small workshops, shops and garages, not homes, so it does not count here. T1 stays unlikely: nothing shows household demand or a feasible home-scale unit. X1's household arm is the direct test.

As a what-if only: if SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE were real (72 of 400 letters of intent for rental versus 32 of 400 for purchase, same machine and cost), T2's lease assumption would gain support within small firms. It would not show a small enough module can be built or that installation and service pay. It is not counted as evidence, so T2 stays kept on public evidence and X1 remains the test.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer product now. Kardex's public record shows B2B automated storage for industrial, office and dealership parts customers, plus pre-owned entry units. It shows no household sales, consumer prices or small-firm payback. Of the options considered, only a dealer-led, leased small-business offer (T2) has any public support, and that support is marketing language. Run the two-arm probe (X1) before any product or channel build, using the stated thresholds.
final.target_customer: Small firms that lose staff time to searching for stock or parts (dealership parts counters, workshops, small sellers), reached through existing dealers and partners, not households.
final.value_proposition: A lower-cost entry into automated storage, offered as a lease or pre-owned unit with service, that cuts search and picking time and frees floor space, with payback shown in staff hours.
final.next_action: Run X1 over about 10 weeks for an estimated 20,000 EUR (analyst estimate, not a company figure). Proceed to a dealer pilot only if the small-business arm reaches at least 10 qualified enquiries per 1,000 visitors and at least 50 percent choose the lease. Keep T1 under review if the household arm reaches 2 per 1,000 and the small-business arm does not.
final.uncertainty: No Kardex sales, margin, pricing or AutoStore partner terms were public, so I could not check whether a small or leased unit is profitable. The dealership and pre-owned pages are company claims with no volumes. I found no independent study of small-business or household demand. T1's feasibility at home scale is untested.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.target_customer: Small firms that lose staff time to searching for stock or parts (dealership parts counters, workshops, small sellers), reached through existing dealers and partners, not households.
arguments.value_proposition: A lower-cost entry into automated storage, offered as a lease or pre-owned unit with service, that cuts search and picking time and frees floor space, with payback shown in staff hours.
arguments.next_action: Run X1 over about 10 weeks for an estimated 20,000 EUR (analyst estimate, not a company figure). Proceed to a dealer pilot only if the small-business arm reaches at least 10 qualified enquiries per 1,000 visitors and at least 50 percent choose the lease. Keep T1 under review if the household arm reaches 2 per 1,000 and the small-business arm does not.
arguments.uncertainty: No Kardex sales, margin, pricing or AutoStore partner terms were public, so I could not check whether a small or leased unit is profitable. The dealership and pre-owned pages are company claims with no volumes. I found no independent study of small-business demand or household demand. The only lease-versus-purchase figures come from a SIMULATED case, which I have not counted. T1's feasibility (a home-scale unit) is untested.

result.title: Simulated compact storage-module payment offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

It says nothing about whether a module could be built small and cheap enough, whether installation and service pay at that scale, or whether private households would buy. T1 concerns household and prosumer demand at a premium price, which this result does not test. The result would leave T1 unchanged and would not move the B2B recommendation.

T1.claim: Kardex's closest route to individual-scale buyers is through small businesses that already run parts counters or workshops (for example dealership parts departments and small repair shops), not households. A compact, lower-cost unit sold to these small-premises operators would be bought because floor space is scarce and retrieval time costs them money, so Kardex could capture value through its existing commercial sales and service channel.
T1.who_benefits: Small workshop, parts-counter and small-business operators with limited floor space and high retrieval-time costs; Kardex, through reuse of its existing dealer and channel relationships.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Operators who lose staff time and sales to slow, cluttered parts retrieval will pay for a smaller automated unit when the payback on saved time and recovered floor space is visible within their budget, which a large industrial system cannot offer them.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Kardex sells compact units and recurring service through its existing commercial channel, earning hardware margin plus maintenance revenue from a customer segment just below its current minimum project size.

X1.name: Small-operator demand test for a compact unit
X1.method: Recruit small parts operators (independent auto parts counters and small repair workshops) in one region. Each is shown a compact-unit concept, a proposed price band and a simple payback model. Operators who agree to a paid site survey have their current retrieval times and floor use measured. A separate, small consumer arm tests whether households in a retail or design-channel setting show purchase intent at a premium price against shelving-level prices.
X1.sample: Proposed: 15 small-operator sites in one region; 60 consumer respondents recruited online, targeted at garage, workshop and home-office users.
X1.measure: Share of operators who sign a paid site survey (proposed deposit of EUR 150 each); measured retrieval time per part and floor space used; payback estimate per site; consumer purchase intent at two price points.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 5 of 15 operators (33%) sign a paid site survey, and measured retrieval times show payback under 3 years at the proposed price band.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Few operators sign (under 3 of 15), and consumer intent is concentrated at shelving-level prices, with sharp drop-off at premium prices.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a costed compact prototype only if at least 5 of 15 operators sign the paid survey (33% or more) AND at least 3 surveyed sites show estimated payback under 3 years. If fewer than 3 sign or no site shows payback under 3 years, stop the consumer and small-operator line and keep capital in industrial systems. Thresholds are proposed, not derived from company data.

revisions.reason: SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not real demand, so it is not cited as evidence. Even if it were real, it would bear on payment structure (purchase letters of intent 72 vs rental 32 in the hypothetical arm), not on whether small operators have a retrieval-time problem worth a compact unit, or whether a module could be built and serviced at a viable cost. It would refine the price-structure question in the test rather than change T1's core claim. My belief is unchanged. The only real support for T1 remains the company's own dealership application page, which is a company claim.

Hypothetically, if SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE were real, it would bear on T2 only weakly: it shows that the upfront-payment structure changes choice among recruited small-workshop owners, which is a question about small operators, not households. It does not test whether households would pay a premium for storage automation. The result is SIMULATED and is not evidence, so my belief in T2 is unchanged, and I do not use it as support for either theory.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer proposition now. Keep the primary investment in industrial systems. The only differentiated route worth a cheap test is a compact unit for small commercial operators (parts counters, small workshops, garages) sold through existing commercial channels. Scale up only if test X1 shows real willingness to pay and measured payback. Individual household demand is unsupported by anything I could read.
final.target_customer: Small commercial parts and workshop operators with limited floor space and high retrieval-time costs (hypothesis, unverified).
final.value_proposition: A compact automated storage unit that cuts retrieval time and recovers floor space for small operators, with recurring service revenue for Kardex.
final.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed, roughly EUR 14,000 and 10 weeks, estimated): recruit about 15 small operators in one region, offer a paid site survey with measured retrieval times and payback, and apply the decision rule (proceed only if at least 5 of 15 sign and at least 3 sites show payback under 3 years). In parallel, look for Kardex's own consumer sales and AutoStore partner terms, which I could not find in public sources.
final.uncertainty: I found no evidence of Kardex consumer sales or a consumer product. My sources were three company pages and one Wikipedia page; the Wikipedia excerpt concerns business data storage history and is not relevant to consumers. Kardex's consumer sales share, AutoStore partnership terms, unit costs, and small-customer margins are not public. The T1 claim rests on a company application page, not independent demand data. The test figures (sample, threshold, cost) are my proposals, not observed facts. Household demand (T2) is untested.

Kardex or independent sources show an existing consumer or small-business product line with measurable sales
Measured retrieval-time savings for small operators are too small to pay back a compact unit at any viable price
Public or partner data show AutoStore-based small units are already sold at scale to small operators by others, removing the gap
Consumer intent tests (real, not simulated) show strong purchase intent at premium price points through a retail channel

position.recommendation: Do not build a new differentiated consumer product yet. Treat the existing US and Canadian retail lines as the evidence base: Sika already sells professional-grade products to DIY buyers under a retail brand. Before any redesign, measure whether those retail packs sell and earn margin, and run the proposed two-arm test (X1) to see whether a warranty or installer layer adds conversion beyond shelf access. Keep T2 open because the only support for it is Sika's own statement that specialist products are kept away from DIY use.

frame.objective: Decide whether Sika AG should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example homeowner waterproofing, sealing or bonding) beyond its contractor, distributor and industrial business. The decision should rest on evidence that such a proposition would earn returns above its cost, and on a clear view of how far Sika already reaches individual buyers.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact, no access to internal sales or contract data.
Test budget assumed at EUR 20,000 and 12 weeks maximum (analyst assumption, not a company figure).
Only 8 searches in total; 7 remaining after the brief.
Sika's existing consumer reach is unknown and must be established before theorising.
Channel margins, distributor exclusivity and product liability terms may not be public and must be flagged as unknown.
Consumer products carry different regulatory, labelling, warranty and retail-shelf requirements from professional products.
alternatives: No expansion: keep the contractor, distributor and industrial model, and reach homeowners only indirectly through existing trade channels.
Packaged existing products through DIY retail and online: sell current sealants and waterproofing in consumer packs with minimal redesign.
Differentiated use-case product: redesign one homeowner job (for example bathroom or roof leak repair, or floor bonding) with simplified packs, instructions and a warranty.
Referral service layer: a consumer advice and booking route that sends homeowners to Sika-approved installers, earning product sales and referral value without owning the retail sale.
License or partner route: license a Sika formulation to a consumer brand or retailer that owns the shopper relationship, taking a royalty.
Different customer group: target small professional tradespeople or builders' merchants who buy in small quantities, rather than end consumers.

T1.claim: Homeowners already buy Sika-grade products when they are packed for simple jobs and placed on retail shelves. Sika's consumer value comes from retail access to existing products, not from new product design.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners who need a simple repair, and retailers who gain a trusted brand for the aisle. Sika gains volume from the same formulations.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Retail availability and clear pack sizes reduce search and purchase friction for simple DIY jobs. A recognised professional brand on the shelf signals quality, so the buyer chooses it over cheaper generics.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika sells existing products to retailers at wholesale margin, with packaging and retailer marketing as the main added cost. Value is captured as incremental volume without new R&D.
assumptions: Retailers will stock Sika-branded packs at acceptable margin.
Homeowners' jobs can be completed with existing products and no special training.
Sika already has the packaging and channel capability in some markets (for example US and Canada).
predictions: Sika's retail-pack sales grow faster in markets where it already has shelf placement than in markets where it does not.
Retail consumers buying Sika packs choose them mainly for brand and availability, not for a new feature.
Margins on retail packs are lower than on contractor sales but cover the packaging cost.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners already buy Sika-grade products when they are packed for simple jobs and placed on retail shelves. Sika's consumer value comes from retail access to existing products, not from new product design.

T2.claim: Homeowners will not buy specialist chemicals for DIY use unless the failure risk is removed. A consumer proposition works only when it bundles guidance, a warranty or a certified installer route, so value is captured through installer referral and warranty-backed kits rather than through product sales alone.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who want a guaranteed result without learning technical application, and Sika, which can attach its installer network and warranty to a consumer job.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The company's own annual report says its specialised products need trained applicators because improper use causes failure or safety hazards. A homeowner facing that risk pays for certainty: a warranty, step-by-step guidance, or a booked professional, instead of a tin with instructions.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika earns a product margin plus a referral or booking fee, or a premium on warranty-backed kits. The installer network does the work, so Sika avoids owning installation liability.
assumptions: Homeowners will pay a premium for guaranteed results over cheaper DIY alternatives.
Sika or its partners can offer a warranty without unacceptable liability.
Installer referrals convert to paid jobs at a rate that covers the referral cost.
predictions: Homeowners' conversion from enquiry to purchase is higher for a booked-installer offer than for a DIY kit alone.
Warranty-backed kits command a higher price than the same product sold without a warranty.

result.brief: Sika AG makes construction chemicals and industrial adhesives and sealants, including waterproofing, concrete admixtures, roofing, flooring and bonding systems, for contractors, distributors and manufacturers in the building and automotive industries. It is a listed group headquartered in Baar, Switzerland, with subsidiaries in 103 countries. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Some of its financial and contractual detail may not be public, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. arguments.objective: Decide whether Sika AG should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example DIY or homeowner waterproofing, sealing, or bonding), beyond its contractor, distributor and industrial business. The decision should rest on evidence that a consumer proposition would earn returns above its cost, and on a clear view of how far Sika already reaches individual buyers.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact, no access to internal sales or contract data.
Test budget assumed at EUR 20,000 and 12 weeks maximum (analyst assumption, not a company figure).

Sika's existing consumer reach is unknown and must be established before theorising.

alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the current contractor, distributor and industrial model and serve homeowners only indirectly through existing trade channels.
B. Serve existing DIY/retail channels with current products: sell packaged versions of existing sealants and waterproofing through retailers and online, with minimal redesign.
C. Differentiated use-case product: redesign a product for one homeowner job (for example bathroom or roof leak repair, or floor bonding) with simplified packaging, instructions and a warranty.

D. Digital or service route: a consumer-facing advice, specification or booking layer that sends homeowners to Sika-approved installers, capturing value through products and referrals rather than owning the retail sale.

position.recommendation: Do not build a new differentiated consumer product yet. Sika already sells some pro-grade sealants, adhesives and patchers to DIY buyers through US retail, so the first step is a low-cost price and repeat test of a single-task, pro-grade pack against a plain pack. Expansion beyond that waits for the test result. Treat acquisition as a separate option that T2 predicts is the only route to brand power.

frame.objective: Decide whether Sika AG should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for individual buyers and one specific use case, beyond its contractor, distributor and industrial B2B chemicals, and identify what evidence would justify that investment rather than assume it.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or internal data

alternatives: No expansion: keep the B2B focus on contractors, distributors and industrial manufacturers and spend nothing new
Route expansion: sell existing consumer-grade sealants, waterproofing and adhesives through retail and DIY channels without redesigning products
Product redesign: build a packaged, simplified or pre-mixed consumer product for one home-use task such as bathroom waterproofing or tile repair
Customer-group shift: reach homeowners and small renovators through installer or handyman channels rather than end consumers directly
Partnership or licensing: supply a consumer brand or retailer with Sika formulations and let them own the shopper relationship
Acquisition of an existing consumer DIY sealants or adhesives brand

T1.claim: Individual buyers pay for a professional-grade brand on a single, low-risk home task. Sika's existing 'pro-grade' reputation carries over to a packaged DIY line sold through retail, so Sika can capture margin by placing its existing sealant, adhesive and patching products on shelf under a simple, task-specific label.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and DIYers who want proven, pro-used products for one job, and Sika through retail placement of existing formulations.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who fear failure on a visible job (leaks, cracked tiles) choose the brand professionals use over cheaper generic products, especially when the pack states one clear use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika sells existing formulations in consumer packs at a price premium over generic DIY products, with little new product development, through retailers it already serves.
assumptions: Pro-brand reputation transfers to DIY buyers
Retail shelf space can be won for existing formulations without redesign
Price premium over generic products is sustainable after retailer margin

Repeat purchase rises when packs state a single clear use
Sales lift is larger in markets where Sika already has a retail listing (e.g. US Pro Select) than where it has none
T1.first_claim: Individual buyers pay for a professional-grade brand on a single, low-risk home task. Sika's existing 'pro-grade' reputation carries over to a packaged DIY line sold through retail, so Sika can capture margin by placing its existing sealant, adhesive and patching products on shelf under a simple, task-specific label.

T2.claim: Individual buyers buy on price and shelf convenience, not on professional credentials. Consumer demand for sealants and adhesives is captured by whoever owns the shopper relationship and retailer shelf, so a pro-grade formulation earns no premium unless it is sold under a consumer brand built for DIY buyers, such as Everbuild.
T2.who_benefits: Retailers and DIY-focused brand owners who control shelf placement and shopper loyalty, and budget buyers who get cheaper generic products.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: DIY buyers compare visible price and pack size at the shelf and rarely know whether a product is pro-grade, so a professional reputation does not drive their choice.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika earns margin only by acquiring or building a consumer brand that holds shelf position and pricing power; supplying formulations to a retailer's own-label brand yields thin margin.
assumptions: Buyers do not pay a premium for pro-grade claims alone
Retailers capture most of the margin on own-label or unbranded lines
Consumer brand ownership, not formulation, is the scarce asset

X1.name: Pro-grade label price and repeat test on one online marketplace
X1.method: Run a 10-week paid listing test on one marketplace with one existing Sika-type sealant formulation sold in three pack variants at the same retail price band: (a) pro-grade label naming one home task, (b) same formulation in plain packaging with no professional claim, (c) generic-branded equivalent from a competitor for reference. Randomise listing exposure across variants and track sales, price realised, and repeat purchase.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 6000 shopper sessions per variant on the marketplace, roughly 3 to 4 weeks per variant rotation, with cost capped at EUR 20000 including media and product.
X1.measure: Units sold per 1000 sessions, realised price per unit of coverage, and 90-day repeat purchase rate for each variant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Variant (a) sells at a higher realised price per unit of coverage than (b) and (c), and its repeat rate is higher than (b).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Variant (a) shows no price premium over (b) and (c); units sold depend on listing position and price, not on the professional claim.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a retail pilot only if variant (a) realises at least 10 percent more per unit of coverage than both (b) and (c) with a 90-day repeat rate at least 5 percentage points higher than (b). If the premium is under 5 percent or repeat is not higher, reject the stand-alone pro-grade consumer line and treat the consumer route as brand-acquisition only.

revisions.reason: The simulated what-if, if it were real, would concern application help rather than the pro-grade label, so it does not test T1's price-premium claim. T1 is kept unchanged. The simulated result is not cited as evidence.

The read evidence does not yet separate T2 from T1. The Everbuild acquisition was stated as a merchant-channel move, and the Bostik Amazon listing is consistent with either an owned shopper relationship or a pro-label premium. T2 is kept as a live rival until the marketplace test runs. The simulated what-if is not cited.
Recording again that the simulated what-if changes nothing for T1. T1 is still untested on price premium, and nothing read so far separates it from T2. No simulated result is cited.

What-if only, SIMULATED and not real data. If it were real, it would show that application help raised purchases in a recruited group, a different mechanism from the pro-grade label. It does not test T1's price-premium claim, so T1 is kept. It is excluded from the finish evidence.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new differentiated consumer product yet. Sika already sells some pro-grade sealants, adhesives and patchers to DIY buyers through US retail, and it bought a UK consumer-facing sealant brand, Everbuild, in 2013. The first step is a low-cost price and repeat test of a single-task, pro-grade pack against a plain pack. Redesign or acquisition should wait for that result. Sika's own annual report says its specialised roofing, flooring and structural products are not marketed for DIY, so any consumer case is narrow.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and DIY buyers doing one visible, low-risk task, such as resealing a bathroom or window, who buy at retail or online. Contractors and distributors remain the core customers.
final.value_proposition: A proven, professional-grade sealant or adhesive packed for one named home task, so the buyer knows which product fits the job. Whether this earns a price premium is untested.
final.next_action: Run the proposed marketplace test X1 (proposed, not run; EUR 20000, 12 weeks). Compare a pro-grade-labelled single-task pack with a plain pack and a generic reference. Proceed only if the pro-grade pack realises at least 10 percent more per unit of coverage than both comparators and has a 90-day repeat rate at least 5 points higher than the plain pack.
final.uncertainty: Sika's consumer sales, margins and retail listings are not public, so I could not size the market or check whether US Pro Select is profitable. The Everbuild acquisition dates from 2013 and I found no current data on its consumer share. The only evidence on consumer price premium is a company marketing claim and a competitor's launch notice. These show pro-grade products are sold to consumers, not that buyers pay more for them. I found no evidence that contradicts T1, but none that confirms it either. The test thresholds are my proposals, not company figures.
