position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer investment yet. The only evidence for demand is Sika's own marketing and the existence of DIY lines in the US and Canada. Nothing I read shows that task-labelled packs sell, or that homeowners would pay for certified application. Favour T1 as the working hypothesis because it has a live retail precedent, and test it cheaply before deciding. If the pilot fails both arms, keep the contractor focus.

frame.objective: Decide whether Sika AG should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example DIY or homeowner sealing, waterproofing or repair) beyond its contractor, distributor and industrial channels, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The objective is an investment decision, not a claim that consumer demand exists.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no company contact or internal contractual or financial data.
Some financial and contractual detail (channel margins, existing consumer brands, retailer agreements) may not be public and must be flagged as unknown.
Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
Search budget is 8 searches, 7 remaining; read sources carefully.
Company's intentions are unknown; nothing in the brief describes what Sika wants.
alternatives: No expansion: keep the contractor, distributor and industrial focus and make no consumer investment.
Differentiated consumer product for a specific use case sold through existing retail partners (for example a DIY sealant or waterproofing kit for homeowners).
Product redesign of existing professional products into easier-to-use formats for trade and DIY buyers, without a separate consumer brand.
Different route to buyers: sell through online or trade-counter channels to small contractors and homeowners, instead of building a new product.
Partner or licence: supply formulations or contract-manufacture for an existing consumer brand, capturing value without owning the consumer relationship.
Different customer group: target small builders, renovators or property managers as a professional-but-small-volume segment, not individual consumers.

T1.claim: A retail product labelled for one specific homeowner repair, sold at the same price as an unbranded equivalent, sells more units through an existing Sika-linked retail partner. The bundled application kit is dropped from the claim, because the (simulated) evidence suggests bundled extras may not help.
T1.who_benefits: Retail partners who want a trusted brand for home-improvement shelves; DIY buyers who want professional-grade performance in a task-specific pack; Sika, which captures a premium per pack and extends brand reach to homeowners.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A homeowner facing a specific repair (for example a leaking joint or a small patch) will pick a product that is labelled for that job and trusted as professional-grade, rather than a generic product, because the task is clear and the brand signals performance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Sika earns a higher price per small pack than bulk pro supply, sells through existing retailer relationships with a shared margin, and keeps the professional product line separate so the consumer line does not undercut contractor sales.
assumptions: Retail partners in the target market will stock a Sika-branded task-specific product and accept its margin.
Homeowners in the chosen use case judge products by brand and visible task labelling more than by price.
Packaging and instructions can reduce misapplication enough that warranty and safety exposure stays acceptable.
The retail route is already commercially proven in the US and Canada, so the step is an extension, not a new channel.
predictions: In a test retail store, a task-labelled Sika pack outsells an unbranded equivalent at the same shelf price by a clear margin over 12 weeks.
Retail buyers in the chosen market agree to shelf space at a margin Sika finds acceptable.
Return and complaint rates for the consumer pack stay below the rate for comparable retail sealants.
T1.first_claim: Sika already sells consumer-facing lines through retail partners in some markets (Sika Pro Select in the US, Sakrete in Canada). A consumer proposition for one use case is most valuable when it extends that retail route with a pro-grade product repackaged for a specific DIY task, so the retailer's shelf and the Sika name carry the sale.

T2.claim: Sika's own annual report says its specialised products are not marketed for DIY because misapplication can cause performance failures and safety hazards. So the value of a consumer extension is capped by liability and brand risk, and the stronger lever is a trained-applicator or certified-installer route that brings homeowners to professional application rather than selling them product to apply themselves.
T2.who_benefits: Trained applicators and distributors who want more homeowner jobs; Sika, which keeps control of application quality and protects its brand from failures; homeowners who get a warranted result instead of a risky DIY job.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A homeowner with a roof, floor or waterproofing job that is too risky or too large to do safely will hire a certified applicator if one is easy to find and the product comes with a warranty tied to certified application, so the purchase shifts from a product to a service.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Sika earns on product sold into certified-applicator jobs, plus referral or certification fees from the applicator network, and avoids the warranty and claims costs of unsupervised DIY application.
assumptions: Homeowners will pay for a certified application if the warranty benefit is visible and the price gap is not too large.
Applicators will join a Sika-certified network in return for referred jobs and product margin.
Failures from DIY misuse would fall on Sika's brand and warranty even when it is not the seller.
The annual report's stated position reflects a real constraint and not only a marketing choice.
predictions: A warranty offer tied to certified application converts more homeowner enquiries than a DIY kit at the same price point.
Certified applicators accept referral and certification terms when they see a steady flow of homeowner jobs.
Claims rates on jobs done by certified applicators are lower than on comparable unsupervised DIY jobs.
T2.first_claim: Sika's own annual report says its specialised products are not marketed for DIY because misapplication can cause performance failures and safety hazards. So the value of a consumer extension is capped by liability and brand risk, and the stronger lever is a trained-applicator or certified-installer route that brings homeowners to professional application rather than selling them product to apply themselves.

assessments.quote: offer pro contractors and DIY'ers the same superior performing products developed and used on the most spectacular projects throughout the world
assessments.does_not_show: Sales volume, shelf share, retailer margins or whether DIY buyers choose the Pro Select range over cheaper alternatives. It is Sika's own marketing claim and says nothing about demand or whether task-labelled packs would outsell unbranded ones.

assessments.quote: These products are not marketed for DIY or general retail because improper application could lead to performance failures or safety hazards.
assessments.does_not_show: Whether this applies to the whole range or only to the specialised roofing, flooring and structural products it names. It does not show that homeowners would hire certified applicators, that a warranty would convert enquiries, or what applicator networks cost. It also sits awkwardly with the US Pro Select page, which markets DIY lines, so the company's position is not consistent across sources.

assessments.quote: nominal sales in the home improvement market in North America and Europe grew slightly in 2024, with increases of 1.6 percent and 1.2 percent respectively
assessments.does_not_show: Anything about Sika's own consumer sales, the share of DIY buyers who choose a pro-brand product, or whether task-labelled packs outsell unbranded ones. It is aggregate market size, so it neither supports nor contradicts T1's specific claim.

X1.name: Task-labelled pack vs unbranded equivalent; applicator warranty vs DIY kit (pilot)
X1.method: Two-arm field pilot with one retail partner in one market (proposed). Arm A: a task-labelled Sika pack for one homeowner repair (for example a joint or small patch) placed next to an unbranded equivalent at the same shelf price. Arm B: a certified-applicator warranty offer versus a DIY kit at the same price, shown through the retailer's website and a regional landing page. Track units, enquiries, returns and complaints. Data comes only from the pilot, not from Sika internal records.
X1.sample: Proposed: one retail chain with about 40 stores or one online listing, 8 to 10 weeks. Arm A needs enough store-weeks to detect a 20 percent unit difference. Arm B needs at least 300 homeowner enquiries per arm (estimated) to compare conversion.
X1.measure: Units per store-week for Arm A (task-labelled vs unbranded). Conversion from enquiry to purchase or booking for Arm B. Return and complaint rate per 100 units or jobs for both arms. Estimated cost 18000 EUR, about 10 weeks (estimated, within the 20000 EUR and 12-week limits).

prediction_by_theory.T1: The task-labelled pack sells at least 20 percent more units per store-week than the unbranded equivalent at the same price, with returns no higher than comparable retail sealants. The DIY kit converts enquiries at least as well as the warranty offer.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The certified-applicator warranty offer converts at least twice as many homeowner enquiries as the DIY kit at the same price, and the task-labelled pack shows no unit uplift over the unbranded equivalent.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed with a retail consumer pack (T1) only if Arm A shows at least 20 percent unit uplift over the unbranded equivalent with a return rate no more than 1.5 times the category average, and the retailer accepts a margin Sika can live with. Favour the applicator route (T2) if Arm B warranty conversion is at least 2 times the DIY kit and Arm A uplift is below 10 percent. If neither threshold is met, do not invest; keep the contractor focus (no expansion). Results between these bands are inconclusive and trigger a repeat with a larger sample.

revisions.reason: If the simulated offer test were real, it would weaken one part of T1. In that hypothetical, a kit with a smoothing tool and step-by-step guide bought less than the same cartridge with standard label instructions (32 versus 72 purchases per 400 assigned). This suggests that added application help, at least as a bundled kit, does not drive purchase in that group. It does not test task-labelled packaging at shelf price, and it is simulated, so it cannot be cited as evidence. It does not show demand beyond the recruited group, kit margins, or retailer stocking.
revisions.new_claim: A retail product labelled for one specific homeowner repair, sold at the same price as an unbranded equivalent, sells more units through an existing Sika-linked retail partner. The bundled application kit is dropped from the claim, because the (simulated) evidence suggests bundled extras may not help.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer investment yet. Keep the contractor, distributor and industrial focus as the default. Before any spend, run a small, cheap pilot to test whether a task-labelled product sells through a retail partner at a usable margin. The public evidence shows that Sika already sells DIY-positioned lines in some markets (the US Pro Select range and the Canadian Sakrete products). It does not show that these lines grow, what share of sales they make, or what they earn. Sika's own annual report says its specialised products are not marketed for DIY because misapplication risks failure and safety hazards, so the case is strongest for simpler, lower-risk products, not for roofing, flooring or structural systems.
final.target_customer: Homeowners doing one specific, low-risk repair (for example a sealant joint or small patch), buying through an existing retail partner. This is a hypothesis to test, not an established segment.
final.value_proposition: A product labelled for one specific repair, carrying the Sika name and professional-grade performance, sold at a premium to unbranded equivalents through retail. Whether this premium exists is untested.
final.next_action: Scope the pilot with a retail partner: a task-labelled pack against an unbranded equivalent at the same shelf price, for 8 to 10 weeks, with a proposed budget of about 18000 EUR. Ask Sika's own data (not available to me) for existing DIY line sales, margins and returns. Decide only if the pilot meets the threshold: at least 20 percent unit uplift, returns no more than 1.5 times the category average, and a retailer margin Sika accepts. If the pilot fails, keep no expansion. A separate applicator-warranty route (T2) could be tested alongside.
final.uncertainty: High. I found no measured consumer sales, shelf share, retail margins, or return rates for any Sika consumer line. The Canadian and US sources are company marketing claims. The market data is aggregate and says nothing about Sika's share. The Everbuild acquisition (2013) shows a UK merchant-market route but not a DIY one. Contractual and financial details are not public. Both theories remain uncertain, and the simulated result I was shown is not evidence and is not cited here.
would_change_if: Sika's internal or public figures show existing DIY line sales that are small, flat or loss-making, which would argue against T1.
A real pilot shows at least 20 percent unit uplift over an unbranded equivalent with acceptable returns, which would strengthen T1.
A real pilot shows certified-applicator warranty offers converting at least twice as well as DIY kits, which would shift the case toward T2.
Retail partners refuse shelf space at a margin Sika can accept, which would argue against any retail consumer proposition.

Public evidence that the annual report's DIY restriction has changed for simpler products, or that roofing or flooring product failures are rising from misuse, which would strengthen the risk concern.

result.title: Simulated home-sealant application offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: If the simulated offer test were real, it would weaken one part of T1. In that hypothetical, a kit with a smoothing tool and step-by-step guide bought less than the same cartridge with standard label instructions (32 versus 72 purchases per 400 assigned). This suggests that added application help, at least as a bundled kit, does not drive purchase in that group. It does not test task-labelled packaging at shelf price, and it is simulated, so it cannot be cited as evidence. It does not show demand beyond the recruited group, kit margins, or retailer stocking.
arguments.new_claim: A retail product labelled for one specific homeowner repair, sold at the same price as an unbranded equivalent, sells more units through an existing Sika-linked retail partner. The bundled application kit is dropped from the claim, because the (simulated) evidence suggests bundled extras may not help.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer investment yet. Keep the contractor, distributor and industrial focus as the default. Before any spend, run a small, cheap pilot to test whether a task-labelled product sells through a retail partner at a usable margin. The public evidence shows that Sika already sells DIY-positioned lines in some markets (the US Pro Select range and the Canadian Sakrete products). It does not show that these lines grow, what share of sales they make, or what they earn. Sika's own annual report says its specialised products are not marketed for DIY because misapplication risks failure and safety hazards, so the case is strongest for simpler, lower-risk products, not for roofing, flooring or structural systems.
arguments.target_customer: Homeowners doing one specific, low-risk repair (for example a sealant joint or small patch), buying through an existing retail partner. This is a hypothesis to test, not an established segment.
arguments.value_proposition: A product labelled for one specific repair, carrying the Sika name and professional-grade performance, sold at a premium to unbranded equivalents through retail. Whether this premium exists is untested.
arguments.next_action: Scope the pilot with a retail partner: a task-labelled pack against an unbranded equivalent at the same shelf price, for 8 to 10 weeks, with a proposed budget of about 18000 EUR. Ask Sika's own data (not available to me) for existing DIY line sales, margins and returns. Decide only if the pilot meets the threshold: at least 20 percent unit uplift, returns no more than 1.5 times the category average, and a retailer margin Sika accepts. If the pilot fails, keep no expansion. A separate applicator-warranty route (T2) could be tested alongside.
arguments.uncertainty: High. I found no measured consumer sales, shelf share, retail margins, or return rates for any Sika consumer line. The Canadian and US sources are company marketing claims. The market data is aggregate and says nothing about Sika's share. The Everbuild acquisition (2013) shows a UK merchant-market route but not a DIY one. Contractual and financial details are not public. Both theories remain uncertain, and the simulated result I was shown is not evidence and is not cited here.
would_change_if: Sika's internal or public figures show existing DIY line sales that are small, flat or loss-making, which would argue against T1.
A real pilot shows at least 20 percent unit uplift over an unbranded equivalent with acceptable returns, which would strengthen T1.
A real pilot shows certified-applicator warranty offers converting at least twice as well as DIY kits, which would shift the case toward T2.
Retail partners refuse shelf space at a margin Sika can accept, which would argue against any retail consumer proposition.

Public evidence that the annual report's DIY restriction has changed for simpler products, or that roofing or flooring product failures are rising from misuse, which would strengthen the risk concern.

X1.name: Retail pack-format pilot with installer-callback tracking
X1.method: Controlled in-store pilot across two matched retail regions. In each region, sell three existing Sika repair SKUs in two pack formats: the current trade-style pack and a consumer pack with step-by-step instructions and a recognised brand panel. Rotate formats across stores on a fixed schedule to remove store effects. Track sell-through, and survey a sample of buyers after 6 weeks on whether they used the product themselves and whether they called an installer for any failure.
X1.sample: Proposed: 12 retail stores (6 per region), 3 SKUs, roughly 10 weeks of sales, and about 150 buyer follow-up surveys.
X1.measure: Units sold per store-week by format; share of buyers self-applying (not via a contractor); installer call-back rate within 6 weeks; price realised per unit by format.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer-pack sell-through per store-week is at least 25% above trade-pack sell-through, most buyers self-apply, and realised price is higher per unit with no rise in installer call-backs.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Consumer-pack sell-through is no more than 10% above trade-pack sell-through, buyers mostly hand the job to an installer or do not apply the product themselves, and call-back rate is high for self-applied units.

X1.decision_rule: Favour T1 if consumer-pack sell-through is at least 25% above trade-pack and call-back rate among self-applied buyers is at or below 15%. Favour T2 if the uplift is 10% or less, or if self-applied buyers call an installer at more than 30%. Anything between is inconclusive and triggers a larger test, not a launch decision.

revisions.reason: SYN-SIKA-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not evidence. Reasoning as if it were real: the kit offer with instructions converted 32 of 400 against 72 of 400 for the cartridge alone, a lower completed-purchase rate. That cuts against the core T1 mechanism that a step-by-step, brand-led consumer pack wins purchases on ease of use. It would also make the price-premium prediction harder to hold. It applies only to a recruited group, a single product, and purchases not returned in 30 days, so it would weaken T1 for kit-style packs without ruling out retail sales of other formats.
revisions.new_claim: Homeowners buy repair products at retail when a recognised brand and existing retail shelf presence make the product easy to find and trust. Ease of use via an added kit is not assumed to raise purchases; that must be tested separately.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new standalone consumer brand or direct-to-consumer channel yet. Sika already reaches DIY buyers through retail partners in the US, by its own account, so the real question is whether a consumer-formatted version of existing non-isocyanate repair products sells and holds price. Test that cheaply with pilot X1 (proposed cost about 15,000 EUR, 10 weeks, estimated). Keep polyurethane products out of consumer packs until handling and labelling rules are checked. Treat the installer-led model as the default for waterproofing until the pilot says otherwise.
final.target_customer: Homeowners doing small repair or sealing jobs who buy at retail, and the retail partners who stock them. Not general consumers buying waterproofing systems, which the evidence suggests still runs through installers.
final.value_proposition: Existing Sika repair chemistry in a retail-ready, clearly labelled pack from a recognised brand, priced above the trade equivalent. This is a hypothesis, not a validated offer.
final.next_action: Run pilot X1 with retail partners: matched stores, trade vs consumer pack formats on three existing non-PU SKUs, sell-through and installer call-back tracked for 10 weeks. Request existing retail sell-through and any consumer-line sales data from Sika, since these are not public.
final.uncertainty: High. Sika's financial and contractual detail for consumer or retail lines is not public, so size, margin and profitability are unknown. Sika consumer evidence is company marketing plus a 2013 acquisition article giving a merchant-channel rationale. Bostik items are competitor evidence. The EU diisocyanate rule covers professional users; I did not check US equivalents. The simulated result was excluded from evidence. Beliefs are uncertain on T1 and T2.

T1.claim: Households will return drink containers more often if they can drop off bulk bags at a collection point and get the deposit back without sorting, so a TOMRA-run consumer collection service would increase its share of container volume and earn per-container fees from deposit operators.
T1.who_benefits: Households with large volumes of containers, and deposit system operators who need higher return rates to meet targets

X1.name: Paid convenience pilot versus free return point, priced consumer demand test
X1.method: Offer a paid or subscription bulk-return option (bag drop with pickup or drop-off at a partner store) in a single metro with a deposit scheme already live. Randomise households by postcode cluster to: (a) free return point only, (b) free return plus paid bulk option at a stated price, (c) free return plus free bulk option. Track returns and paid sign-ups. Use an online pre-order with a refundable deposit as a demand check.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 1,200 households across 6 postcode clusters, 400 per arm, recruited through a panel provider. Estimated cost within EUR 20,000 budget (analyst assumption).
X1.measure: Share of households taking up the paid option within 4 weeks; containers returned per household per week in each arm; willingness to pay for bulk return.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Free bulk option raises containers returned per household versus free return point only; paid option still gets measurable uptake, showing the operator should pay for collection capacity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Paid option gets near-zero uptake when a free return point is nearby; free bulk option changes returns little; value lies in retailer and operator contracts, not consumer payment.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if paid uptake is below 5% of households in the paid arm and free bulk raises returns by less than 10% per household, keep T2 and do not build a consumer proposition. If paid uptake is at or above 15% and returns rise by at least 10%, T1 is supported and a consumer service merits a further pilot. Between these thresholds, the result is inconclusive.

revisions.reason: If SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE were real, it would weaken T2's prediction that a paid private return service gets near-zero uptake. In that hypothetical, a doorstep collection offer at the same fee gained 72 active paid sign-ups per 400 (18%) against 32 (8%) for store drop-off. That would mean some households pay for removing the return trip, though it is one simulated group, with no test of pricing, store partners or whether the fee covers cost. This is a simulated what-if, so it does not count as evidence and I do not rely on it for the recommendation.
revisions.new_claim: A paid return service may find uptake where the return trip is the main cost to the household, but willingness to pay is untested and the value to TOMRA would still depend on operator and retailer contracts.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the core investment in the obligated B2B channel (retailers and deposit operators, where regulation creates demand for return points and machines). Treat bulk bag-drop and home collection as operator-contracted services, and run the proposed paid-convenience pilot (X1) before any consumer-facing build. The existing consumer footprint is mostly company-reported: a North American bag-drop acquisition and a New South Wales app. Neither shows consumers paying TOMRA directly.
final.target_customer: Not chosen. Obligated retailers and deposit system operators are the evidenced buyers. Households are a possible later segment, pending the pilot.
final.value_proposition: For obligated retailers and operators: return-point machines and collection services that meet scheme obligations. A consumer convenience offer is a hypothesis, not a proposition yet.
final.next_action: Scope and price the X1 pilot (proposed: about 1,200 households, three arms, about EUR 18,500, 10 weeks) and seek a deposit operator or scheme partner to co-fund it. Also search for TOMRA's own disclosure of consumer-channel revenue and of how bag-drop and app services are priced, which I could not find.
final.uncertainty: High. I could not access TOMRA's contracts, pricing, consumer revenue, or how much of its machine demand comes from retailer obligations versus operators. The evidence on consumer behaviour is one company-authored North American claim about bag drop, a Canadian operator blog post on depot convenience with no cited figures, and regulatory descriptions that do not say who pays. The X1 test is only proposed; no data have been collected. Theory T1 (convenience generates paid operator demand) is still uncertain.
would_change_if: X1 pilot shows paid uptake at or above 15% of households and containers returned rising by at least 10%: T1 would be supported and a consumer pilot would merit funding.

It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-owned product yet. The only consumer-facing activity I found is TOMRA's own myTOMRA app and bag-drop acquisition, both presented in company claims. If TOMRA wants to test further, it should run a low-cost pilot in which an operator or municipality pays for a convenience service, and it should treat consumer willingness to pay for hardware as unproven.

frame.objective: Decide whether TOMRA should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, beyond its B2B reverse vending and sorting business, and what evidence would justify that investment. First establish whether any consumer-facing business already exists.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company intent is implied
Search budget is 8 with 7 remaining; test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions

Claims made by TOMRA itself are company assertions, not proof of consumer demand
alternatives: No expansion: remain B2B (reverse vending for deposit systems, sensor sorting for recyclers, mining and food)
Consumer-facing return-point proposition for households, such as home or retail return convenience
Product redesign: adapt existing sorting or vending hardware into a smaller consumer-grade unit
Different route to buyers: sell through retailers or deposit operators as a consumer service rather than direct consumer sales
Different customer group: municipalities or brand owners funding consumer return and recycling services
Consumer-facing data or traceability service, such as deposit credits or a circular-economy app, rather than hardware

T1.claim: Households return containers more when returning is convenient and refunds are paid digitally or in bulk. A consumer-facing return service (app payout, bag drop, mapped return points) therefore raises return rates in deposit systems that give no retailer obligation, and the operator or government pays TOMRA a per-container or service fee for that lift.
T1.who_benefits: Deposit scheme operators and state governments that need higher return rates; households who avoid queuing and carrying bags.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Friction is the barrier to returning containers. Removing it through a digital payout, a map to return points or a bag drop changes the cost of returning, so more people return containers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA sells the software, app and collection logistics as a service to the scheme operator, billed per container or per year. The consumer does not pay directly.
assumptions: Return rate is limited by convenience rather than by lack of deposit value or by lack of motivation
Scheme operators will pay for consumer-facing tools that lift return rates
The app or bag drop is the marginal cause of extra returns, not reverse vending machines alone
predictions: Regions that add a digital payout or bag drop show a larger rise in return rate than matched regions without one
Return rate gains are largest where no retailer obligation exists, as in NSW
Operators renew or expand these services when return rate targets are set
T1.first_claim: Households return containers more when returning is convenient and refunds are paid digitally or in bulk. A consumer-facing return service (app payout, bag drop, mapped return points) therefore raises return rates in deposit systems that give no retailer obligation, and the operator or government pays TOMRA a per-container or service fee for that lift.

T2.claim: Households will not pay for a consumer-owned return device or service, because the container deposit is small and the return is a chore. Any consumer-facing proposition therefore has to be paid for by a third party such as a brand owner or a municipality, which makes the consumer a passive user rather than a customer, and TOMRA's margin depends on that third-party contract rather than on consumer demand.
T2.who_benefits: Brand owners with extended producer responsibility obligations and municipalities that pay for collection; these payers, not households, would be the buyers.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A household does not return containers because the value of a single deposit is low compared with the effort. A paying third party changes the economics: it wants the containers returned and will fund the collection point, so the household gets a free service and has no reason to buy a device.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA sells machines and collection services to a brand owner or municipality under a contract, with the consumer as an unpaid user.
assumptions: Household willingness to pay for a return device or service is near zero
Extended producer responsibility or municipal budgets are large enough to fund collection
Households respond to free convenience but not to paid convenience
predictions: Pilots where consumers must pay for a return service see low uptake compared with free ones
Collection points funded by brand owners or municipalities carry the largest volumes
Contract revenue, not consumer sales, makes up most of any consumer-facing business

assessments.does_not_show: This is TOMRA describing its own rationale for building the app. It does not show that the app raised return rates, how many of the 10 million sessions led to a return, whether the NSW operator paid TOMRA for it, or how much of the value came from the app versus the reverse vending machines. It supports that the mechanism was attempted, not that it works.

assessments.does_not_show: This is about a different company's home composter, not TOMRA or return devices. It does not show household willingness to pay for return equipment, the price at which a return device would sell, or whether a free or operator-funded service would meet the same resistance. It shows only that a consumer hardware category needed demonstrations to sell, which is consistent with T2 but does not test it.

assessments.quote: Respondents also overwhelmingly chose to visit that specific retail location partially or mainly due to the convenience of the bottle return system offered by the retailer.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a 2013 New York survey of self-reported shopping choices, so it shows that convenience matters to where people return containers, not that a consumer-facing service raises return rates. It also shows the value going to the retailer through footfall, not to a deposit operator or to TOMRA. It partly undercuts T1's value capture, because a retailer that offers returns may keep the benefit and not pay a vendor for it. The survey does not give return rates or effect sizes.

X1.name: Matched-district return-convenience pilot with paid-device price test
X1.method: Two-part test. Part A: a matched-pair field trial with a partner collection point operator, where treatment districts get a digital refund payout and a mapped return-point service and control districts keep usual returns. Part B: an online and in-store willingness-to-pay survey that offers a consumer-owned return device or paid return service at several price points, with a free operator-funded option alongside.
X1.sample: Part A: 4 matched district pairs, roughly 2,000 households per arm (proposed). Part B: about 800 respondents in the partner's catchment area (proposed).
X1.measure: Part A: containers returned per household per week, measured from partner scan data, with the matched control. Part B: stated take-up at each price point and the share who choose the free option when it is offered.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Treatment districts show a clear rise in returns over control, and the operator would pay for the service once the uplift is shown.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Treatment shows little or no rise over control in Part A, or Part B shows near-zero paid take-up, so consumers will not pay and value must come from a third-party contract.

X1.decision_rule: Keep T1 only if Part A shows a relative return-rate uplift of at least 15% over control with a 95% interval excluding zero, and Part B shows paid take-up at or below 10% at every price tested (which means value must come from an operator contract, the T1 model). Reject T1 if Part A uplift is below 5%. If uplift is between 5% and 15%, treat the result as inconclusive and do not invest beyond the pilot. Thresholds are proposed, not observed.

revisions.reason: The simulated result SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE is labelled SIMULATED and states that no study was conducted, so I cannot cite it. Real evidence still leaves T2 open. The only direct support is an analogy from a different company's home composter, which shows that consumer hardware needed demonstrations to sell. It does not test household willingness to pay for return services. The X1 pilot is the way to test T2.

The simulated result SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE is excluded because it is labelled SIMULATED and no study was conducted. It is not evidence for or against T1. The real evidence for T1 is still indirect: TOMRA's own account of the NSW app, the company's bag-drop acquisition, and a 2013 survey showing that convenience drives where people return containers. None measures a return-rate uplift from an operator-paid service. T1 stays as the favoured hypothesis, to be tested in X1.

What-if only. If SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE were real, its paid sign-ups (72 of 400 for doorstep collection, 32 of 400 for store drop-off after 30 days) would show that some households pay for a return convenience, which would weaken T2's claim that willingness to pay is near zero. It is SIMULATED, so I do not count it as evidence and I do not change my belief. It is kept only as a hypothesis for the X1 pilot to test. The real evidence still leaves T2 open.

final.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-owned hardware product now. TOMRA already has a consumer-adjacent presence through the myTOMRA app in New South Wales and the bag-drop collection business it acquired in the northeastern U.S., but the evidence for both comes from TOMRA's own announcements, with no independent return-rate data. The most promising route is a service that an operator, municipality or brand owner pays for, because it raises returns. Test that before any hardware investment. The pilot is proposed at EUR 18,500 over 12 weeks; this is an estimate, not a company figure.
final.target_customer: Deposit-scheme operators and governments that need higher return rates, and possibly brand owners or municipalities funding collection. Households are the users rather than the paying customer, on the current evidence.
final.value_proposition: Convenient returns (digital refund payout, mapped return points, bag drop) that lift return rates, sold as a per-container or service fee to the party that pays for collection.
final.next_action: Run the matched-district pilot in X1 with a partner collection operator, plus the paid-device willingness survey. Before that, ask for TOMRA's deposit-system and collection contract terms, which are not public, to learn whether any consumer service is already priced per container. Decide on investment only after the pilot's decision rule is applied.
final.uncertainty: High. I could not find TOMRA's contract terms, the revenue or margin of its consumer-facing services, or any independent measurement of return-rate uplift from the NSW app or the bag-drop service. The NYPIRG survey is from 2013 and concerns retailer-offered returns, so it may not apply to a TOMRA service. T2's core claim, that households will not pay, is untested; the only related evidence is an analogy from another product. The simulated result SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE is excluded from all evidence I rely on.
would_change_if: Part A of X1 shows a relative return-rate uplift below 5% over matched control, which would reject T1
Operators or brand owners will not pay a per-container fee for a return convenience service even after uplift is shown
Part B shows paid take-up above 10% at a price that covers collection cost, which would support a consumer-paid model over T1
TOMRA's own contract data show that NSW app or bag-drop revenue is small or unprofitable
Independent evaluation shows that retailer-offered returns capture the footfall gain, leaving no value for an operator-paid service

prediction_by_theory.T1: Treatment districts show a clear rise in returns over control, and the operator would pay for the service once the uplift is shown.

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1.claim: Households take up a return service when it fits an existing routine such as a store trip, not necessarily when it removes all effort. Platform value comes from routing and payout, with operator fees as the capture mechanism. Whether doorstep collection pays at any fee is unproven.
T1.who_benefits: Households with many containers who value time saving; deposit system operators and producers who need collection rates; TOMRA as platform owner that captures fees or data.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Current return effort (sorting, counting, travelling to a machine) is a cost. A digital payout or bag-drop removes part of that cost, so more containers are returned and more refunds are claimed when the service is convenient.
T1.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA earns from operators or brand owners who pay per collected container or per service, and possibly from app usage data. Consumers pay nothing directly.

T1.first_claim: Households will pay for or use a digital return service (app-based payout, locating return points, bag-drop collection) because it removes the time and hassle of counting and carrying containers. Where a scheme does not oblige retailers to host return points, a platform that aggregates refunds and collection can capture value from the operator or brand-owner side.

T2.claim: Households do not return containers mainly because of effort. They hold containers because the deposit value is too small to motivate a trip. A consumer product that raises the value per return, for example by bundling refunds into a donation or a loyalty credit, would change behaviour more than convenience alone, and a manufacturer that owns the refund mechanism could capture a share of that value.
T2.who_benefits: Households that hold containers; charities or retailers that receive donated or credited refunds; TOMRA if it captures a fee on the refund mechanism.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A small deposit makes a return trip seem not worth it. If the refund is donated or converted into a larger reward, the perceived value of each return rises, so more people make the trip.
T2.how_value_is_captured: TOMRA earns a transaction or platform fee on refund routing, or sells the machine and software that enables donation or credit at the point of return.

X1.name: Convenience versus value-per-return pilot at existing machine sites
X1.method: Randomised pilot across sites in one deposit-scheme market where TOMRA or a partner already runs machines. Sites are split into three arms for 12 weeks: (a) control with cash refund only; (b) convenience arm with digital payout and a return-point map added; (c) value arm with a donation or credit option added at the machine. Container counts and app or donation uptake are logged per site. Scheme terms are not changed.
X1.sample: Proposed: 30 sites, 10 per arm, selected to be comparable on footfall. Estimated 150 to 200 weekly active returners per site.
X1.measure: Containers returned per site per week, relative to the control arm's baseline in weeks 1 to 2. Secondary: share of refunds taken as digital payout or donation.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The convenience arm raises returns per site by a larger margin than the value arm, because the cost of returning falls rather than the reward rising.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The value arm raises returns per site by a larger margin than the convenience arm, because the reward per return rises rather than the cost of returning falling.

X1.decision_rule: Back T1 if the convenience arm's uplift is at least 1.5 times the value arm's uplift and both are above 5 percent over control. Back T2 if the reverse holds by the same margin. If neither arm clears 5 percent, or the two uplifts are within 1.5 times of each other, neither theory is supported and the investment case stays unproven.

The result also does not test deposit value (T2), and it is limited to one recruited group, so it does not decide between the theories. Under this what-if, T1 would need a narrower claim: the return trip and its fit with routine matter, not only how little effort it takes.

TOMRA already reaches individuals indirectly, through the myTOMRA refund app in New South Wales and the bag-drop collection business it acquired in the northeastern US. final.value_proposition: A refund and collection service that raises return rates through digital payout, return-point routing and possibly bag-drop, with TOMRA earning fees from operators or producers. Its value depends on evidence not yet gathered.

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: SIMULATED, hypothetical only, not real data. If this result were real, it would weaken the simple form of T1. The doorstep-collection offer, which removes the most effort, got fewer active sign-ups after 30 days (32) than the store drop-off offer (72). So reducing effort alone does not explain uptake. The result also does not test deposit value (T2), and it is limited to one recruited group, so it does not decide between the theories. Under this what-if, T1 would need a narrower claim: the return trip and its fit with routine matter, not only how little effort it takes.
arguments.new_claim: Households take up a return service when it fits an existing routine such as a store trip, not necessarily when it removes all effort. Platform value comes from routing and payout, with operator fees as the capture mechanism. Whether doorstep collection pays at any fee is unproven.

Treat the consumer route as a platform or service extension of existing channels, not a new device line.

arguments.value_proposition: A refund and collection service that raises return rates through digital payout, return-point routing and possibly bag-drop, with TOMRA earning fees from operators or producers. tool_result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-branded proposition yet. Keep the B2B model as the base, and test a paid collection option with a deposit operator or retailer before any consumer investment.

frame.objective: Decide whether TOMRA should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing B2B reverse vending and sensor sorting, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. First establish how far TOMRA already reaches individual buyers.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked and nothing here describes its intentions
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state what could not be found
Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget is 8 in total, 7 remaining, so evidence searches must be targeted
Every observed number must come from a source read; proposed numbers must be labelled as proposed or estimated
alternatives: No expansion: keep the current B2B and deposit-system model and invest only in core machines
Consumer-facing product redesign: a home or consumer version of existing sensor sorting or reverse vending
Different route to existing buyers: reach consumers through retailers or deposit operators, for example an incentive or app layer on existing machines
Different customer group: consumer brands, municipalities or households as direct buyers of recycling or sorting services
Adjacent use case: food or packaging quality sorting sold to small producers such as farmers or packhouses rather than end consumers
Partnership or licensing of the consumer use case to a third party rather than building it in-house

T1.claim: Return convenience affects behaviour, but the claim that doorstep or bag collection is the paid-for convenience is unsupported; the return point's location may matter more, which would favour a retailer or operator capturing the value.
T1.who_benefits: Households who dislike carrying bags to a return point, and TOMRA plus deposit system operators if they earn per-container or per-collection fees.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Return rates depend on effort. When collection moves to the doorstep or a drop-off point that takes whole bags, the time cost falls, so more containers return and more consumers use the service.
T1.how_value_is_captured: A fee per bag or per collection, or a share of unredeemed deposits, paid by deposit operators or retailers, earned from TOMRA's existing reverse logistics and machine network.
assumptions: Unredeemed deposits or handling savings are large enough to fund a paid collection service
Consumers value convenience enough to change habits, and the effect is not limited to a small, already-motivated group
Deposit operators will outsource collection rather than run it in-house
Regulation permits a collection channel that is not a retailer return point
predictions: In markets with bag drop or doorstep collection, return rates rise compared with markets that rely only on in-store machines
Paying households or operators will sign recurring collection contracts with a per-bag fee
Bag drop volumes grow where retail return points are scarce
T1.first_claim: Households will pay for convenience in returning deposit containers, through bag drop or home collection, and a manufacturer that already runs the machines and logistics can capture a service fee from that demand.

T2.claim: Retailers and deposit system operators, not consumers, control the return relationship and the regulatory obligation, so the value of any consumer-facing layer stays with them and TOMRA's best return is to keep selling machines and sorting systems on a B2B basis.
T2.who_benefits: Retailers and deposit system operators, who keep the customer contact and the compliance duty; TOMRA keeps a machine-supply role without carrying consumer risk.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers return containers where the scheme places a machine or a return point, so the behaviour follows the placement decision made by the retailer or operator, not any product the manufacturer brands for households.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Equipment sales and service contracts with retailers and operators, priced per machine or per transaction, with no direct consumer billing.
assumptions: Schemes assign the return-point duty to retailers, as in England and Northern Ireland guidance
Consumers judge return points by location and reliability rather than by brand
Operators prefer to keep consumer contact and will not hand it to a machine maker
predictions: Where schemes assign the return duty to retailers, TOMRA sells machines but not a consumer-branded service
Retailers that switch manufacturers do so on price and uptime, not on consumer-facing features
Consumer complaints about machine uptime are the main driver of supplier switching
T2.first_claim: Retailers and deposit system operators, not consumers, control the return relationship and the regulatory obligation, so the value of any consumer-facing layer stays with them and TOMRA's best return is to keep selling machines and sorting systems on a B2B basis.

assessments.quote: Bag drop is a convenient collection method whereby consumers can drop off entire bags of empty beverage containers at collection points and have their deposit refunded. It is a well-established and popular complement to reverse vending machines and redemption centers in North America, with strong growth potential.
assessments.does_not_show: It is TOMRA's own claim, with no volumes, return-rate effect, consumer willingness to pay, or fee level. 'Popular' and 'strong growth potential' are unquantified. It is also a North American market, not the European schemes where the other sources sit.

assessments.quote: However, it added, a number of retailers decided to switch RVMs to an alternative manufacturer. The statement comes as some consumers have complained machines were not working when they tried to return bottles and cans and collect their deposits.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a news report of a statement by an unnamed party, not an audit. It does not give the number of retailers, the reason for switching, or whether uptime or price drove the decision, and it does not show that consumers judge by brand rather than location.

assessments.quote: Respondents also overwhelmingly chose to visit that specific retail location partially or mainly due to the convenience of the bottle return system offered by the retailer.
assessments.does_not_show: It is a 2013 survey in New York State, with no sample size or response rate in the excerpt. It shows that return convenience affects store choice, not that households would pay a fee for home or bag collection. The value it shows goes to the retailer through store traffic, which supports T2's capture logic at least as much as T1's.

X1.name: Paid bag-drop pilot with household sample
X1.method: Offer a paid doorstep or bag-drop collection option to a random subset of households in one region, against a matched control region with only in-store return. Track containers returned and willingness to pay. Propose a short price test at two fee levels (proposed).
X1.sample: Proposed: about 600 households across 2 matched areas, with 300 in the bag-drop arm, recruited via a deposit operator or retailer partner
X1.measure: Share of deposit containers returned per household per month, uptake of the paid option at each fee, and whether the retailer or operator will sign a per-bag fee

prediction_by_theory.T1: Uptake of the paid bag-drop option is high enough at a fee of about 1 euro per bag that return rates rise materially in the bag-drop arm versus control, and a deposit operator agrees to pay the per-bag fee.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Households take up the collection option only where the retailer or operator subsidises or runs it; no operator signs a per-bag fee and uptake without subsidy stays low, so return rates in the arm barely move.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a consumer-facing investment only if (a) paid uptake is at least 25 percent of the arm at the proposed fee and (b) return rates in the bag-drop arm are at least 10 percentage points above control, and (c) at least one operator signs a per-bag fee commitment. Otherwise keep the B2B model (T2).

revisions.reason: SIMULATED, NOT REAL DATA. If this hypothetical result were real, a store drop-off offer (72 active sign-ups per 400) would have beaten doorstep collection (32 per 400) at the same fee. That would count against the part of T1 that says home collection is the convenience households pay for, and support the view that the return point itself, which retailers control, is what drives behaviour. It would not show that households pay for any collection service. This is a what-if only and is not cited as evidence.
revisions.new_claim: Return convenience affects behaviour, but the claim that doorstep or bag collection is the paid-for convenience is unsupported; the return point's location may matter more, which would favour a retailer or operator capturing the value.

final.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-branded or direct-to-household proposition now. Keep the B2B model (reverse vending and sensor sorting sold to retailers and deposit operators) as the base. Before any consumer investment, test a paid collection option with a deposit operator or retailer partner, at a proposed budget of 18,000 EUR over 10 weeks.
final.target_customer: No consumer target is recommended yet. The only candidate for a test is households in a deposit scheme, reached through a deposit operator or retailer partner.
final.value_proposition: Not yet established. The candidate is a paid bag or doorstep collection service, with TOMRA earning a per-bag or per-collection fee from operators, but no evidence I read shows households would pay for it.
final.next_action: Run the proposed X1 test with a deposit operator or retailer partner, since the operator holds the consumer relationship and the scheme duty. Measure return rates, paid uptake at two fee levels, and whether an operator will sign a per-bag fee. Proceed only if the decision rule is met.
final.uncertainty: Much is unknown. I could not find TOMRA's own consumer revenue, contract terms or how far it already reaches individual buyers in Europe; the C&C bag-drop acquisition is a company claim about North America with no volumes. The only consumer-behaviour evidence I read is a 2013 New York survey with no sample size in the excerpt, and a 2024 Irish news report of unnamed retailers switching machines. The SIMULATED update is not evidence. Proposed test figures (600 households, 1 euro fee, 25 percent uptake, 10 point return gap) are my estimates.
would_change_if: Real data showing households in a deposit scheme pay for bag or doorstep collection at a fee that covers TOMRA's cost, with uptake above the 25 percent threshold
Evidence that TOMRA already sells to individual consumers at scale, which would change the starting position
An operator or retailer signing a per-bag fee commitment, which would support the service model
Evidence that retailers control supplier choice mainly on price and uptime, which would confirm T2 and rule out a consumer layer
Independent (non-company) evidence on return-rate effects of bag drop versus in-store return

arguments.method: Offer a paid doorstep or bag-drop collection option to a random subset of households in one region, against a matched control region with only in-store return. Track containers returned and willingness to pay. Propose a short price test at two fee levels (proposed).

result.title: Simulated home container-collection offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: SIMULATED, NOT REAL DATA. If this hypothetical result were real, a store drop-off offer (72 active sign-ups per 400) would have beaten doorstep collection (32 per 400) at the same fee. That would count against the part of T1 that says home collection is the convenience households pay for, and support the view that the return point itself, which retailers control, is what drives behaviour. It would not show that households pay for any collection service. This is a what-if only and is not cited as evidence.
arguments.new_claim: Return convenience affects behaviour, but the claim that doorstep or bag collection is the paid-for convenience is unsupported; the return point's location may matter more, which would favour a retailer or operator capturing the value.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-branded or direct-to-household proposition now. arguments.target_customer: No consumer target is recommended yet. The only candidate for a test is households in a deposit scheme, reached through a deposit operator or retailer partner.
arguments.value_proposition: Not yet established. The candidate is a paid bag or doorstep collection service, with TOMRA earning a per-bag or per-collection fee from operators, but no evidence I read shows households would pay for it.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed X1 test with a deposit operator or retailer partner, since the operator holds the consumer relationship and the scheme duty. arguments.uncertainty: Much is unknown. The only consumer-behaviour evidence I read is a 2013 New York survey with no sample size in the excerpt, and a 2024 Irish news report of unnamed retailers switching machines. The SIMULATED update is not evidence. Proposed test figures (600 households, 1 euro fee, 25 percent uptake, 10 point return gap) are my estimates.

The real objective is to find where individual buyers would pay for braking performance or upgrades in a way Brembo can capture, without damaging its OEM and aftermarket business.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Continued sales of replacement parts via distributors and workshops, with no new consumer channel and no added marketing spend

position.recommendation: Do not build a standalone direct-to-consumer proposition now. Keep the trade and installer channel as the main route. Run the low-cost choice experiment (X1) before any investment. T1 is not yet rejected: the evidence on brand premium is thin and one-sided, and the experiment should test it directly.

frame.objective: Decide whether Brembo N.V. should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case beyond its OEM supply and aftermarket replacement parts, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The decision turns on whether individual buyers form a value pool Brembo can capture profitably without damaging OEM relationships.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company; no knowledge of its intentions
Brembo's current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be verified, not assumed
OEM contracts, aftermarket margins and channel agreements are likely not public
Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget is limited (7 searches remaining)

alternatives: No expansion: keep OEM supply and aftermarket replacement parts as they are
Aftermarket channel deepening: improve availability, distribution or brand presence for independent workshops
Direct-to-consumer performance upgrade kits for enthusiast car owners, sold online or through retail partners
Product redesign for a specific consumer use case such as track day or towing, sold through existing OEM or aftermarket routes
Licensing or co-branding with consumer automotive accessory or tuning brands instead of an own consumer channel
Adjacent consumer product outside brakes, such as e-bike or cargo-bike braking, that uses the Brembo engineering brand

T1.claim: Car enthusiasts buy visible performance brake upgrades as a identity and status purchase, so a Brembo-branded big-brake kit sold direct to them could command a price premium over generic kits.
T1.who_benefits: Enthusiast car owners who want a visible, track-proven upgrade; Brembo, which owns the heritage and could capture the premium margin.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Motorsport heritage and the sporty look signal status to other enthusiasts, so buyers pay for the badge and the look, not only for stopping power.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Brembo sells complete kits through its own online store or retail partners at a price above generic kits, keeping the brand premium and the margin that would otherwise go to kit resellers.
assumptions: Enthusiast buyers value the Brembo badge enough to pay a visible premium over non-branded kits
Brembo can sell direct without channel conflict with installers and distributors
Buyers will install kits themselves or pay a workshop, and are willing to accept the homologation and liability limits of the product
predictions: Brembo-branded kits hold a price premium over comparable non-branded kits in the same market
Demand is concentrated in track-day and sporty-car communities, not in mainstream car buyers
Conversion from enthusiast traffic to purchase rises when the product is shown with motorsport heritage imagery
T1.first_claim: Car enthusiasts buy visible performance brake upgrades as a identity and status purchase, so a Brembo-branded big-brake kit sold direct to them could command a price premium over generic kits.

T2.claim: Individual buyers do not value Brembo's brand enough to pay a premium direct; the brand's value is captured through installers and distributors, so a direct consumer channel would only add cost and channel conflict.
T2.who_benefits: Independent workshops and distributors, who keep the installation and resale margin; Brembo, which keeps its trade relationships rather than taking on direct selling.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Most buyers choose a brake upgrade on the advice of a workshop or fitter, who recommends a product they trust and earns a margin on installation, so the brand reaches buyers through that trusted intermediary, not through advertising.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Brembo keeps selling through its existing trade channels and earns the brand premium there; it would only capture direct consumer value by funding an own channel, which carries marketing, logistics and liability cost.
assumptions: Buyers rely on workshop or fitter advice for brake purchases, especially where safety is concerned
Workshops and distributors would resist a manufacturer selling direct to the same buyers
Direct selling would need consumer marketing spend that exceeds the extra margin captured
predictions: Share of Brembo-branded aftermarket sales that goes through installers stays high where direct-to-consumer kits are offered
Buyers who reach a Brembo kit online are routed to a partner installer rather than buying direct at checkout
Direct online sales add little incremental volume without a workshop or fitter endorsement
T2.first_claim: Individual buyers do not value Brembo's brand enough to pay a premium direct; the brand's value is captured through installers and distributors, so a direct consumer channel would only add cost and channel conflict.

assessments.quote: going to be tricky to justify
assessments.does_not_show: This is one reviewer's view of one mountain-bike brake kit in Europe. It does not measure car enthusiasts, Brembo's price premium against non-branded kits, or how many buyers were deterred. It is a single review, not sales data.

assessments.quote: Designed and tested specifically for track day enthusiasts
assessments.does_not_show: The page is a company product description. It does not say how the kit is bought, whether installers or distributors take a margin, whether Brembo sells direct, or whether direct sales conflict with trade partners. It cannot tell T2 from T1.

X1.name: Enthusiast choice experiment on brand premium and purchase channel
X1.method: Online discrete-choice survey with embedded price and channel attributes. Each respondent sees pairs of big-brake kits for their car, varying brand (Brembo heritage vs unbranded equivalent), price, and purchase route (buy direct online from manufacturer vs buy via a partner installer who fits it). Analyst-run via a panel and enthusiast community recruitment, with no company data.
X1.sample: Proposed: 400 respondents who own a car they say they would modify for performance, recruited from a panel plus enthusiast forums, quota-matched to Italy, Germany and UK. Estimated fieldwork cost covers panel fees and analysis.
X1.measure: Share of choices for the Brembo-badged kit at each price premium over the unbranded kit; relative utility of purchase route (direct online vs installer-fitted); stated willingness to buy direct without installer advice.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Brembo badge carries a positive price premium: at least a 15% premium is chosen by a majority of respondents who value the heritage look, and direct online route is valued at least as highly as installer route.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Brand premium is small or absent; installer-fitted route is strongly preferred over direct purchase, and most respondents who would buy direct still want installer confirmation before buying a braking product.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 50% of respondents choose the Brembo kit at a 15% premium over the unbranded kit AND direct online route scores within 10% of installer route, favour T1 and treat a direct consumer proposition as worth a pilot. If installer route is preferred by more than 20 percentage points, or the Brembo premium is below 5% at 50% choice share, favour T2 and keep the trade channel. Otherwise, treat as inconclusive and do not invest.

revisions.reason: No real source I have read tests whether buyers need installer advice. The only real evidence bearing on T1 is one review that price is hard to justify, which is weak. The simulated trial in SYN-BREMBO-UPDATE is not evidence and is not cited here. Had it been real, it would point to trial through a partner shop mattering, which is consistent with T2, but it concerns bicycle brakes and a single hypothetical group. T2 stays uncertain.

The simulated trial in SYN-BREMBO-UPDATE is not evidence and I do not cite it. Had it been real, it would bear most on T1's purchase channel, since it concerns trial and purchase in a different product. It would not show a brand premium. The real evidence on T1 is one review saying the price is hard to justify, and a company page that targets track-day enthusiasts. Neither confirms a premium. T1 stays uncertain and is still open to the choice experiment.

Recording that the simulated bicycle-brake trial changes nothing for T2. It is not real evidence, so I do not cite it. My view stays uncertain, because no real source tests whether car-brake buyers need installer advice.

What-if only. SYN-BREMBO-UPDATE is SIMULATED, not real data. Taking it as if real: a demo ride at a partner shop raised purchases in a bicycle-brake group, which would fit T2 that trial through a trusted intermediary matters. But it does not measure car-brake demand or Brembo's price, so it would change nothing about my recommendation. T2 stays uncertain. This simulated result is excluded from the evidence I rely on in finish.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a standalone direct-to-consumer proposition now. Keep the trade and installer channel as the main route to enthusiast buyers. Before any investment, run the proposed low-cost choice experiment (X1), about EUR 12,000 over 6 weeks (analyst estimate), to test whether a Brembo brand premium exists and whether buyers need installer routing. The evidence I could read establishes neither point.
final.target_customer: Car enthusiasts who modify for track-day or sporty performance and already buy aftermarket brake upgrades. Motorcycle and bicycle buyers are not established by the evidence I read.
final.value_proposition: A Brembo-badged performance kit with motorsport heritage, sold through or with a partner installer. Whether a direct channel adds value is untested.
final.next_action: Run the X1 choice experiment. Decision rule as proposed: favour a direct pilot only if at least 50% choose the Brembo kit at a 15% premium and the direct route scores within 10% of the installer route. Separately, request Brembo's direct online sales and channel margins through a formal channel, since these are not public.
final.uncertainty: Large. Not found: OEM contracts, aftermarket margins, channel agreements, and whether bremboparts.com sells direct or only routes buyers to retailers. Brembo already markets kits to enthusiasts online (company claim). The SEMA source is US off-road, not Brembo. The only critical evidence is one mountain-bike review. No real source tests installer dependence for car brakes. Safety and liability limits are not assessed. Budget and timing are analyst assumptions.

X1 shows installer route preferred by more than 20 points, or a premium below 5%: favour T2 and keep the trade channel

arguments.name: Enthusiast choice experiment on brand premium and purchase channel
arguments.method: Online discrete-choice survey with embedded price and channel attributes. Each respondent sees pairs of big-brake kits for their car, varying brand (Brembo heritage vs unbranded equivalent), price, and purchase route (buy direct online from manufacturer vs buy via a partner installer who fits it). Analyst-run via a panel and enthusiast community recruitment, with no company data.
arguments.sample: Proposed: 400 respondents who own a car they say they would modify for performance, recruited from a panel plus enthusiast forums, quota-matched to Italy, Germany and UK. Estimated fieldwork cost covers panel fees and analysis.
arguments.measure: Share of choices for the Brembo-badged kit at each price premium over the unbranded kit; relative utility of purchase route (direct online vs installer-fitted); stated willingness to buy direct without installer advice.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Brembo badge carries a positive price premium: at least a 15% premium is chosen by a majority of respondents who value the heritage look, and direct online route is valued at least as highly as installer route.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Brand premium is small or absent; installer-fitted route is strongly preferred over direct purchase, and most respondents who would buy direct still want installer confirmation before buying a braking product.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 50% of respondents choose the Brembo kit at a 15% premium over the unbranded kit AND direct online route scores within 10% of installer route, favour T1 and treat a direct consumer proposition as worth a pilot. If installer route is preferred by more than 20 percentage points, or the Brembo premium is below 5% at 50% choice share, favour T2 and keep the trade channel. Otherwise, treat as inconclusive and do not invest.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a standalone direct-to-consumer proposition now. Keep the trade and installer channel as the main route.
