tool_result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Treat the enthusiast brake kit as a hypothesis to test cheaply. Public sources show a market for personalising vehicles and that Brembo already sells performance kits to enthusiasts, but nothing I read shows owners pay a premium for the Brembo name, and one review says the price is hard to justify. Run the proposed pre-order test before committing capital.

frame.objective: Decide whether Brembo N.V. should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond OEM supply and aftermarket replacement parts, and identify the evidence that would justify that investment. The company has not asked this question and nothing here reflects its intentions.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no access to internal financials or contracts
Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget of 8 (7 remaining); challenge_theory and read_source draw on it
Report which financial or contractual details could not be found
Observed numbers must come from sources read; proposed numbers must be labelled as proposed or estimated
alternatives: No expansion: remain OEM supplier plus aftermarket replacement parts
Deepen the existing aftermarket channel with performance upgrade parts sold through current distributors
Differentiated consumer kit for enthusiast car or motorcycle owners, sold direct or online, or via a certified service network
Different customer group: independent workshops or fleet operators rather than end consumers
Product redesign for a new consumer use such as e-bike or mobility-scooter braking
Licensing or co-branding the Brembo name to consumer accessory makers

T1.claim: Enthusiast owners buy visible big-brake upgrades as a styling and identity purchase, so a branded kit sold to them can earn a price premium over generic performance brakes.
T1.who_benefits: Enthusiast car owners who want a visible, track-capable brake upgrade; Brembo, which owns the performance brand.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: The Brembo name and motorsport heritage signal performance and status, so owners pay more for the badge and look than for the measurable stopping gain.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Brembo sells complete kits direct or online at a premium price above what generic upgrade kits fetch, keeping the margin that distributors would otherwise take.
assumptions: A meaningful group of owners buys brake upgrades mainly for looks and image
Owners will pay a premium for the Brembo name over cheaper kits
Direct or online sale can reach these owners without a large marketing cost
predictions: Kit buyers spend more on styling and badge-related features than on measured braking performance
Price premium over comparable non-branded kits persists after controlling for fitment and kit specification
Demand concentrates among owners who already modify their cars visually
T1.first_claim: Enthusiast owners buy visible big-brake upgrades as a styling and identity purchase, so a branded kit sold to them can earn a price premium over generic performance brakes.

T2.claim: Installer or certified-fitter endorsement may matter for purchase, but only if it substitutes for owner technical doubt; a demo ride alone is not assumed to raise conversion.
T2.who_benefits: Installers and workshops that want reliable, warrantied upgrades to offer; owners who trust the installer's advice; Brembo, if it controls the installer relationship.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Owners lack the technical knowledge to judge brake fitment and safety, so they follow the installer's recommendation, and an installer certified by Brembo has a reason to recommend Brembo kits.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Brembo earns margin on kits and on installer certification or training fees, and avoids being sold through unbranded distributors that take the margin.
assumptions: Owners rely on installer advice more than on brand research when buying brakes
Installers have a commercial reason to choose a certified brand
Certification adds enough trust or fitment safety to justify the installer's cost
predictions: Installer recommendation is the most common reason cited for brand choice in upgrade purchases
Owners of cars fitted by certified installers show higher repeat or referral purchase than those fitted elsewhere
Brand awareness among owners who never visited an installer is lower than among those who did
T2.first_claim: Owners do not choose the brake brand themselves; a fitting installer or independent workshop recommends it, so a consumer proposition only works if it is sold through a certified installer network that Brembo controls.

assessments.quote: along with a truly sporty look
assessments.does_not_show: It is Brembo's own marketing claim. It does not show that owners buy for looks, that they pay a premium over cheaper kits, or how many buy it.

assessments.quote: but they come at a price (€750 for the kit) that’s going to be tricky to justify
assessments.does_not_show: One reviewer's view on one product in one market. It does not show what owners actually paid, whether they bought for looks, or whether a premium holds across buyers.

assessments.quote: roughly one-fourth of drivers purchased products within the industry to personalize their vehicles last year
assessments.does_not_show: This is a US survey of vehicle accessories in general, mostly off-road parts. It says nothing about brake kits, European buyers, or whether personalisation buyers pay a premium for a brake brand.

assessments.quote: Designed and tested specifically for track day enthusiasts and for drivers who demand maximum performance from their vehicle
assessments.does_not_show: Nothing about who fits or recommends the kit, whether installers are certified, or how owners choose a brand. It is Brembo's marketing for the product, so it cannot test T2.

X1.name: Channel and message test for enthusiast brake kit (proposed)
X1.method: Run a controlled pre-order test on a single kit (proposed). Arm A: direct-to-consumer online page, styling and performance message, at a premium price point. Arm B: same kit offered through a small set of certified installers, with installer recommendation as the message. Arms run in parallel in two European markets (proposed).
X1.sample: Proposed: about 2,000 enthusiast visitors per arm from targeted online ads and forums, plus 6 partner installers for arm B. Estimated budget within 20000 EUR.
X1.measure: Refundable pre-order conversion rate per arm at the premium price, and share of buyers who cite look, performance or installer advice as reason (short post-purchase survey).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A converts at a clear premium-price rate and buyers cite look and identity more than installer advice; a premium holds across arms.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B converts better than Arm A, and buyers cite installer advice as the main reason; the premium collapses in arm A without installer endorsement.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed: continue to a full channel plan only if one arm converts at least 2 percent of visitors at the premium price and that arm's buyers cite its own main driver in at least 60 percent of responses. If neither arm reaches 1 percent, reject both theories' commercial case and do not invest.

revisions.reason: SYN-BREMBO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not evidence. Treated as a what-if: if a real offer test showed a free demo ride converting less than a specification-only offer (32 versus 72 purchases per 400), then a physical trial or installer demo would not by itself lift conversion. That would weaken the claim that installer recommendation drives purchase, and would point to specification and trust content instead. Real evidence for T2 is still absent.
revisions.new_claim: Installer or certified-fitter endorsement may matter for purchase, but only if it substitutes for owner technical doubt; a demo ride alone is not assumed to raise conversion.

final.recommendation: Do not build a new consumer proposition yet. Brembo already sells performance kits to enthusiasts through its parts catalogue, so the question is whether a differentiated, premium-priced consumer offer adds margin. The public evidence shows personalisation demand and a marketed performance kit, but nothing shows owners pay a premium for the Brembo name. Run the proposed pre-order test (X1) at a bounded cost before any capital commitment.
final.target_customer: Enthusiast car and motorcycle owners who already modify their vehicles visually or for track use (hypothesis; not validated).
final.value_proposition: A branded, track-capable brake upgrade kit, sold with clear fitment and performance specification, whose premium rests on motorsport heritage and visible performance. This is a hypothesis to test, not a proven proposition.
final.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed, about 18000 EUR over 10 weeks, within the 20000 EUR and 12-week assumptions) comparing a direct online offer against an installer-led offer at the premium price, and apply the decision rule: proceed only if one arm converts at least 2 percent of visitors and at least 60 percent of its buyers cite its own main driver. Also seek the consumer sales share and the price premium over the existing kit range.
final.uncertainty: Brembo's consumer sales volume, margins, distributor terms, installer network and current bremboparts.com pricing could not be found in public sources. The evidence on T1 is one company claim, one review that calls the price hard to justify, and a US market survey on accessories in general. T2 has no real evidence at all. The SEMA result covers US off-road accessories, not brake kits. Test X1 is proposed only and has not been run; its sample and threshold are analyst estimates.
would_change_if: A real pre-order test shows a premium converting at or above 2 percent of visitors in one arm, with buyers citing look or performance, which would strengthen T1
Installer-led sales convert clearly better and buyers cite installer advice, which would favour T2 and a certified-installer network
Brembo's consumer sales show the premium over generic kits is not sustained, or the review's price concern holds in sales data
Public or company data show distributors already capture the enthusiast margin, making direct sales less attractive
A real demo-ride or trial result shows trial raises conversion, which would reopen T2

arguments.name: Channel and message test for enthusiast brake kit (proposed)
arguments.method: Run a controlled pre-order test on a single kit (proposed). Arm A: direct-to-consumer online page, styling and performance message, at a premium price point. Arm B: same kit offered through a small set of certified installers, with installer recommendation as the message. Arms run in parallel in two European markets (proposed).
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 2,000 enthusiast visitors per arm from targeted online ads and forums, plus 6 partner installers for arm B. Estimated budget within 20000 EUR.
arguments.measure: Refundable pre-order conversion rate per arm at the premium price, and share of buyers who cite look, performance or installer advice as reason (short post-purchase survey).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A converts at a clear premium-price rate and buyers cite look and identity more than installer advice; a premium holds across arms.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B converts better than Arm A, and buyers cite installer advice as the main reason; the premium collapses in arm A without installer endorsement.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed: continue to a full channel plan only if one arm converts at least 2 percent of visitors at the premium price and that arm's buyers cite its own main driver in at least 60 percent of responses. If neither arm reaches 1 percent, reject both theories' commercial case and do not invest.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Treat the enthusiast brake kit as a hypothesis to test cheaply. Run the proposed pre-order test before committing capital.

result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: SYN-BREMBO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not evidence. Treated as a what-if: if a real offer test showed a free demo ride converting less than a specification-only offer (32 versus 72 purchases per 400), then a physical trial or installer demo would not by itself lift conversion. That would weaken the claim that installer recommendation drives purchase, and would point to specification and trust content instead. Real evidence for T2 is still absent.
arguments.new_claim: Installer or certified-fitter endorsement may matter for purchase, but only if it substitutes for owner technical doubt; a demo ride alone is not assumed to raise conversion.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a new consumer proposition yet. Brembo already sells performance kits to enthusiasts through its parts catalogue, so the question is whether a differentiated, premium-priced consumer offer adds margin. The public evidence shows personalisation demand and a marketed performance kit, but nothing shows owners pay a premium for the Brembo name. Run the proposed pre-order test (X1) at a bounded cost before any capital commitment.
arguments.target_customer: Enthusiast car and motorcycle owners who already modify their vehicles visually or for track use (hypothesis; not validated).
arguments.value_proposition: A branded, track-capable brake upgrade kit, sold with clear fitment and performance specification, whose premium rests on motorsport heritage and visible performance. This is a hypothesis to test, not a proven proposition.
arguments.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed, about 18000 EUR over 10 weeks, within the 20000 EUR and 12-week assumptions) comparing a direct online offer against an installer-led offer at the premium price, and apply the decision rule: proceed only if one arm converts at least 2 percent of visitors and at least 60 percent of its buyers cite its own main driver. Also request, through public channels or a conversation if the company chooses, the consumer sales share and the price premium over the existing kit range.
arguments.uncertainty: Brembo's consumer sales volume, margins, distributor terms, installer network and the existing bremboparts.com pricing could not be found in public sources. The evidence on T1 is one company claim, one review that calls the price hard to justify, and a US market survey on accessories in general. T2 has no real evidence at all. The SEMA result is US off-road accessories, not brake kits. Test X1 is proposed only and has not been run; its sample and threshold are analyst estimates.

Installer-led sales convert clearly better and buyers cite installer advice, which would favour T2 and a certified-installer network
Brembo's existing consumer sales show a premium over generic kits is not sustained, or the review's price concern holds in sales data
Public or company data show distributors already capture the enthusiast margin, making direct sales less attractive

X1.name: Heritage messaging and channel split test for performance brake kits
X1.method: Run a 10-week online test with a partner aftermarket retailer or marketplace selling one Brembo upgrade kit in two arms. Arm A uses motorsport-heritage messaging and a premium price point. Arm B uses spec-sheet messaging at the same price. Within each arm, split traffic between direct online checkout and a 'book a fitting at a partner workshop' option, to see whether the workshop route drives conversion. Compare conversion rate, price acceptance and workshop-booking share.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 4,000 qualified visitors from enthusiast car and motorcycle audiences in one European market, with roughly 1,000 per cell across four cells, plus 15 to 20 partner workshops in the same market.
X1.measure: Conversion rate per cell, share of buyers choosing the workshop route, and revealed price acceptance at the premium price versus a 15 per cent lower price in a follow-up cell.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Heritage messaging converts higher than spec messaging at the premium price, and the gap holds across the direct and workshop routes, because the brand itself drives purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Direct online conversion stays low in both message arms, and most completed purchases come through the workshop-booking route, so message effects are small by comparison.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed: treat T1 as supported only if heritage messaging lifts direct-route conversion by at least 20 per cent relative to spec messaging, with the difference clear of noise at 95 per cent confidence. Treat T2 as supported if at least 60 per cent of completed purchases come through the workshop route and direct-route conversion is under half the workshop-route rate. If neither threshold is met, neither theory is supported and the consumer proposition should not be funded on this evidence.

revisions.reason: SIMULATED result, not real data. If it were real, it would bear on the channel and messaging side of T1 rather than the premium claim. Specification-only messaging converted more buyers (72) than a demo-ride offer (32) at the same price, which gives no support to the idea that experiential routes add value. It does not test whether a heritage brand earns a price premium over rivals, and the result is a what-if for a bicycle-brake trial in one recruited group. My belief in T1 is unchanged: still uncertain, with the one real observation on price still pointing against it.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer-facing brake proposition on the evidence so far. Brembo already offers upgrade kits to enthusiasts through its own parts site, so the question is whether a differentiated, separately funded consumer proposition adds value beyond that. I found no sales or margin data to answer it. Before any investment, run the proposed price and channel test (X1, about EUR 18,500 over 10 weeks, a proposed estimate) to see whether heritage messaging and the workshop route lift conversion. Treat both theories as unproven.
final.target_customer: Enthusiast car and motorcycle owners who buy performance upgrades. This is a hypothesis to test, not a validated segment.
final.value_proposition: A branded performance upgrade kit whose motorsport heritage supports a price premium over generic kits. Not yet supported: the only real price observation found pointed the other way.
final.next_action: Ask Brembo, through appropriate channels, for its existing consumer-kit sales, pricing and margin data for the bremboparts.com range, and for any installer-network data. Then run test X1 if the data does not already settle the premium question.
final.uncertainty: High. I have no Brembo sales, margin, contract or channel data, which is likely non-public. The evidence is three sources: one company marketing page, one independent product review of a single mountain-bike kit at EUR 750, and a US accessory market statistic that does not cover brakes or Europe. Nothing I read shows willingness to pay for a Brembo-branded kit, or who decides which brake brand is fitted. The workshop-channel theory (T2) has no supporting evidence at all.

Test X1 shows most purchases coming through the workshop route with direct conversion under half of it, which would support T2 and point to an installer-led channel instead
Independent evidence that European enthusiast buyers pay a premium for brand over rival kits at comparable specification

result.title: Simulated bicycle-brake trial offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Treat the premium compact CNC idea as an unproven option. Keep the industrial focus, review the Rover A line and its aftermarket, and run the proposed X1 test (EUR 18,000 estimated, 10 weeks) before any hardware investment. Read the evidence as: a competitor has tried it, Biesse itself marketed a compact machine to craftsmen in 2012 and 2022, and nothing I read shows premium demand or sales outcomes.

frame.objective: Decide whether Biesse should build a differentiated proposition for individual (consumer or prosumer) buyers for a specific use case, or keep its focus on industrial manufacturers. Find out whether individual buyers can be reached profitably and what evidence would justify the investment.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact, internal financial or contract data, and no assumed company intentions; company claims are claims, not proof of demand.
Search budget of 8 searches (7 left) and one frame_problem call.
Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12 weeks are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.
Core products are industrial CNC machining centres, edgebanders, saws and complete lines sold to furniture, window and door, construction, automotive and aerospace manufacturers.
First establish how far Biesse already reaches individual buyers rather than assume it does not.
Note any financial or contractual detail that could not be found.
alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the industrial focus and invest in existing lines, service and aftermarket.
B. Product redesign: a smaller, lower-cost machine for a specific use case (for example a cabinet or door shop bench CNC) sold through existing industrial channels.

C. Different route to buyers: sell or lease a compact machine to individuals and small workshops through retailers, marketplaces, hobbyist channels, or a partnership with a consumer brand that already reaches them.
D. Different customer group: target small craft workshops, makers or training schools, a segment between hobbyists and industry, with a product and service package.
E. Consumer-facing software, design or subscription layer (for example cutting-file or design services) selling to owners of existing or third-party machines, without selling hardware to individuals.
G. Exit from or de-prioritise any consumer ambition and focus on industrial customers and aftermarket revenue.

T1.claim: Individual and small-workshop buyers will pay a premium for a compact CNC that carries industrial build quality and precision, because they want a machine that lasts and is accurate, not a cheap toy. A manufacturer already known for industrial machines could capture that premium by offering a scaled-down version of its engineering.
T1.who_benefits: Makerspaces, serious hobbyists and small craft workshops who want durable, precise machines; Biesse, if it can sell them at a margin without damaging its industrial brand.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who have used low-end desktop CNCs and found them inaccurate or fragile would pay more for a machine with industrial-grade frames, spindles and software. The Felder case suggests a competitor believes this segment exists.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Higher unit price for the compact machine, plus recurring revenue from tooling, cutting files, software licences and service contracts, sold through a channel Biesse can reach.
assumptions: A meaningful number of individual or small-workshop buyers are willing to pay well above entry-level desktop CNC prices.
Build quality is a purchase criterion they can perceive before buying, not only after years of use.
Biesse can produce a compact machine at a cost that leaves margin at that price without diverting engineering from industrial lines.
Sales through a channel reachable by individuals can be done without damaging the industrial brand.
predictions: Among makerspace and small-workshop buyers surveyed, a meaningful share will say build quality and accuracy outweigh price when comparing desktop CNCs.
Competitors who launched premium compact machines will show growing listings or dealer networks in this segment over the next two years.
Buyers who pay the premium will also buy recurring consumables or software at a higher rate than entry-level owners.
T1.first_claim: Individual and small-workshop buyers will pay a premium for a compact CNC that carries industrial build quality and precision, because they want a machine that lasts and is accurate, not a cheap toy. A manufacturer already known for industrial machines could capture that premium by offering a scaled-down version of its engineering.

T2.claim: Individual buyers of desktop CNC machines are price-sensitive and mainly want a cheap entry tool, so an industrially engineered compact machine would be over-engineered for them and would sell mainly to existing industrial customers as a secondary item, not as a profitable consumer line.
T2.who_benefits: Entry-level desktop CNC sellers and hobbyists, who gain cheap machines; Biesse would benefit only by staying in its industrial core and avoiding a costly, low-margin consumer line.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Hobbyists compare desktop machines mainly on price and on whether the machine can do a simple job. Engineering built for industrial precision adds cost they will not pay for, so demand stays with cheap machines and the premium never materialises.
T2.how_value_is_captured: No meaningful consumer value capture for the manufacturer; the value stays with low-cost entrants and with Biesse's existing industrial installed base, where service and spare parts are sold.
assumptions: Hobbyist and makerspace buyers rank price above build quality when choosing a desktop CNC.
The desktop segment is dominated by low-cost entrants with thin margins.
Industrial-grade engineering cannot be made cheap enough to match entry prices without losing its advantage.
A consumer line would divert engineering and sales resources from the industrial core.
predictions: In surveys or sales data, price ranks above accuracy and durability for desktop CNC buyers who are not professionals.
Premium desktop machines sell in small volumes and fall in price or disappear from catalogues within a few years.
Companies that moved into consumer desktop CNC report low margin or return to industrial focus.
T2.first_claim: Individual buyers of desktop CNC machines are price-sensitive and mainly want a cheap entry tool, so an industrially engineered compact machine would be over-engineered for them and would sell mainly to existing industrial customers as a secondary item, not as a profitable consumer line.

assessments.quote: We wanted to offer a desktop CNC machine without compromising on our commitment to quality.
assessments.does_not_show: This is a competitor's stated intention, not proof that hobbyists or workshops will pay a premium for industrial build quality. It shows one firm chose to try, not that the market responds. The article gives no sales, price or volume figures.

assessments.quote: Despite the possibility of creating a product that could be over-engineered for hobbyists, we took on the challenge,
assessments.does_not_show: The quote shows the competitor recognised an over-engineering risk for hobbyists. It does not show that hobbyists rank price above build quality, nor the volumes, margins or outcome of the product. It is one firm's own framing.

assessments.quote: With the CNC, dimensions are much more accurate and if you are working at the top end of the market, it’s a key consideration.
assessments.does_not_show: This is Biesse's own marketing of one UK craftsman's view. It shows that accuracy matters to at least one small high-end workshop, not that a premium is paid, how many such buyers exist, or whether individual hobbyists value accuracy the same way. Biesse published it, so it is not independent.

X1.name: Premium compact CNC willingness-to-pay test with small workshops and makerspaces
X1.method: Run a controlled demand test: show a compact CNC concept (price-anchored) to makerspace managers and small craft workshops, with two variants, one emphasising industrial accuracy and warranty, one emphasising low price. Record pre-orders or refundable deposits and a conjoint-style trade-off question. Estimated, not observed.
X1.sample: Proposed: 40 to 60 prospects across makerspaces, small furniture and door workshops, and craft schools in two countries; plus a landing page test reaching 2,000 hobbyist visitors (estimated).
X1.measure: Share choosing the accuracy/quality variant at or above a proposed premium threshold (e.g. at least 25% above entry-level desktop price); refundable deposit conversion rate; stated trade-off ranking of accuracy versus price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: A meaningful share (proposed: 25% or more of qualified prospects) will choose the accuracy variant at a premium and convert to deposits; accuracy ranks above price in trade-off answers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Few prospects (under 10%) choose the premium variant; price ranks first; deposit conversion is concentrated on the cheapest variant.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a product feasibility study only if at least 25% of qualified prospects pick the premium variant AND at least 10% place a refundable deposit at the premium price. If under 10% pick the premium variant, reject the consumer hardware line and keep the industrial focus with aftermarket service.

revisions.reason: No real evidence yet shows that buyers pay a premium for industrial accuracy in compact CNCs. The Felder article and Biesse's own 2012 and 2022 marketing show the idea has been tried or marketed, but none gives sales, prices or outcomes. The simulated update is excluded from evidence; it concerns software simplicity rather than build-quality premium and would not change T1 either way. T1 stays uncertain.

No real evidence has tested T2 directly either. The Felder article acknowledges an over-engineering risk for hobbyists, but that is the competitor's own framing. The simulated update is excluded; as a what-if it concerns software simplicity at a fixed machine and price, so it would not decide between price-led and accuracy-led demand. T2 stays uncertain alongside T1.

Treating SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE as a what-if only: if it were real, it would say that at equal machine, price and warranty, simpler template software roughly doubled deposits among small workshops and hobbyists. That bears on the software and ease-of-use mechanism, not on whether buyers pay a premium for industrial accuracy, so it would not confirm or reject T1. It would suggest a separate theory for later. It is not counted as evidence and changes no belief or recommendation.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the industrial focus. The only plausible near-term option is a small test of a compact, accuracy-led machine for small high-end workshops and makerspaces, and only if the test shows real premium demand. Stop short of any individual-buyer hardware line.
final.target_customer: Small high-end craft and carpentry workshops, and makerspaces, not individual hobbyists. This is a hypothesis, not a finding.
final.value_proposition: Industrial-grade accuracy and build quality in a compact CNC, with the Rover A line as the existing reference. This is a hypothesis that buyers will pay for it; the evidence I found does not show that they will.
final.next_action: Before any hardware work, check whether the Rover A entry-level line is still sold, and at what price and to which buyers, using Biesse's public catalogue and dealer pages. Then run a test along the lines of X1 (proposed EUR 18,000, 10 weeks, estimated) with a pre-set threshold: proceed only if at least 25% of qualified prospects choose the premium variant and at least 10% place a refundable deposit at the premium price; otherwise keep the industrial focus with aftermarket service.
final.uncertainty: High. I found no sales, price, margin or volume data for any Biesse compact or consumer product. Sources are dated (2011, 2012, 2018) or are company marketing (2012, 2022). I did not establish how far Biesse reaches individual buyers today, which was the first question. Internal financials, dealer agreements and the status of the Rover A line are not public to me. The one simulated result is a what-if and I have not counted it as evidence.
would_change_if: Public or dealer data shows the Rover A entry line sold poorly or was withdrawn, which would favour T2.
A real test (like X1) shows at least 25% of qualified prospects choosing the premium accuracy variant with deposits, which would support T1.
Evidence that hobbyists rank price well above build quality in purchase decisions, which would favour T2.
Evidence that ease of use or software, not build quality, drives choice among small buyers, which would point to a different theory and a software-led proposition (alternative E).
Biesse's own disclosures on compact product margins or channel conflict with dealers, which could rule out any consumer-reaching route.

arguments.name: Premium compact CNC willingness-to-pay test with small workshops and makerspaces
arguments.method: Run a controlled demand test: show a compact CNC concept (price-anchored) to makerspace managers and small craft workshops, with two variants, one emphasising industrial accuracy and warranty, one emphasising low price. Record pre-orders or refundable deposits and a conjoint-style trade-off question. Estimated, not observed.
arguments.sample: Proposed: 40 to 60 prospects across makerspaces, small furniture and door workshops, and craft schools in two countries; plus a landing page test reaching 2,000 hobbyist visitors (estimated).
arguments.measure: Share choosing the accuracy/quality variant at or above a proposed premium threshold (e.g. at least 25% above entry-level desktop price); refundable deposit conversion rate; stated trade-off ranking of accuracy versus price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: A meaningful share (proposed: 25% or more of qualified prospects) will choose the accuracy variant at a premium and convert to deposits; accuracy ranks above price in trade-off answers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Few prospects (under 10%) choose the premium variant; price ranks first; deposit conversion is concentrated on the cheapest variant.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed to a product feasibility study only if at least 25% of qualified prospects pick the premium variant AND at least 10% place a refundable deposit at the premium price. If under 10% pick the premium variant, reject the consumer hardware line and keep the industrial focus with aftermarket service.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Treat the premium compact CNC idea as an unproven option. Keep the industrial focus, review the Rover A line and its aftermarket, and run the proposed X1 test (EUR 18,000 estimated, 10 weeks) before any hardware investment. Read the evidence as: a competitor has tried it, Biesse itself marketed a compact machine to craftsmen in 2012 and 2022, and nothing I read shows premium demand or sales outcomes.

result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not build a separate consumer-branded proposition now. Biesse already sells a compact, lower-cost CNC to small businesses (Rover A Edge, 2012 source), so the cheapest next step is to check whether that dealer-led small-shop line is still sold and how well it performs, before testing any new product. Use the 12-week pre-order test only if that check shows a gap in the small-shop segment, and do not spend on a hobbyist consumer line on current evidence.

frame.objective: Decide whether Biesse S.p.A., a B2B maker of wood, glass, stone and advanced-materials processing machinery, should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for an individual-buyer use case, and what evidence would justify that investment rather than staying with industrial customers.
constraints: Outside-in analysis using public sources only; no company contact or internal data
Search budget: 7 searches remaining; read sources before theorising
Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state what could not be found
Do not assume the company's existing consumer reach; verify it
Company claims are not proof of demand
alternatives: No expansion: stay B2B industrial only, focused on existing furniture, window/door and construction customers
Product redesign: simpler or smaller machines for small workshops, sold through existing dealers
Different route to buyers: dealer, online or retail channel, or training and software subscriptions for existing machine owners and small shops
Different customer group: small craft and prosumer makers (hobbyists, small cabinet shops) as a distinct segment
Services or aftermarket: consumables, tooling, software and training around existing machines rather than new consumer hardware
Partnership or licensing with a consumer brand or retailer instead of an own consumer proposition

T1.claim: Hobbyists and makerspace members want a compact, quality desktop CNC, and a manufacturer that already makes industrial CNC could sell a scaled-down model through makerspaces and dealers at a premium.
T1.who_benefits: Makerspace operators, serious hobbyists and small craft shops; Biesse would gain a new revenue line and brand reach.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Makerspaces make desktop CNC the core tool for making things in three dimensions, so demand comes from people who value build quality and want a machine that lasts.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Biesse sells compact hardware plus consumables, software and training, using its existing manufacturing and dealer network.
assumptions: Makerspaces and hobbyists buy machines at prices that cover a compact Biesse product's cost
Industrial engineering can be scaled down without losing the quality buyers pay for
Biesse's brand carries over to the hobbyist segment
predictions: Makerspace operators would sign up for a pilot at a price above rival desktop machines
Repeat buyers would purchase consumables and software at a margin
Conversion from enquiry to order would be low unless a dealer or training is included
T1.first_claim: Hobbyists and makerspace members want a compact, quality desktop CNC, and a manufacturer that already makes industrial CNC could sell a scaled-down model through makerspaces and dealers at a premium.

T2.claim: Individual buyers see industrial CNC as a tool for professionals and will not pay a premium for a consumer-branded machine from an industrial maker. Biesse's value stays in serving existing business customers, and any consumer move would be sold through its own dealers to small cabinet shops rather than to hobbyists.
T2.who_benefits: Existing industrial customers and dealers would keep the value; small cabinet shops, a commercial rather than consumer segment, would be the most plausible buyers.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers judge a machine by its job, not its brand. Hobbyists choose on price and ease of use, and they go to rival desktop makers that already own the consumer niche. Small shops buy when a machine pays back through work done.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Biesse keeps its margin in B2B sales and aftermarket service, and only adds a small-shop line sold through existing dealers.

Small cabinet shops are a real segment that can pay for a compact machine with service

predictions: Hobbyist enquiries would convert poorly relative to small-shop enquiries

It does not show that individual hobbyists bought it, the volumes sold, whether the product is still in the range, or the prices. It shows only that Biesse already offers a compact, lower-cost machine, which is a small-shop product rather than a consumer one.

X1.name: Compact CNC demand test across two buyer segments
X1.method: Offer one compact-CNC concept at a proposed price to two segments in parallel: makerspace operators and serious hobbyists via a landing page and makerspace partner sign-ups, and small cabinet shops via an existing-dealer lead form. Count refundable deposits and signed letters of intent, not survey intent. Run as a single pre-order campaign with no production commitment.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3 to 5 partner makerspaces, a paid online audience of roughly 3,000 hobbyists and makers, and about 40 small cabinet shops reached through 2 to 3 dealers in one country.
X1.measure: Refundable deposits and signed letters of intent per segment at the proposed price, plus cost per deposit and share of enquiries that reach a deposit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Makerspace and hobbyist segment produces deposits at a price above rival desktop machines, with a conversion rate that makes a premium line plausible.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Hobbyist segment produces few deposits and price-sensitive enquiries; small cabinet shops produce more letters of intent, asking for service, financing and dealer support rather than a consumer brand.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: proceed to a compact-line feasibility study only if the hobbyist and makerspace segment yields at least 25 refundable deposits at the proposed price within 12 weeks, and the deposit rate is at least 2% of qualified enquiries. If not, and small shops yield at least 5 letters of intent, favour the dealer-led small-shop route (T2). If neither threshold is met, do not expand.

revisions.reason: The new source is a SIMULATED what-if with no real study behind it, so it does not change my belief. Even if it were real, it would only show that a recruited group preferred standard professional CAD/CAM software over simplified template software for one compact router. That is consistent with small-shop buyers valuing professional tools, so T2 stands. It is not evidence of real demand and is not cited in the finish. The kept evidence for T2 remains the 2012 Rover A Edge statement.

The SIMULATED result bears most on T1, because it concerns whether simplified software for hobbyist-style buyers beats professional tools. It is not real data, so it changes nothing. Even as a what-if, it shows the recruited group preferred standard professional CAD/CAM over template software, which cuts against a simplified consumer line. I keep T1 as uncertain-to-unlikely on the real evidence, which is trade commentary and a competitor's launch statement. The result is not cited in the finish.

Suppose SYN-BIESSE-UPDATE were real, labelled SIMULATED, so this is a what-if. It would support T2: when buyers of a compact router weigh professional CAD/CAM against simplified template software, the standard professional tools won more deposits, which fits small workshops that want professional tools from a dealer rather than a consumer-style product. It would not show that such a machine could be built at a viable price or that the market is large enough. The real evidence still rests on the 2012 Rover A Edge statement, so T2 stays kept. This simulated result is not cited in the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not build a separate consumer-branded proposition now. Keep the core in B2B industrial machinery. Biesse already offers a compact, lower-cost CNC aimed at a 'larger audience' of businesses, so the first step is to confirm whether that small-shop line is still sold and how it performs. Only if that check shows an unmet small-shop gap should a low-cost pre-order test be run, and it should not target hobbyists.
final.target_customer: Small cabinet and carpentry workshops served through existing dealers. The evidence I found does not support hobbyists or makerspaces.
final.value_proposition: A compact, professionally engineered machine with dealer support, service and professional software for small workshops, using the existing Rover A Edge line as the starting point. Not a consumer product.
final.next_action: Check public information on whether the Rover A Edge or a successor is still in Biesse's current range, its price band and dealer coverage. If it is current, rule out a new consumer line. If a small-shop gap appears, run the proposed 12-week, 18,000 EUR pre-order test (proposed, not run), with a threshold of at least 5 letters of intent from small shops.
final.uncertainty: I found no evidence that Biesse sells to individual consumers today. The compact CNC source is from 2012, so its current status is unknown. I could not find financial data, sales volumes, dealer contracts or pricing; these are likely non-public. The T1 hobbyist premium is untested: the sources are trade columns and a competitor's launch statement. The test figures (sample, budget, thresholds) are my proposals. The SIMULATED result was used only as a what-if and is not evidence.

arguments.name: Compact CNC demand test across two buyer segments
arguments.method: Offer one compact-CNC concept at a proposed price to two segments in parallel: makerspace operators and serious hobbyists via a landing page and makerspace partner sign-ups, and small cabinet shops via an existing-dealer lead form. Count refundable deposits and signed letters of intent, not survey intent. Run as a single pre-order campaign with no production commitment.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 3 to 5 partner makerspaces, a paid online audience of roughly 3,000 hobbyists and makers, and about 40 small cabinet shops reached through 2 to 3 dealers in one country.
arguments.measure: Refundable deposits and signed letters of intent per segment at the proposed price, plus cost per deposit and share of enquiries that reach a deposit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Makerspace and hobbyist segment produces deposits at a price above rival desktop machines, with a conversion rate that makes a premium line plausible.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Hobbyist segment produces few deposits and price-sensitive enquiries; small cabinet shops produce more letters of intent, asking for service, financing and dealer support rather than a consumer brand.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: proceed to a compact-line feasibility study only if the hobbyist and makerspace segment yields at least 25 refundable deposits at the proposed price within 12 weeks, and the deposit rate is at least 2% of qualified enquiries. result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. tool_result.title: Simulated small-workshop CNC software offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer-facing proposition on the evidence so far. If anything is pursued, it should be a clinic-led test around the intelligent prosthetic knee, not a direct-to-consumer launch. The public sources I could read show that Nabtesco makes a welfare product and a B2B gear and door business, but none show individual buyers, sales channels, prices or volumes. Our challenge search found no source contradicting T1, but it also found no direct evidence for it.

frame.objective: Determine whether Nabtesco should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific individual-buyer use case, and what evidence would justify that investment, given its current B2B portfolio of reduction gears, automatic doors, transport components and welfare parts.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions assumed
Company financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state the gaps
Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
8 searches in total (7 remaining), so evidence gathering must be targeted
Must first establish how far Nabtesco already reaches individual buyers, for example through prosthetics, door products or consumer-facing channels
alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B component supplier to robot makers, building owners and transport operators
Product redesign: adapt existing welfare components such as prosthetic knee joints for individual users through a direct or clinic-led offer
Different route to buyers: sell the same product to individuals through prosthetists, clinics or online channels
Different customer group: supply reduction gears and actuators to consumer robotics or personal mobility makers (B2B2C)
Consumer-adjacent building products: residential automatic doors or home access products sold via installers or retailers to homeowners
Platform or service model: maintenance, monitoring or subscription services for the installed base of doors and gears

T1.claim: Individual buyers of Nabtesco's intelligent prosthetic knee would pay a premium for it only when a prosthetist or clinic recommends and fits it, so the value is captured through the clinical channel rather than direct consumer sales.
T1.who_benefits: Lower-limb amputees and their prosthetists, who need a fitted, adjustable device; Nabtesco, which would capture margin on a premium component sold through clinics.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Users buy a prosthetic knee because a clinician prescribes and tunes it, and funding (insurance or public health) decides what they can access. Going direct to consumers removes the fitting and reimbursement that make the device usable.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Nabtesco sells components or systems to prosthetic makers and clinics, earning a premium on the microprocessor knee; the consumer price is set by the clinic and funder, not by Nabtesco.
assumptions: Prosthetic knee purchases are mediated by clinicians and payers
Patients value the microprocessor knee enough to pay a premium when a clinic recommends it
Nabtesco's welfare line already sells through orthopaedic channels
predictions: Clinics account for most fittings; direct-to-patient sales would be near zero without a clinician
Adoption varies with reimbursement rules across countries
A direct online offer would convert few buyers without fitting support
T1.first_claim: Individual buyers of Nabtesco's intelligent prosthetic knee would pay a premium for it only when a prosthetist or clinic recommends and fits it, so the value is captured through the clinical channel rather than direct consumer sales.

T2.claim: Individual buyers want a home-scale, self-installed access or mobility product, so a consumer offer would be captured by sales through retailers or installers to homeowners rather than by Nabtesco's current building and transport customers.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners and older or disabled residents who want easier access; retailers and installers who would sell and fit the product; Nabtesco, if it could sell a compact, lower-cost door or actuator to these buyers.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners buy when the product is cheap enough, simple to install and sold where they already shop. Current automatic doors are priced and specified for commercial buildings, so consumers do not see them as an option.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Nabtesco sells a redesigned, lower-cost unit through installer or retail channels, earning margin on a product line it does not yet sell to households.
assumptions: Homeowners would pay for an automatic door or access product if the price and installation fit a home
Retail or installer channels can reach these buyers at acceptable cost
Commercial door know-how transfers to a smaller residential product
predictions: Demand concentrates among buyers with accessibility needs rather than general consumers
Installer margins would decide adoption more than end-user price
A residential product would need a different price point than the commercial range

assessments.does_not_show: Who buys the knee, whether clinicians or payers mediate the sale, what it costs, or how many units are sold. It is the company's own description of a product, so it does not show demand or the sales channel.

assessments.quote: Thanks to their high reliability, Nabtesco’s precision reduction gears are preferred by a range of domestic and overseas robot manufacturers in the joints of their industrial robots, giving us a large share of the market.

X1.name: Channel-and-demand interview and landing-page test
X1.method: Structured interviews with prosthetists, lower-limb amputees and home-access installers, plus a landing-page test offering two routes: clinic-referred and direct-to-consumer enquiry for a prosthetic knee, and an installer-referred enquiry for a residential automatic door or access product. Measure where buyers say they would buy and what price they would accept.
X1.sample: Proposed: 15 prosthetists, 40 lower-limb amputees recruited through clinics and patient groups, 15 residential installers or retailers, and a landing page open for 6 weeks.

result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated home automatic-door safety offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
